PULSE BIOSCIENCES $PLSE HIT A NEW HIGH ON A TRIAL THAT HASN'T FINISHED ENROLLING:

Pulse Biosciences PLSE at $53.11, Friday's close, -$1.32 / -2.43% from Thursday's $54.43 close. The Miami company, 116 employees, built a technology called nano-pulse stimulation - a burst of electrical pulses that destroys targeted cells without heat - and is now running it through two separate heart trials for atrial fibrillation, the most common heart-rhythm disorder there is.

Six ways of reading this market tonight, and the same question keeps showing up in different clothes: what has a company actually banked, against what the price has already assumed it will bank. Nowhere is that gap wider right now than here. On Wednesday, September 9, an analyst at Freedom Capital Markets started coverage with a Buy rating and a $73 target, and the stock spiked to $58.90 intraday - a fresh one-year high - before giving back almost the entire move to close at $52.97. A stock trading like that is being priced off an outcome nobody has proven yet, not off what it sold last quarter: $0.4M of revenue.

The Momentum Len5 flagged Pulse first on its watch for exactly this shape of strength - a price near the top of its one-year range, the recent run and the longer run agreeing, on real volume. Both check out: the stock has run roughly 19% since Needham initiated it at Buy on August 17 at a $44.54 close, and it is up more than four times over from last November 20's $12.56 low. Wednesday's spike traded 1.56 million shares, nearly double its own two-week average of about 817,000 - real volume behind the move, even if most of the day's gain didn't survive the close.

What actually supports the price, on the clock: the nPulse Cardiac Catheter trial - a single-arm study testing whether Pulse's pulsed-field technology can stop recurrent, drug-resistant atrial fibrillation - passed the halfway point of enrollment this quarter, and management moved its completion target up to early Q4 2026, three months ahead of the original plan. A second trial, testing a surgical version of the same technology, is enrolling toward mid-2027. Both are aiming first for a CE Mark - Europe's version of FDA clearance - with filing later this year and approval targeted for mid-2027. Neither trial has a stated date yet for U.S. approval, the market that would actually turn this into a real revenue line.

None of it is free. The August 6 second-quarter report: revenue $0.4M, a GAAP net loss of $24.7M, or $0.36 a share - wider than the $0.29 loss analysts modeled - and a cash burn of $18.7M for the quarter against $101.6M in the bank. Pulse raised $46.8M selling shares directly into the market through its at-the-market program in the quarter alone, plus another $10.7M since, and just opened a new $75M version of that program on top of a $125M shelf - pre-cleared paperwork to sell more stock later - still untouched. The trials are being funded by continuously issuing new shares, which is also, mechanically, why each existing share is worth a little less every time it happens.

VERDICT: real trial progress, on a real and growing unmet need, priced by two analyst notes three weeks apart rather than by anything Pulse has actually sold. CHANGE IT: enrollment finishing on schedule in early Q4 keeps the case alive into that CE Mark filing; a delay, or a miss on the safety and effectiveness data once the trial reads out, is what unwinds it. Pulse reports again November 4. WATCH the cash burn holding near $18M-$19M a quarter between now and then - that number is the clock on how long today's cash buys before the next share sale.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Chubb Limited, ticker CB, at $339.21 (overnight), +$0.96 / +0.28% from Friday's $338.25 close. Chubb underwrites property and casualty insurance for consumers and businesses worldwide and is the largest P&C insurer that trades publicly. Fourth of 54 names on this watch, which wants a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought under what it's worth. The rebuild half is hard to argue with: Chubb's combined ratio - claims and expenses as a share of every premium dollar, where anything under 100 means an underwriting profit - improved to 83.8% in the July 21 quarter from 85.6% a year earlier, while premiums written grew 3.6% to $14.7B and adjusted profit rose 18.2% to $7.26 a share. Underwriting discipline that consistent should command a premium price; instead the stock trades near 12 times trailing profit, 7.3% under its own July 29 high of $365.91. VERDICT: the moat gets proven every quarter, and the market still isn't charging for it. CHANGE IT: a combined ratio moving back above 90 - a bad catastrophe season eating the underwriting edge - is the specific thing that turns cheap-and-durable into just cheap. Chubb reports again October 20.

DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Dolby Laboratories, ticker DLB, at $64.48, Friday's close, +$1.86 / +2.97% from Thursday's $62.62 close. Dolby licenses the audio and video standards built into most of the world's TVs, soundbars, and streaming apps - Atmos surround sound, Vision high-dynamic-range picture - collecting a small royalty on hardware it never manufactures. Eleventh of 51 names on this watch, which wants settled earning power bought cheaply with no credit taken for the balance sheet. The mispricing here looks like timing, not quality: the July 30 quarter posted revenue of $305M, down from $316M a year earlier, because licensing deals renew in lumps rather than on a smooth schedule, not because fewer devices are shipping with Dolby inside them. Meta and Alibaba both joined its video distribution program this quarter, and Dolby's own next-quarter guide - $362M-$392M of revenue, $1.13-$1.28 of adjusted profit a share - sits more than 60% above what it just posted, the deferred deals landing all at once. VERDICT: a high-margin licensing business trading at a discount created by its own lumpy calendar. CHANGE IT: if that guided jump doesn't show up when Dolby reports again November 17, deal timing stops being the excuse and the licensing model itself becomes the question.

GROWTH LEN5:
PulteGroup, ticker PHM, at $118.65 (overnight), +$0.39 / +0.33% from Friday's $118.26 close. The Atlanta company builds homes across 25 states and runs its own mortgage and title businesses for the buyers who need them. Nineteenth on this watch, which wants profit growth the price hasn't already charged for - and at about 12 times trailing profit, this one hasn't been charged for yet. The July 22 quarter beat estimates at $2.48 a share against $2.38 modeled, even as that profit fell 18% from $3.03 a year earlier on a thinner gross margin, what's left of a home's sale price after paying to build it. Still growing underneath the profit decline: net new orders rose 6% to 7,536 homes, order value rose 5% to $4.1B, and the community count - the number of active subdivisions selling homes at once - averaged 1,074, up 8%. Management's own next-quarter map puts gross margin at 24.5%-25.0%. VERDICT: more stores selling, at a thinner markup in each one. CHANGE IT: two quarters of that margin band holding instead of guided down again is what turns order growth into profit growth. PulteGroup reports again October 22, but the Federal Reserve's interest-rate decision this Wednesday, September 16, is the nearer date that matters more - it sets the mortgage rate every one of these buyers has to qualify against.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
Aura Minerals, ticker AUGO, at $87.54 (overnight), +$0.46 / +0.53% from Friday's $87.08 close. The Miami company mines gold, copper, and other metals across five sites in the Americas. Tenth of 30 names on this watch, which wants a business early as well as fast - and fast is the real half here. The August 5 quarter marked a twelfth straight quarter of rising trailing-12-month cash profit, a record $802M, on 75,437 ounces of gold equivalent produced. Early is not what's on offer: a company founded in 1946 running five operating mines is a producer, not a startup, which is why it sits well down this list rather than at the top. The quarter itself missed estimates, $1.15 a share against $1.38 modeled, because the cost of pulling an ounce out of the ground rose 9% to $1,985 during an infrastructure turnaround at one mine, while the price Aura actually realized per ounce sold fell 9% to $4,416 as gold cooled off its own high. Even with both moving the wrong way at once, that's still roughly $2,431 of margin on every ounce sold. VERDICT: real, growing profit on an aging streak, dented by one quarter's cost spike rather than broken by it. CHANGE IT: costs settling back down at that one mine when Aura reports again November 5 confirms this was a one-off; a second spike says the infrastructure problem is structural.

INCOME LEN5:
Zions Bancorporation, ticker ZION, at $68.75, Friday's close, +$0.46 / +0.67% from Thursday's $68.29 close. The Salt Lake City bank lends to consumers and businesses across eight Western states under seven different local brand names. Twentieth on this watch, which wants cash reaching owners that the business itself funds - and the headline number here is not the one to trust. The July 20 quarter reported $3.05 a share, which would make the $0.48 quarterly dividend, about 2.7% here, look barely worth mentioning, but $252M of that profit was one-time: $215M from selling long-held Visa shares, plus $37M from a small-business investment fund marked up on paper rather than sold. Strip both out and adjusted profit was $1.74 a share, still a real beat of the $1.56 estimate, funded by net interest margin - the gap between what a bank earns on loans and pays out on deposits - holding at 3.27% and loans growing at a 4.7% annualized pace. On that adjusted number the dividend takes under 28 cents of every profit dollar. VERDICT: a real, well-covered payout, temporarily wearing a headline number that isn't real. CHANGE IT: margin or loan growth actually slipping - not visible yet - is what would make this payout worth worrying about; a one-time gain rolling off when Zions reports again October 19 is not that.

Put the six side by side and the same instrument keeps reading differently depending on where you point it. A trial that hasn't finished is already sitting in Pulse's price. A record quarter that already happened isn't yet sitting in Chubb's. Before a price tag tells you anything else about a stock, check which side of that gap it's standing on.

text:
I was hiking up a steep mountain in Tennessee once and the path was thin and had a drop off that went waaaay down. When someone passed by, you basically had to hug the mountain until they passed. This guy was afraid of heights and his wife yelled at him for being a baby and stupid and a coward and walked off and left him there - halfway up the mountain! He had his eyes squeezed shut and he was literally grasping onto grass and weeds growing out of the mountainside until his knuckles were white. He was absolutely terrified. My girlfriend and I couldn’t believe how his wife was acting and that she left him there. 
My girlfriend and I stopped to talk to him and we offered to slowly walk him back down the mountain. He wasn’t moving. We offered to stay there at least until his wife came back down the mountain and he said he’d be okay. He clearly was not going to be okay.  I talked him through getting his breathing under control. I didn’t try to tell him his fears were unfounded or stupid. (They really weren’t. One wrong turn and you really could fall to your death. There were signers saying as much.) But what I did do was reassure him he was okay in the moment - for that moment - and that all he had to do was stay okay until the next moment. And then the next and the next. And I told him that we wouldn’t leave him there and that we would stay with him and help him at least down to a part of the path that was much broader - at whatever pace he needed to do that in. Told him we had all day if he needed it. Whenever someone walked by, my girlfriend and I put our hands gently on his back and gently told him he was okay. 
He finally insisted that we move on, that his wife was only going to a certain point to see a waterfall and then was coming back down.  I offered my walking stick in case he thought it would help him keep balance better when he did start his journey back down. He refused. Reluctantly, my girlfriend and I moved on.  And we saw his wife coming back down the mountain about ten or fifteen minutes after we’d left her husband’s side. I don’t recall exactly what she said, but my girlfriend gave his wife a piece of her mind when we crossed paths with her. 
Anyhow, phobias may seem irrational to those who don’t suffer from any, or at least not from the same type. But the terror and panic for someone with a phobia is real and it’s debilitating.  For this guy to face that fear to experience the look down, however brief, was a brave thing to do. And him crawling slowly and on his stomach may seem comical to some, but that’s what he needed to do to work his way through the fear and panic of the phobia. I’m proud of whoever this man is.

Sverre Vinje, a 102-year-old Navy veteran of World War II, delivered an emotional performance of “God Bless America” during a Milwaukee Brewers game.

Fans Chant ‘USA! USA!’

The attacks of September 11, 2001, claimed nearly 3,000 lives and remain one of the defining tragedies in modern American history.

Across the country, Americans gathered to remember the victims, honor first responders and reflect on the unity that followed the attacks.

Against that backdrop, hearing a 102-year-old World War II veteran perform “God Bless America” created an especially powerful moment.

A Veteran Representing a Generation

Vinje served in the U.S. Navy during World War II, connecting his personal story to one of the most consequential periods in American history.

Decades later, at 102 years old, he stood before a stadium crowd and delivered a patriotic song that has become deeply associated with American identity.

His performance offered a remarkable reminder of the generations of Americans who served their country.

A Standing Ovation From the Crowd

When Vinje finished singing, fans rose together to honor him.

The standing ovation, cheers and repeated “USA!” chants transformed the performance into one of the night's most memorable moments.

For many in attendance, the tribute represented more than a musical performance—it was a gesture of respect for a veteran and a reflection of national pride during a significant anniversary.

A Memorable American Moment

As the nation commemorated 25 years since 9/11, Sverre Vinje's performance provided a moving display of patriotism, remembrance and respect for military service.

At 102 years old, the World War II veteran stood before the crowd and received a thunderous ovation, with fans joining together in a simple but powerful message:

USA! USA!

text:
Alex Idrache’s story begins in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, where he grew up in a working-class neighborhood and watched U.S. troops conduct humanitarian missions, an experience that planted the earliest seeds of his military ambition. His father, Dieujuste, had dropped out of school at 14 to support the family, but he instilled in Idrache a fierce belief in education as the only reliable path forward. When Dieujuste immigrated to the United States and later brought Idrache over in 2009, the young Haitian teenager arrived barely speaking English but determined to seize the opportunity his father had fought for.

Within a year, Idrache enlisted in the Maryland Army National Guard, joking later that he first said yes because they offered him a free T-shirt, but beneath the humor was a deep sense of purpose. His leaders encouraged him to apply to the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, and against steep odds, he was accepted in 2012. Idrache battled language barriers, cultural adjustment, and the academic rigor of one of America’s most demanding institutions, ultimately graduating in 2016 at the top of his class in physics. A photo of him crying during the ceremony went viral worldwide; he later explained that the tears came from realizing how far he had traveled, from a Haitian slum to standing among the nation’s future military leaders.

After West Point, Idrache earned one of the Army’s most competitive assignments: training as a UH-60 Black Hawk pilot. His career quickly became a full-circle story. In 2021, when a devastating earthquake struck Haiti, Idrache returned as part of Joint Task Force Haiti, flying hundreds of missions, delivering nearly 600,000 pounds of aid, rescuing civilians, and translating French and Haitian Creole for ground teams. His journey, from a boy who once believed Haitians “don’t grow up to be pilots” to a U.S. Army captain serving his birth country from the sky, has become a modern emblem of perseverance, education, and the immigrant version of the American dream.

During his early years at West Point, long before the viral photo and long before he became a Black Hawk pilot, Idrache would routinely volunteer for extra duties that most cadets avoided: late-night hallway checks, early-morning accountability rounds, and the tedious administrative tasks that keep a company running.

He wasn’t doing it for recognition; he did it because he felt he owed something to the institution that had taken a chance on a kid who arrived in America barely speaking English. Senior cadets later said they remembered him not for his grades, which were exceptional but for the way he quietly made everyone else’s load lighter. It was his way of repaying a debt he believed he could never fully settle.

text:
The rupture between Russia and Europe objectively strengthened certain components of the transatlantic relationship. Europe became more dependent on American military protection while the United States simultaneously acquired greater importance as an energy supplier.

This does not prove that Washington designed the war, the sabotage, or Europe’s energy rupture in order to obtain those outcomes.

But there is no intellectual obligation to pretend that those outcomes do not exist.

Asking who gains power after a crisis is not the same as proving who caused the crisis.

It simply means refusing to study history without studying interests.

And here a curious European asymmetry toward China emerges.

Russia increasingly becomes a strategic enemy. China is described as a competitor and systemic rival, yet remains a gigantic trading partner.

Europe could begin economically replacing Russia, although at considerable cost.

It cannot easily replace China.

China does not simply stand opposite the West.

China exists within a considerable part of the chains through which the West reproduces its material life.

To radically contain China, the West would have to contain part of itself.

And here perhaps another comfortable category must be abandoned.

We continue speaking about the United States, China, Russia and Europe as though we were observing only states confronting one another across a map.

Yet a considerable portion of contemporary power no longer occupies territory in that way.

Capital can be legally incorporated in one country, financed in another, produce in a third, pay taxes in a fourth, and move among all of them.

Platforms cross borders.

Data do not spontaneously recognize sovereignty.

Supply chains transform the planet into an economic geography superimposed upon political geography.

A form of power therefore emerges that, at least in its aspiration, needs no flag.

Perhaps another map has been laid over the old map of territories, peoples, borders and states: the map of transnational economic spaces.

The United States retains extraordinary instruments of state power: currency, military force, technology, financial capacity, sanctions and regulatory reach. Yet some corporations born within its territory possess interests extending far beyond its borders.

The American State and transnational capital can cooperate extraordinarily well when their interests converge.

But they are not necessarily the same subject.

Russia offers another configuration.

Following the oligarchic experience after the Soviet Union, the State attempted to recover authority over capital that had acquired extraordinary international mobility.

An oligarch could hold his fortune in London, register companies across several jurisdictions, own assets throughout Europe and still belong to the Russian elite.

Sanctions brutally reminded us of something globalization appeared to have forgotten:

Capital may claim to have no flag until geopolitics gives it one again.

China once again presents the most fascinating paradox.

It participates in the global economy, receives capital, exports capital, produces for the world and also depends upon the world.

But it retains a political institution that intends to establish the ultimate boundary of that circulation.

Capital may enter without a flag. China reminds it that the territory it enters still has one.

Perhaps therein lies one of the fundamental contradictions of our time.

Two geographies exist upon the same planet.

One is made of territories, peoples, borders, states and flags.

The other is made of capital, platforms, data, finance, algorithms and supply chains.

One asks who governs the territory.

The other asks where value may circulate.

For a long time, they could complement one another.

But when their interests diverge, a question globalization believed it had rendered obsolete returns:

Who has the final say?

China still appears to answer: sovereignty.

text:
3/
Ben-Gurion’s counter-strategy
Israel did not view the Horn passively.
In July 1958, David Ben-Gurion proposed a discreet regional grouping—one not necessarily formal or public—to counter Nasser’s growing influence. The idea involved Ethiopia, Sudan, Türkiye, and Iran, with the United States expected to provide political, financial, and moral support.
•U.S. State Department FRUS: memorandum of conversation, London, July 27, 1958
•U.S. State Department FRUS: Embassy Tel Aviv cable, March 1960
•JSTOR: “Seizing Opportunities: Israel and the 1958 Crisis in the Middle East”
There was no formal U.S.–Israel–Ethiopia military triangle. But there was a strategic overlap: Ethiopia’s territorial integrity, Kagnew Station, Israeli diplomacy in Africa, Red Sea access, and resistance to Nasserist expansion all intersected.
This is the geopolitical context in which Cairo’s anti-Ethiopian, anti-Israeli, and anti-Western messaging should be read.

Sadat and the Ogaden War
Sadat altered Egypt’s public ideology, shifted toward Washington, and later made peace with Israel. But he did not remove Egypt from the Horn’s strategic contest.
During the 1977–78 Ogaden War, Siad Barre’s Somalia invaded Ethiopia. Two U.S. representatives reported to President Carter that Sadat said Egypt had already supplied more than $30 million in arms to Somalia and was prepared to offer further military support under certain conditions.
•Washington Post, January 27, 1978: Egypt and Sudan seen pledging military help to Somalia
•U.S. State Department FRUS index: Egyptian military aid to Somalia and the Ogaden War
•U.S. State Department Milestones: “Buried in the Sands of the Ogaden”
Ethiopia defeated the Somali invasion with decisive Soviet arms, advisers, and Cuban troops. Somalia’s defeat weakened Siad Barre’s regime and helped set the stage for the long crisis that ended in state collapse.
The evidence does not prove that Egyptian-supplied RPGs were the weapons used to shoot down U.S. Black Hawks in Mogadishu in 1993. That claim needs serial numbers, manifests, or chain-of-custody evidence that has not been produced.
But Egypt’s willingness to arm Ethiopia’s principal regional adversary at this decisive moment remains an important fact.

Kagnew closed; Ethiopia lost the coast
Kagnew Station closed in 1977. Its closure followed the Ethiopian Revolution, the Derg’s break with Washington, mounting insecurity in Eritrea, the growing value of satellite communications, and Ethiopia’s move toward the Soviet bloc.
Nasser did not personally oversee the closure; he had died in 1970.
•Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training: “The U.S. Expulsion from Eritrea, 1977”
•The Baffler: “Listening Devices”
•U.S. State Department FRUS: Kagnew and Eritrean insurgency
Then, in 1993, Eritrea’s internationally observed referendum formalized independence. Ethiopia became landlocked and lost sovereign control of its Red Sea coastline.
Cairo did not single-handedly produce that result. The EPLF won a war. The Derg collapsed. Eritrean nationalism was real. Ethiopia’s transitional authorities accepted the referendum. International observers recognized it.
But the strategic outcome was unambiguous:
•Ethiopia lost its sovereign Red Sea coast.
•The U.S. facility at Kagnew was already gone.
•The earlier Ethiopia-centered strategic environment around Eritrea was transformed.
•Israel’s former strategic relationship with Ethiopia could no longer rest on Ethiopia’s control of Eritrean territory and coastline.
States do not need to engineer every event to benefit from its outcome. The question readers should consider is which states benefited most from a more constrained, landlocked Ethiopia.

text:
When the West Dominates, It Is Power. When Others Rise, It Is a Threat.

Sea, Space and Cyberspace Are All Under Siege
The freedom of the global commons helped the world thrive economically and politically. China and Russia want to end it.

13 September 2026

A new Bloomberg Opinion analysis by Hal Brands offers a revealing picture of how the changing global balance is described in Western strategic commentary.

The argument is that sea, space and cyberspace — the "global commons" — are under siege, with China and Russia challenging the system that the United States helped build and, for decades, overwhelmingly dominated.

There is an important question beneath the argument:

When Washington exercised "command of the commons", it was presented as the infrastructure of global stability. When other powers begin acquiring comparable strategic leverage, the vocabulary changes — to "revisionism", "coercion", "threat" and "contested commons".

That does not make every Chinese, Russian or Iranian action benign. Nor does it make every American action illegitimate.

But it exposes something fundamental about geopolitics:

Power rarely describes itself as power. It describes itself as order.

And when the balance shifts, yesterday’s "order" can become today’s contested system.

The emerging question is therefore not simply who controls the seas, satellites, or networks.

It is who gets to define the rules — and whose power is still considered legitimate when the world becomes genuinely multipolar.

Source: Bloomberg Opinion | Hal Brands | 13 September 2026

text:
That rumor is true: in late August 2026, the retail price of gasoline in the Northwest Arctic village of Shungnak jumped to $26.82 per gallon.
What Drove the Spike
 * Shallow River Waters: Shungnak, located about 150 air miles east of Kotzebue on the Kobuk River, relies on seasonal summer barges for bulk fuel deliveries. Extremely low water levels on the Kobuk prevented fuel barges from navigating upriver to reach the village.
 * Emergency Air Deliveries: With barges unable to get through and local reserves running dry, the community store had to fly in fuel via cargo aircraft twice over the summer. Aviation freight rates drastically multiply per-gallon handling and transport costs compared to waterborne bulk shipments.
 * Overnight Doubling: Local store management noted that prior to the air-delivered inventory hitting the pumps, gas had been selling for $13.99 per gallon. Once the flown-in fuel was factored in, the price nearly doubled overnight to $26.82 (though NANA Regional Corporation shareholders were offered a discounted rate of $21.46).
The price spike arrived right at the height of the fall subsistence hunting season, putting immense financial strain on local residents who depend on boats and off-road vehicles to harvest meat for the winter.

Neither the White House nor the state’s top elected officials have issued a direct emergency response specifically addressing Shungnak’s $26.82 spike, but the situation puts a spotlight on the divide between national energy debates and the realities of the Bush.
The View from Washington (The Oval Office)
 * Out of Sight: Rural Alaska’s micro-logistics rarely make the White House briefing sheet. National energy discussions are framed around national averages ($4-something at the pump) or strategic crude reserves, not remote river navigation.
 * The Policy Gap: Federal energy initiatives tend to push for electrification, EV transitions, and grid decarbonization. While federal grants have funded microgrids and solar-battery installations in parts of rural Alaska, federal policy has virtually no mechanism to intervene when a shallow river cuts off a barge and forces emergency DC-6 fuel flights into a gravel airstrip.
The Congressional Delegation (Murkowski & Sullivan)
 * Dan Sullivan: Frequently points to situations like this to argue against federal restrictions on resource development and shipping, emphasizing that remote Alaskan communities bear the brutal brunt of high energy costs. He regularly uses high rural energy bills to push back on federal environmental mandates.
 * Lisa Murkowski: As a senior member of the Energy and Natural Resources and Appropriations committees, her focus is typically on securing federal infrastructure funding, bulk fuel storage upgrades, and alternative energy development through the Denali Commission. Her office is well aware of off-road logistics, but federal dollars move slowly toward long-term infrastructure, not immediate pump subsidies.
Juneau (Governor Dunleavy & the Legislature)
 * The Reality of Non-Intervention: Historically, neither the governor’s office nor the legislature steps in to subsidize retail gasoline prices for individual communities experiencing supply-chain interruptions. State assistance usually centers on the Power Cost Equalization (PCE) program, which offsets electrical generation costs for residential users in rural utilities—not retail gasoline at the local pump.
 * Treated as Local Logistics: In Juneau, river-freeze and low-water barge issues are generally viewed as local logistical hazards managed by local Native village corporations (like NANA), fuel suppliers, and borough governments rather than a statewide disaster trigger.
The disconnect is evident on the ground: while Juneau and D.C. debate broad resource policies and energy subsidies, villages like Shungnak are left absorbing airfreight prices just to fuel an outboard motor for fall hunting.

text:
ALIBABA $BABA IS 190 BILLION YUAN INTO A 380 BILLION YUAN AI BET:

Alibaba at $108.10 (overnight), -$1.20 / -1.10% from Friday's $109.30 close. The Hangzhou company, 131,462 employees, runs China's largest online marketplaces and rents out the country's largest pile of computing power.

The verdict: Asia traded all night and mostly declined to panic. The one thing being sold in every time zone is a company's willingness to spend enormous sums on artificial intelligence - and Alibaba signed for three years of that in writing, with half the money already gone.

Where Asia sits with the session nearly finished. Japan's Nikkei 225 ended at 63,418, -593 pts / -0.93%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng is at 24,899, +93.83 pts / +0.38%, about two hours from its bell. The Shanghai Composite is at 3,881.07, -7.04 pts / -0.18%, with roughly an hour left. Hong Kong changed its mind partway through: earlier in this same session the Hang Seng sat around 118 points lower at 24,687, and it has spent the whole afternoon on the other side of Friday's close.

Now the American side, where futures - bets on where an index finishes later - are the only live opinion on today's open. Nasdaq-100 futures at 28,993.75, -393.00 pts / -1.34%. S&P 500 futures at 7,616.00, -43.50 pts / -0.57%. Dow futures at 52,516.00, -69.00 pts / -0.13%. Russell 2000 futures at 2,897.00, -7.50 pts / -0.26%.

The technology one is falling more than ten times as hard as the Dow one, and small companies are barely moving. Whatever is being sold tonight has a narrow address.

That address was written on Saturday, September 12. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published an essay, "We Must Pace the Frontier," arguing his own industry should deliberately slow how fast it makes AI models more capable. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman agreed within hours and matched Anthropic's pledge to let outside evaluators inside permanently. Neither firm is listed, so neither is something an ordinary investor can own. The businesses writing cheques on the assumption those two keep sprinting are.

Hangzhou holds one of the largest. August 20, for the three months to June 30:

- Total revenue $39.6B, +9% on a year earlier
- AI cloud and computing revenue $7.1B, +45% - the fastest that business has grown in 22 quarters
- AI product revenue $1.8B, a twelfth straight quarter of triple-digit growth
- Capital spending, meaning money laid out on chips, buildings and equipment: nearly $10B in the quarter alone, +75%

Read the last line against the second. Alibaba laid out about $10B over three months building capacity, while the entire AI cloud business it is building collected $7.1B in the same three months. Capital spending now runs about 25 cents of every revenue dollar the whole group takes in, marketplaces included. Profit counted the way every company must fell roughly three-quarters from a year earlier, and that spending is the reason.

Nor is it one quarter's decision. The three-year plan is 380 billion yuan, roughly $56B, and through the end of June 190 billion of it was spent. Half out, half still to write, against $69.9B of cash and liquid investments.

VERDICT: China's largest single bet on the AI build-out, listed in New York, which is why an American argument about speed lands here first. Alibaba is on none of the six Len5es. Hypergrowth wants a business early as well as fast, and neither half survives the facts: founded 1999, 131,462 employees, group revenue +9%. Quality-Value wants a business almost nobody could rebuild bought under what it is worth, and at about 24 times the last year of profit it is the earnings half in motion, not the price half. CHANGE IT: the first quarter Alibaba spends less than that cloud business collects. WATCH those two figures side by side, about $10B against $7.1B. WHEN: no date announced; the September quarter has landed in November in past years. RISK: the shares already sit 43.9% under last October 2's $192.67, and the remaining 190 billion yuan is committed against demand nobody has booked.

The weekend's other mover is not an opinion. Drones from Iraq damaged Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and Riyadh shut it - the line that moves crude to the Red Sea while avoiding the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, traded at $107.95 a barrel early this morning, +3.19% on the day. Japan buys nearly all the energy it burns, part of why Tokyo finished lower on a night Hong Kong finished higher.

One American company sits on both of tonight's markets and outside the argument entirely. East West Bancorp at $129.17, Friday's close, -$0.20 / -0.15% from Thursday's $129.37 close. The Pasadena, California bank is the largest US lender built around Chinese-American customers and US-China trade, with branches in Hong Kong and subsidiaries on the mainland. Its July 21 quarter: record revenue $791M; net income $364M, or $2.63 a share, +18% on a year earlier; record loans of $59.0B and record deposits of $70.1B. It sits on the Quality-Value Len5 watch - a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought under what it is worth - and at about 12.4 times profit the discount is the half genuinely on offer. Its verdict: Asia exposure with no AI bill attached, and tonight nobody is selling it.

Europe is shut; Germany's DAX last printed at 25,569, +207 pts / +0.82%, on Friday - a closing level, not a live opinion. One caution over the rest: almost nobody trades at two in the morning, so a 1.34% fall in a futures price is a proposal rather than a result, and these overnight gaps fade by the 9:30am ET open more often than they hold.

In seven and a half hours, people who slept through every number above will either confirm tonight or erase it. What none of them can touch is the 190 billion yuan Alibaba has already spent, or the 190 billion still to come. That bill was signed long before anyone asked for a slower frontier, and it does not get to change its mind.

65 year old school bus driver gets caught trying to hookup up with and share meth with a 15 year old. 

​65-year-old Jeffery Seubert initiated contact with an undercover Facebook account operated by Wisconsin detectives. The officer made it clear right out of the gate that the profile belonged to a 15-year-old boy—a fact Seubert explicitly acknowledged multiple times throughout the exchange.

 Despite thinking he was communicating with a juvenile, Seubert steered the conversation toward explicit sexual fetishes and offered to supply methamphetamine, even outlining specific methods of ingestion.

​Within 48 hours, Seubert coordinated a meeting to engage in sexual acts with the decoy at an empty commercial garage arranged by law enforcement. When he arrived at the location, officers ambushed him and placed him into custody.

He walked through the door carrying an auto parts box stocked with a loaded syringe and a prescription bottle packed with meth. A subsequent search of his vehicle uncovered adult bedroom toys and chemical inhalants.

​During his interrogation, Seubert admitted he knew the profile was a minor and made the disturbing disclosure that he worked part-time as an active school bus driver transporting children of all ages.

 While forensic phone extraction found no communication with other juveniles, detectives discovered thousands of web searches and media files depicting besti@lity.

​Seubert was booked into the Marathon County Jail on multiple felony counts, including child enticement, using a computer to facilitate a child sex crime, and possession with intent to deliver methamphetamine.

After posting a $5,000 bond, his case eventually concluded in Marathon County Circuit Court, where he pleaded guilty to felony child enticement under a plea agreement that dismissed the remaining counts.

He avoided extended prison time and received a probation sentence with mandated sex offender treatment and lifetime sex offender registration.

text:
📜 HOOK & AUTHENTIC QUOTE

"We are tired because we are engaged in a form of self-consumption, mistaking our productivity for our existence." 

It sounds like a modern critique of LinkedIn culture, doesn't it? But it was actually written over a century ago by Franz Kafka in his private journals, agonizing over a bureaucracy that demanded every drop of his vitality. 

Kafka didn't live in the age of push notifications, remote work, and personal branding, yet he diagnosed the exact spiritual sickness of our time: the tyranny of hustle culture and chronic burnout.

⚡ THE MODERN MIRROR

Walk into any digital space today, and you will find an invisible, relentless panopticon. We have commodified our breathing. 

Sleep is treated as a weakness. Hobbies must be monetized. Weekends are for "upskilling." We have internalized the factory floor, carrying it inside our skulls wherever we go. 

We check our emails before our eyes fully open, feeding a digital beast that is never satisfied. Burnout is no longer a temporary exhaustion; it is the baseline state of modern existence. We wear our exhaustion like a medal of honor, terrified that if we stop moving, we will discover the terrifying truth: that we have hollowed ourselves out for an altar of endless output.

🧠 DEEP ANALYSIS

1. The Illusion of Agency: Kafka understood that modern systems don't need whips and chains; they convince you to whip yourself. Hustle culture successfully reframed exploitation as "self-actualization." You aren’t being overworked; you are "building your empire." By rebranding labor as identity, the system ensures you cannot rebel without feeling like you are betraying yourself.

2. The Quantification of Worth: We now measure human value in metrics. Impressions, revenue, hours logged, books read, steps taken. Kafka’s characters—most famously in *The Metamorphosis*—wake up transformed into burdens overnight, instantly realizing that their human worth is entirely conditional on their economic utility. When you stop producing, society looks at you with Gregor Samsa’s family: with disgust and inconvenience.

3. The Infinite Horizon: The traditional farmer worked hard, but the harvest ended. Winter came, and the fields rested. Hustle culture, however, offers an infinite harvest. The internet never closes. The algorithm never sleeps. There is always another milestone, another tier, another benchmark. Because the finish line keeps moving, true rest becomes psychologically impossible.

💡 THE PHILOSOPHICAL TAKEAWAY

Kafka’s ultimate warning was this: when you surrender your humanity to a system that only values your output, you eventually wake up and realize you have lost the very self you were trying to "optimize."

The antidote to chronic burnout isn't a better morning routine or a more efficient time-management app. It is a radical, quiet rebellion. It is the realization that your worth is intrinsic, not transactional. 

Sometimes, the most revolutionary act you can commit in a world obsessed with speed is simply to stop, draw a boundary, and remember what it feels like to exist—just for the sake of being alive, not for the sake of being useful.

text:
🚨🚨🚨FACT CHECK🚨🚨🚨

📌 1. EUROPEAN CONVENTION ON HUMAN RIGHTS (ECHR)

Reform says:

“We will withdraw the United Kingdom from the jurisdiction of the European Convention on Human Rights and create a British Bill of Rights, written by Parliament, for the people of the United Kingdom.”
— 2024 Manifesto, p. 24

📌 2. EQUALITY ACT 2010

Reform says:

“We will repeal the Equality Act 2010 and replace it with a simple, clear law that protects people from direct discrimination — but removes the thousands of pages of extra rules, duties, and bureaucratic burdens that have nothing to do with fairness.”
— 2024 Manifesto, p. 27; official policy statement

❌ They REMOVE: indirect discrimination rules, public‑sector duties, positive action requirements, definitions covering multiple protected characteristics — critics say this weakens protections widely

📌 3. EMPLOYMENT / WORKERS’ RIGHTS

“We will review and simplify employment laws to remove unnecessary red tape, costs, and complexity — especially for small businesses. We will keep the National Minimum Wage, health & safety laws, and protection against unfair dismissal — but cut layers of regulation that stop firms hiring and growing.”
— 2024 Manifesto, p. 18–19

❌ They NEVER say “strip away rights” or “remove protections” — their wording: “simplify, reduce burdens, make it easier to create jobs”

• ❌ They EXPLICITLY promise to keep core rights: minimum wage, safety, unfair dismissal

📌 4. ZERO‑HOURS / FLEXIBLE CONTRACTS

“We support flexible working — for employers AND employees. We will remove the ban on exclusivity clauses where it works for both sides, and make it easier to offer and accept flexible hours — while keeping legal safeguards: minimum wage, holiday pay, and safety rules.”
 
❌ They have NOT proposed removing minimum wage, holiday entitlement, or basic protections

• ❌ They NEVER say “lift restrictions on exploitation” — that is their critics’ language, not Reform’s

📌 5. RENTERS’ RIGHTS ACT / NO‑FAULT EVICTIONS

Reform says:

“We will repeal the Renters’ Rights Act and reverse the planned ban on Section 21 ‘no‑fault evictions’ — landlords need certainty to invest and rent out homes; tenants deserve good service too.”
— 2024 Manifesto, p. 31; housing policy

❌ BUT: The Renters’ Rights Act received Royal Assent — but its ban on Section 21 has NOT YET come into force (delayed repeatedly — currently expected no earlier than 2027–2028)

• ❌ Therefore saying “it abolishes no‑fault evictions” is PREMATURE — it has NOT done that yet

• Fact check status: ❌ “which abolishes” = FACTUALLY WRONG — not in force yet — policy stance is correct, timing/effect is wrong!🤦‍♂️

text:
A comprehensive investigation into the Tesla Cybercab without a steering wheel 

A wide-ranging investigation has now begun into the 'Cybercab' robot taxi vehicles introduced by Tesla, which lack a steering wheel. This electric robot taxi service was launched on September 3rd in selected areas of Austin, Texas, USA.
Although this vehicle, with its golden exterior finish and attractive Cybercab branding, has managed to capture the attention of passengers, the absence of a steering wheel or pedals inside has raised serious safety concerns regarding passengers' ability to act in an emergency.

The Cybercab, which can accommodate two people, features upward-opening doors and an elegant cyberpunk finish, distinct from the vehicles of its rival, Waymo. Tesla CEO Elon Musk calls this a true golden age in transportation. He states that the absence of brake pedals in these vehicles, designed for maximum efficiency and autonomous operation, reduces the complexity of the hydraulic system. It is said to be like a comfortable lounge with a TV and an excellent sound system, and in the future, passengers will be able to watch 4K quality videos via Starlink internet connectivity. Additionally, a camera is installed to monitor the interior of the vehicle. Promotional videos have shown that passengers can sleep, watch movies, play games, or participate in video conferences while traveling in this vehicle. Passengers' climate and media settings are saved in their profile and automatically applied for subsequent journeys.

Children under 13 years of age are prohibited from traveling in this vehicle. In a non-emergency, the journey can be stopped using a button on the touchscreen or the 'STOP' button located above. In an emergency, passengers can pull a special lever on the door to exit the vehicle. Instead of sudden braking, the system is designed to pull the vehicle to the side of the road and stop, taking into account the surrounding environment. Furthermore, passengers can contact Tesla representatives through the vehicle's communication system.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) in the United States has launched an investigation into the safety of these vehicles. This will examine whether Tesla's new vehicle complies with Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS). Additionally, the agency is evaluating the Full Self-Driving (FSD) feature in over 3 million Tesla vehicles, which is said to have led to accidents due to camera performance weaknesses under adverse weather conditions. It has also been previously reported that these autonomous vehicles have interfered with ambulances and fire trucks during emergencies, and NHTSA has strongly stated that autonomous vehicles unable to safely interact with first responders pose a danger to the public. Nevertheless, Tesla has previously deployed its Model Y robotaxis in other cities in Florida and Texas.

Supporters of robotaxis say that these vehicles are a safer option for women and passengers with communication difficulties. Their argument is that they reduce accidents compared to human drivers, prevent accidents caused by drunk or fatigued drivers, and offer great convenience to passengers using wheelchairs or those with other health issues. However, there is still a risk regarding the safety of these vehicles when facing unexpected situations. Various videos and reports have been published on social media about incidents where passengers were frightened when the vehicle could not move forward due to people blocking the road, and minor accidents.

text:
October 2011. The National Counterintelligence Executive drops a report on Congress covering two full years of foreign economic espionage, and the headline finding is basically: we are being robbed blind, at a scale we can't even fully measure, and cyber is how they're doing it.

This is the NCIX 2009-2011 assessment, now archived at the National Security Archive at George Washington University. It's an unclassified document, which means it was designed to be read and understood by legislators and the public, not just cleared analysts. That matters, because the language in it is unusually direct for a government counterintelligence product. The report names China and Russia as the primary culprits, doesn't hedge much, and lays out the methodology in enough detail to make clear this wasn't a collection of random incidents. It was systemic.

China gets the harshest characterization. The NCIX assessed Chinese actors as the most prolific of any foreign state, operating across aerospace, defense, information technology, pharmaceuticals, and energy. Not picking one lane. All of them, simultaneously. Russian actors are described differently: more targeted, more focused on government-adjacent research institutions and defense contractors, assessed as particularly sophisticated rather than particularly broad. Two different operational styles, same basic goal.

The tradecraft section is worth sitting with. The NCIX documented four recurring methodologies, and together they paint a picture of how thorough a well-resourced state espionage effort can be. First, insider recruitment: naturalized citizens, temporary visa holders, anyone with legitimate access to sensitive research who could be approached, pressured, or simply paid. Second, cyber intrusions hitting corporate networks, university research systems, and government contractor infrastructure. Third, front companies and joint ventures set up to acquire technology through transactions that looked, on paper, completely legitimate. Fourth, and this one gets underappreciated: harvesting open-source scientific publications and conference participation to aggregate technical intelligence without ever touching a classified system.

That last one deserves more attention than it usually gets. There is a version of this problem that requires sophisticated hackers and covert operations. There is also a version where you just send people to academic conferences and read the journals. The NCIX report flagged both as real, active collection vectors. Not hypothetically. In practice, during 2009-2011.

The economic damage section is honest about what it doesn't know. The report explicitly avoids putting a precise dollar figure on the losses, acknowledging that quantifying intellectual property theft is genuinely hard to do with methodological rigor. But the framing it uses instead is actually more clarifying than a number would be. The assessment warns that foreign acquisition of U.S. trade secrets was compressing the technology development timeline for adversary states. They're not just stealing products. They're stealing years. Decades of R&D investment that American companies and government programs sank into developing a capability, and a foreign state walks away with the results without funding any of it. That compression effect on the technology gap between the U.S. and its competitors is harder to put on a spreadsheet than a dollar figure, but it's the more consequential harm.

The central structural finding of the report is the shift in how espionage is conducted. By the 2009-2011 period, cyber had become the dominant vector for foreign economic espionage, displacing traditional human intelligence collection as the primary methodology. The reason the NCIX gives for this is worth quoting directly in spirit: cyber operations offered scale, deniability, and operational reach that human networks simply couldn't match. You can run a human intelligence network against maybe dozens of targets if you're very well resourced. A cyber operation can run against hundreds of corporate and research targets simultaneously, at minimal operational risk, with built-in deniability if you're caught. The math on that is obvious, and adversary intelligence services did the math.

This tracks with what CSIS was documenting concurrently in its survey of Chinese espionage in the United States. CSIS had been tracking a sustained pattern of technology acquisition operations spanning commercial, academic, and government sectors going back to 2000, and their data showed the 2009-2011 period as a marked acceleration in both volume and sophistication. The NCIX assessment and the CSIS work were looking at the same phenomenon from different angles and reaching compatible conclusions.

The policy downstream from this report is traceable. The NCIX assessment fed directly into the congressional awareness that produced the 2012 House Intelligence Committee report on Chinese telecommunications firm security risks, which was a significant moment in how the U.S. government began talking publicly about Chinese tech companies as national security concerns. It also contributed to legislative efforts to tighten the legal framework around foreign economic espionage. CISA's later nation-state threat assessments built on the analytical framework the NCIX established here, treating Russian and Chinese cyber espionage as persistent, mission-driven operations fundamentally different in character from opportunistic criminal activity. That distinction matters for how you respond to it. Criminal hackers have economic motives you can potentially disrupt. A state intelligence service running economic espionage as national industrial policy has a different set of incentives and a much longer time horizon.

What this report represents, in retrospect, is the U.S. government getting specific in public for the first time about the scope of what was happening. Not a vague warning about foreign adversaries. Named actors, named sectors, documented methodology, honest assessment of what the damage actually meant for American competitiveness. Thirteen years later, the actors are the same. The sectors are largely the same. The methodology has evolved but the core logic hasn't. The 2011 version of this problem and the 2024 version are the same problem, further along.

Greencoat Renewables $GRP.L Deep-Dive Analysis

Energyplay with a juicy dividend yield ~8-9% with dividend cover of 1.5

1. Company Introduction
Greencoat Renewables PLC (GRP.L) is a premier European owner and operator of renewable energy infrastructure. 

It operates a 1.4GW portfolio of wind, solar, and battery assets across Ireland, France, Germany, Spain, and Sweden. 

The shareholder base is heavily institutional, holding roughly 54% of the shares. Top institutional holders include BlackRock at 9%, RBC Brewin Dolphin at 6%, and KBI Global Investors at 6%. Retail and public investors hold the remaining ~46%. 

The company started as an Irish wind farm operator and grew into a pan-European utility-scale generator. 

The future strategy shifts toward "Value Accretive Growth," transitioning from purely operational generation to hybridisation and powering green digital infrastructure like data centers. 

The portfolio capacity is currently split into 74% onshore wind, 22% offshore wind, 3% solar, and 1% battery storage.

2. Product Presentation & Current Developments
The company boasts a young fleet with two-thirds of its assets being less than 10 years old. 

In 2025, generation volumes fell 10% below budget due to low wind resources across Europe. 

Despite this, cash flows remained highly robust with over 80% of revenues contracted, generating €115m in net cash and a 1.5x dividend cover. 

A major recent development is the €156m divestment of an Irish merchant portfolio at a 4% premium to NAV.

Current developments focus on hybridisation by co-locating batteries and solar at 10 existing wind sites, alongside a new Joint Venture (Drogheda Energy Park) to supply green power to hyperscale data centers.

3. Valuation Snapshot
Utilizing real-time market data for September 2026, the stock trades at approximately €0.776 per share. 

This translates to an up-to-date Market Cap of ~€864m. 

Net Debt (strictly without leasing) stands at €1,117m.

This results in an Enterprise Value (EV) of roughly €1,981m. With 2025 EBITDA at €158m, the EV/EBITDA multiple sits at 12.5x.

4. Earnings Snapshot
Revenue for 2025 was €296m, a decrease of €61m compared to 2024, primarily driven by geographic tariff mixes and the absence of a one-off €21m German compensation received in the prior year. EBITDA came in at €158m. 

Net cash generation was €115m. Dividends paid out were €76m, translating to a target dividend of 6.81c per share for 2026. 

NAV per share dropped 10.5c to 99.0c, impacted by P50 revisions and lower short-to-mid-term power prices.

5. Peer Group Comparison
GRP.L operates in the same space as funds like Greencoat UK Wind, Foresight Solar, and Aquila European Renewables. 

Like its peers, GRP has suffered from a persistent discount to NAV, averaging 29% in 2025, due to high interest rates. 

However, GRP distinguishes itself through its strategic pivot toward green digital infrastructure and data center PPAs in Ireland, offering a stronger growth catalyst than peers relying solely on merchant power markets.

6. Forecast 2030
The company forecasts approximately €600m in cash generation potential between 2026 and 2030. Dividend cover is projected to expand to 2.0x by 2030.

Driven by hybridisation and premium PPAs, 2030 EBITDA is estimated to reach the €190m-€200m range. 

With an aggressive deleveraging plan targeting a 45% gearing ratio by 2027, Net Debt will decrease significantly. Assuming EV drops to the €1.7bn-€1.8bn range, the 2030 EV/EBITDA multiple is forecast to contract to a highly appealing 8.5x-9.0x, indicating immense value unlock potential.

7. Acquisition Potential
Trading at a steep discount to its 99.0c NAV, GRP is a prime acquisition target. 

Its highly contracted revenues, with 76% contracted through 2030, and strategic access to the booming Irish data center market make it highly attractive for larger private equity infrastructure funds or major utilities seeking immediate European scale and predictable cash flows.

8. Catalysts / Milestones in the next 6-12 Months
The most immediate catalyst is the €100m share buyback program launching immediately to close the NAV discount. 

Management is also executing over €300m in selective asset disposals over the next 18 months to accelerate deleveraging. 

Further milestones include securing premium Corporate PPAs with tech hyperscalers and advancing the 36MW Drogheda data center JV. 

Additionally, a crucial shareholder continuation vote will occur at the May 2026 AGM.

9. Opportunities / Risks
Opportunities: 
The convergence of digital and energy markets presents a massive opportunity, with GRP positioned to power Irish data centers via premium PPAs. Hybridisation offers a +500bps Return on Equity (RoE) boost by utilizing existing grid connections. 

Risks: 
The primary risks include prolonged periods of low wind resources, further declines in merchant power capture prices, and the execution risk associated with selling €300m of assets in a potentially soft secondary market.

10. Conclusion
Greencoat Renewables is aggressively addressing its NAV discount through self-funded buybacks and deleveraging. 

By pivoting toward high-return hybridisation and data center energy solutions, GRP is transforming from a traditional yield-co into a dynamic growth engine. 

The current valuation offers an incredible entry point for a cash-rich, high-yielding green infrastructure powerhouse.

Next week's summit to feature curated roundtables with Asian, US and EU chip firms

The Big Idea
Government proposing that technologically advanced countries participating in Semicon India 2026 work with India to develop industrial linkages across semiconductor materials, components, equipment and intellectual property (IP)

Core goal: "accelerate matchmaking among interested parties"

Three-day summit in New Delhi beginning September 17

How It Works — The Roundtable Model
Centre identified Indian equipment, sub-assembly and component makers to hold curated roundtable discussions with counterparts from US, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Malaysia and Europe

Indian firms identified for attending — being supported to forge partnerships with foreign entities who are stalwarts in their category within semiconductors

Mentorship element: Indian companies with experience doing business from another specific country — whether via JV or sourcing agreement — will help other Indian companies access that economy

Country-Wise Strengths in Global Chip Value Chain
Malaysia: ~30% of global market share in Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT)

South Korea: Leader in production of memory chips

Japan: Significant share of global upstream semiconductor materials production line — including light-sensitive chemicals (photoresists), high-purity etching gases and wafer-cleaning & coating equipment

US: Leads in fabless chip design and core semiconductor IP

ET Insight — Shifting from 'Silica to Silicon'
India's role shifting from assembly market to a critical tech sovereign

De-risks India's position and elevates the nation

Roundtables organised in response to industry interest

Centre expects incentives being offered to establish domestic manufacturing ecosystem to draw highest number of investment applications under India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) 2.0

ISM 2.0 — What's on Offer
Government providing up to 30% of eligible capital expenditure as support to companies setting up facilities to manufacture:

Semiconductor raw materials like wafers, substrates, chemicals and glasses

Firms installing units for manufacturing or assembling of equipment, sub-assemblies and components

The government is considering a new domestic tourism stimulus program that would offer 1 million travel entitlements to encourage travel in late 2026 and early 2027. Tourism and Sports Minister Surasak Phancharoenworakul announced details of Thai Tiew Thai Plus at Government House on September 11, with registration expected to open on October 1 and each eligible person allowed up to five entitlements.

The government will subsidize accommodation at the actual room rate, capped at 2,000 baht per room per night, and provide co-payment tourism coupons worth 1,500 baht for major destinations and 2,000 baht for secondary destinations. Coupons will cover restaurants, spa and massage services, tourism packages, diving, boat excursions, and other eligible activities, extending support to businesses across the tourism sector.

Travel benefits are expected to run from November 1 to December 15, 2026, and January 16 to February 28, 2027, excluding the peak New Year period. The 4-billion-baht program, financed through loan funds, is expected to generate about 20 billion baht in economic activity. More than 1,000 operators and travelers linked to fraud in previous programs have been blacklisted, while participating accommodations must provide room rates from the previous year to help authorities detect artificial price increases.

Surasak also addressed Wat Phutthaisawan in Ayutthaya province, citing its reclining Buddha image, royal monuments, and riverside prang as important historical, religious, and tourism assets. Despite recent reports involving an individual at the temple, he expects visitors to distinguish individual conduct from the site’s religious and cultural value and continue visiting for worship and its historic attractions.

text:
In 586 BC, Nebuchadnezzar II did something that no conqueror in the ancient world could resist. He took the gold and silver vessels from Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem and carried them back to Babylon.

This was not mere looting. In the ancient Near East, when you sacked a god's house and walked away with his sacred objects, the theology was clear: your god had beaten his god. The defeated deity was either weak, absent, or simply finished.

Nebuchadnezzar placed the vessels inside Esagila, the great temple complex of Marduk in Babylon. He filed them alongside the spoils of every other civilization his army had consumed. The message was architectural: Marduk rules, and the evidence is right there on the shelf.

What he did not know, and what the biblical account insists upon, was that the God of Israel had already left the building.

The prophet Ezekiel, writing during the same years, described the presence of Yahweh departing Jerusalem in stages before the Babylonians ever arrived. The temple was emptied of its meaning before Nebuchadnezzar emptied it of its furniture. The king had captured a house from which the occupant had already walked out.

For decades, the vessels sat in Esagila. Babylon remained the center of the known world. The conquest looked permanent.

Then came the night of circa 539 BCE.

Belshazzar, ruling as regent in Babylon, hosted a banquet. According to the Book of Daniel, he called for the Jerusalem vessels to be brought out. Wine was poured into the Temple cups. Toasts were made to the gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone.

The same night, the armies of Cyrus the Great entered Babylon. The city, whose walls were considered impregnable, fell without the siege its defenders expected. The Achaemenid Persian Empire absorbed Babylon almost peacefully, through internal betrayal and the diversion of the Euphrates.

Belshazzar did not survive the night.

Cyrus, in one of his first administrative acts, reversed the entire theological equation. He issued a decree allowing the exiled peoples of Babylon to return home and take their sacred objects with them. The Jerusalem vessels, which Nebuchadnezzar had treated as trophies of a defeated god, were catalogued, packed, and sent back to Judah.

The empire that had spent fifty years celebrating its conquest of Yahweh was gone. The vessels were not.

Ancient history does not often offer this kind of long arc. A king wins, declares his god supreme, builds his proof into the stonework of his capital, and then watches his entire theological argument collapse within a single generation. The objects he used as evidence against Israel's God outlasted every king who mocked them.

The irony is not subtle. It rarely is, across that many centuries.

Belshazzar's banquet is one of the stranger nights in ancient history. He had fifty years of apparent Babylonian invincibility as context, and he chose that particular evening to pour wine into the Temple cups. The timing is almost too precise to be accidental.
