text:
Annacotty weir and the failure to restore fish passage on the Mulkear

Limerick City and County Council has refused Inland Fisheries Ireland’s (IFI) application to remove Annacotty weir, following a planning process that attracted numerous objections. Salmon, lampreys and eels continue to face a major barrier to upstream migration near the mouth of a river protected as part of the Lower River Shannon Special Area of Conservation (SAC).

The refusal is the latest chapter in a story stretching back to the Office of Public Works’ (OPW) replacement of the old mill weir in the late 1990s. Since then, the lower Mulkear has seen another weir installed, a European-funded conservation project, confident claims about improved lamprey passage, a complaint to the European Commission, and a removal campaign supported by more than 10,000 people. This history explains how the latest project came to fail.

I have spent more than a decade researching and campaigning on this problem. My photographs, videos and persistent campaigning pushed Annacotty weir up the agenda for fish-passage action. I wanted this barrier to become a positive example of community-led river restoration in Ireland. Instead, it has become a case study of how weaknesses in assessment, project management, and public engagement can leave a serious ecological problem unresolved for decades.

Local residents who objected to the project will be an easy target for blame. However, they had every right to question the proposal. IFI was responsible for engaging with them and preparing an application capable of addressing reasonable concerns. The Council’s refusal identified substantive weaknesses in that application. Responsibility for the quality of the application and ultimate planning failure lies with IFI.

The species most seriously affected by Annacotty weir are River Lamprey and Sea Lamprey, both qualifying interests of the SAC. Annacotty weir also delays Atlantic Salmon: under some medium flows, fish have great difficulty negotiating the weir, and those delayed make repeated attempts and expend valuable energy before spawning. The weir also restricts the upstream migration of the critically endangered European Eel. The fact that some fish eventually pass does not mean passage is adequate, particularly where several barriers act cumulatively.

The original Annacotty mill weir is thought to date from around 1749. It lies approximately 2.25 km upstream along the Mulkear from the River Shannon, with Ballyclough, another historic mill weir, a further 1.4 km upstream. However, the present Annacotty weir is a modern structure constructed by the OPW in 1997-98 during the Ballymackeogh-Mulkear drainage works. It replaced the deteriorating old mill weir. The replacement was not included in the Environmental Impact Statement prepared for the flood scheme and apparently does not have planning permission. A deteriorating historic structure was replaced by a substantial modern barrier without an assessment of its consequences for the river’s migratory fish. A Denil fish pass was incorporated, but its design was inadequate and affected by turbulence. Incredibly, some of the baffle boards were never installed.

A further weir was then constructed upstream of Annacotty beneath the Mulkear crossing of the N7 Limerick Southern Ring Road (Phase 1), which opened in May 2004. In an astonishing admission, IFI’s own reports state that “an agreement was reached with the contractors” to install a three-channel Crump weir and fish counter. The account has been repeated several times and appears again in IFI’s latest fish-counter report for 2025. IFI has not identified any corresponding environmental assessment or statutory authorisation for this structure. No separate planning permission has been located in the records reviewed.

The fisheries authorities had arranged another permanent structure to be constructed in a river already obstructed downstream – in an agreement whose terms and authorisation have not been made available. Counting salmon does not remove the need to protect other species. A small side pass was provided, but its presence does not demonstrate effective passage for lampreys or eels.

The implications are considerable. A new weir across a protected river was apparently added to road construction works through an agreement with the contractors. On the available record, the structure appears to have been installed without a documented environmental impact assessment or identifiable planning consent. A contractor agreement establishes neither environmental acceptability nor statutory authorisation. More than twenty years later, the public record still needs to explain what was authorised and assessed, and the basis on which this agreement was made.

Mulkear LIFE was a €1.74 million EU-funded conservation programme that ran from 2009 to 2014, coordinated by IFI (and their predecessors). Improving fish passage on the River Mulkear was one of its central objectives. Plastic lamprey tiles were installed at Annacotty and Ballyclough weirs in 2011. On 31 August that year, the Irish Examiner reported the project manager’s declaration: “We have proven that this fish pass works”.

Claims about the success of these lamprey tiles were widely promoted through media events, conferences, and videos. Interpretative signs at the weir stated that lamprey passage had exceeded 93%. IFI began recommending the tiles for use on other rivers and won an award for this work from the Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management (CIWEM).

But IFI has never produced verifiable evidence demonstrating that the tiles worked at Annacotty weir. I have never witnessed a successful ascent using them, despite spending hundreds of hours at the site documenting the difficulties faced by lampreys. The final Mulkear LIFE technical report containing the project’s passage claims is no longer available from either the project website or the European Commission website. The published peer-reviewed studies by Rooney et al. (2015) and Bracken et al. (2018) provided no evidence of lamprey passage through the tiles.

The Rooney et al. (2015) telemetry paper reported that none of the 20 tagged lampreys released below Annacotty weir in 2011, after the tiles were installed, was recorded ascending it. The single Annacotty ascent recorded in 2010 preceded the tiles. Three fish ascended Ballyclough weir in 2011, but they had been carried above Annacotty before release. The paper therefore provided no evidence of passage through the tiles at Annacotty weir. The authors expressly acknowledged that the expected increase in passage at Annacotty weir was not observed. This was despite contemporaneous claims of success in media reports and at the CIWEM awards.

The later Bracken et al. (2018) eDNA study found no significant difference in concentrations at the sampled locations before and after one of the lamprey-tile passes was reinstated. Nevertheless, the paper stated that the addition of a lamprey-specific pass, “although assisting in ascent”, had no significant effect on upstream eDNA concentrations. Nothing in the results demonstrated that the tiles had assisted ascent. The possibility that they provided no benefit was not properly examined.

A substantial part of Ballyclough weir was removed by Mulkear LIFE in August 2013. No Appropriate Assessment was completed for this project, and no planning application was made. A March 2013 screening document described partial removal combined with a 60-metre rock ramp. The works were not completed as described in that document.

That works of this scale were again progressed outside the planning system within the SAC is highly problematic. Partial removal has provided long-term benefits, but that did not make the short-term damage I documented acceptable.

I brought these matters to the European Commission in February 2015. Its proposed closure arrived in June 2016, repeating IFI’s unsupported assertion that the tiles provided passage for more than 90% of Sea Lamprey. The Commission said it had no scientific information showing that the passes were ineffective. 

However, the basis of my complaint was that IFI had not produced scientific evidence to support its claim. The Commission treated the absence of proof of failure as a reason to accept it. IFI repeatedly promoted the tiles as a success through the media, websites, interpretative signs and conferences, so the onus was on IFI to substantiate those claims with scientific evidence. I had observed the tiles in operation and reported my findings to the Commission, explaining why their steep slope, flow velocities and the behaviour of lampreys made the claimed passage performance implausible. Those observations and technical concerns required an evidence-based response.

I also challenged disturbance from capturing lampreys at their spawning grounds for the telemetry study. The Commission’s response emphasised the researcher’s qualifications and licences, without explaining why that timing and location were necessary.

I raised the issue of sediment impacts on downstream spawning grounds at Annacotty as a result of the partial removal of Ballyclough weir. The Commission dismissed this and said that there was no spawning recorded by IFI immediately downstream of Ballyclough weir. However, almost all of the river and sea lampreys in the River Mulkear spawn only 1.4 km downstream of the construction area. This was clearly within the zone of impact of the works. I asked for the water quality monitoring results that IFI claimed to have. None were supplied in the responses. IFI disputed my account of the works and silt release, but the Commission did not explain how it reconciled those disputes with my photographs and evidence. 

I also asked for the recorded justification for treating the works as conservation management, and the formal approval for Ballyclough. The Commission cited National Parks and Wildlife (NPWS) funding, support, and steering-group membership. Those were not the records I had requested. I had already reported that NPWS had confirmed to me that it held no record of Ministerial approval for the partial removal of Ballyclough weir.

On 22 September 2016, the Commission closed my complaint, declaring the project’s objectives were achieved and that lamprey passage was now adequate. Yet in 2021, IFI’s own barrier assessment classified Annacotty as a complete barrier to adult lamprey under the conditions assessed. By 2026, IFI was seeking permission to remove the weir. 

My complaint was not handled properly. The Commission closed it without answering my central evidential challenges. Similar concerns about complaint handling have reached the European Ombudsman. The handling of a complaint is itself open to scrutiny and closing a file does not settle the scientific questions it raised. 

Mulkear LIFE had a budget of €1.74 million. In May 2022, €99,481 was announced for Annacotty weir assessment and planning. These figures may also do not include ordinary IFI expenditure or any additional planning funds. Successive funding and interventions have still not delivered effective passage at Annacotty weir. IFI should now publish a full account of expenditure, decisions, and results across this history.

In March 2021, I launched the petition to remove Annacotty weir. It reached 10,000 signatures that December. I explicitly asked IFI to work with me and other committed people, and offered my ecological expertise voluntarily. This was a campaign to deliver a solution. 

I proposed a local steering committee, including community representatives and myself, and a riverside park as part of a wider restoration project. Local people could have helped shape the river’s future while retaining a valued public place. But IFI did not take those proposals forward. Despite the campaign’s support and my long involvement, I was not included in any aspect of the project.  

IFI did hold isolated public meetings in 2022 and 2025. But national water policy had identified Annacotty weir as a pilot for collaborative ecological design and engagement beyond normal planning consultation. That commitment raised the standard against which the process should be judged. Holding two consultation events did not answer why IFI did not involve the campaign or establish the proposed local steering group. 

IFI’s planning material did not explain how Annacotty weir was selected as a national fish-passage priority or acknowledge the campaign that had pushed it into public view. The petition attracted more than 10,000 signatures, Annacotty weir was subsequently named as a national pilot, but the campaign itself was omitted from the application. Those who had built public support, including me, were sidelined. I chose Annacotty weir for my campaign because it is a fish passage barrier that happens to be located five minutes from my home and because solving it could demonstrate what effective fish-passage restoration looks like.

Residents were entitled to ask how weir removal would affect their surroundings. Exploring public access, the mill’s history and the appearance of the restored river should have been part of the design process. The failure to build that shared project helped leave people feeling that change was being imposed on them. IFI missed an opportunity to turn a popular ecological campaign into a community restoration project.

The earlier publicity about lamprey tiles then returned in a damaging way. The planner’s report records an objection invoking the Mulkear LIFE lamprey tiles as a reason why removal was unnecessary. The old success claims had become part of the argument against the new solution. IFI needed to account for those claims and explain the continued passage failure. This history had practical consequences for public trust and the application.

IFI lodged application 26/60806 in July 2026. The Council refused it on 8 September without requesting further information. Its four grounds concerned the description of the development, heritage assessment, bridge stability and river-channel processes, and flooding and temporary construction works. These were matters the application needed to resolve before it could secure permission.  

The heritage package contained conflicting accounts of how much historic weir fabric survived the 1997-98 reconstruction. The Department identified that discrepancy. The assessment also needed to address the protected mill structures, their settings, construction access and the proposed temporary removal of entrance gates. Establishing what remained and designing around it was basic project preparation. A modern replacement weir beside historic buildings required a coherent heritage baseline, not contradictory accounts.  

Hydraulic modelling, geotechnical work and a flood-risk assessment had been submitted. Yet important questions about local scour, bridge blockage and the temporary piped causeway remained unresolved. Reports had been commissioned, but the package did not adequately answer the risks identified by the Council. Neither the heritage discrepancies nor those engineering gaps demonstrate that restoration is inherently unworkable. They demonstrate that this application had not made its case.  

Ecology was not a formal refusal reason; the Council’s internal referral recommended permission subject to conditions. However, this does not place the submitted ecological material beyond scrutiny. For a state agency proposing major instream works within an SAC, the assessment should have been exemplary – and it was not.

The aquatic baseline relied principally on a late-September survey at five locations. It recorded small numbers of lampreys and assessed habitat suitability, but did not include targeted surveys of lamprey migration or spawning. The application provided limited information on when and where lampreys would be most vulnerable within the proposed working area.

The measures intended to protect lampreys during construction were insufficiently defined. The Natura Impact Statement (NIS) proposed an instream working period of July to September, but qualified this as “where practicable” and stated that lamprey spawning periods would be avoided only “where feasible”. July can overlap Sea Lamprey spawning and the period when eggs and newly hatched larvae remain within the riverbed. The proposed fish rescue referred generally to electrofishing isolated working areas and inspecting excavated sediment for ammocoetes as works proceeded. It did not provide a detailed lamprey-specific rescue methodology or make a firm commitment to avoid the most sensitive period. 

The treatment of accumulated sediment was also inadequate. The NIS acknowledges that approximately 800 metres of river is impounded upstream of Annacotty weir, causing increased deposition of fine sediment, and accepts that removal will mobilise this material downstream. It recognises the resulting risks of increased turbidity, habitat smothering and the clogging of gravels used by spawning lampreys and salmon. However, it does not quantify the stored sediment or adequately predict the scale, duration and depositional footprint of its release, including its effects on the principal lamprey spawning area downstream. It also does not consider whether sediment released during the earlier works at Ballyclough contributed to the accumulated material. Instead, the assessment relies on the assertion that substantial accumulation is unlikely and that any sediment pulse will be temporary.

The fine sediments upstream are also likely to provide ammocoete habitat, particularly for Brook Lamprey and possibly smaller numbers of River and Sea Lamprey. Removal of the weir and the resulting increase in flow velocities will alter or remove some of this depositional habitat. That does not mean the weir should be retained - restoring natural river processes remains the correct objective. However, the habitat change and the protection of lampreys already present within the sediment needed to be properly assessed and addressed.

The upstream Crump weir was another major omission. Although identified in the ecological reports and hydraulic model, the application did not assess passage through it under the conditions that would follow removal of Annacotty weir. The NIS also asserted that migratory fish could continue moving through “appropriately sized” pipes in the temporary causeway, without specifying their configuration or demonstrating suitable depths and velocities for lampreys. The sediment controls and maintenance of fish passage depended on the same temporary structure whose hydraulic capacity and blockage risk the Council found had not been adequately assessed.

These deficiencies do not weaken the ecological case for removing Annacotty weir. They show that an important and potentially transformative restoration project was submitted without the detailed, species-specific and ecological assessment supported by firm mitigation commitments that work of this scale in a Natura 2000 river required.

However, the Council’s decision also deserves scrutiny. Roads and Flood Risk officers recommended further information. The Conservation Officer also recommended it if the application was not invalidated over its description. The Department requested a revised underwater archaeological assessment. The planner nevertheless treated the heritage issues as making the proposal unacceptable in principle and declined to pursue further information.

I consider that this was disproportionate. The public-notice problem required a proper procedural remedy, but the technical advice identified a route to further investigation and amended proposals. The Council should have given that route greater weight. IFI’s inadequate preparation and the Council’s decision to refuse rather than seek the necessary information have left the ecological problem where it was.

The outcome is a serious failure of delivery. Residents who objected exercised a statutory right; the more than 10,000 people who backed removal were equally entitled to expect a competent project. IFI cannot transfer responsibility for the refusal to either group.

IFI should now state publicly whether it intends to appeal, submit a properly prepared new application, or abandon the project. A renewed project needs accountable leadership, a published timetable, a comprehensive environmental assessment, and a design that addresses Annacotty weir and the upstream counter together. It should give something back to the community, such as a riverside park, and give local people and campaigners a meaningful role. Effective interim passage measures are also needed immediately. I proposed such measures more than five years ago, but not one was implemented.

My original campaign petition linked Annacotty weir to the much greater challenge of the ESB dams on the main Shannon. I wanted to begin here and build the case for tackling Ardnacrusha dam and Parteen weir. If the agencies cannot deliver at this relatively small barrier, what confidence can we have that they will address the larger ones?  

The national record gives reason for concern. Clondulane Weir on the River Blackwater still stands despite a ministerial direction in July 2006 requiring its removal. Fish passage at Fermoy weir located upstream from here was restored only when the weir collapsed by itself. 

I hoped Annacotty weir could become a case study in successful fish-passage restoration. It has instead become another case study in Ireland’s failure to deliver it. The problem is not simply a lack of money: publicly documented funding commitments across the wider Mulkear LIFE programme and Annacotty planning already approach €2 million, before ordinary IFI expenditure and any further planning funds are counted. What is missing is accountability and competent project preparation and management. 

The latest run of River Lamprey has arrived at Annacotty to meet the same concrete barrier. After years of programmes, claims, reports and public expenditure, effective passage has still not been delivered. Ten years after the European Commission declared passage adequate, the problem I challenged remains unresolved. This is unacceptable. We need an independent review of what went wrong, accountability for the decisions taken, and a new restoration project developed with the local community, backed by robust ecological and engineering assessments, secured funding and a clear timetable for delivery. It should not be this difficult to remove a redundant barrier from a protected river. The lampreys cannot wait another decade.

𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗥 𝗙𝗥𝗨𝗜𝗧 𝗙𝗔𝗥𝗠𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗜𝗡 𝗞𝗘𝗡𝗬𝗔: 𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗧𝗢 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪 𝗖𝗔𝗥𝗔𝗠𝗕𝗢𝗟𝗔 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗙𝗜𝗧
💰 𝗞𝗦𝗵 𝟮,𝟬𝟬𝟬

Are you looking for an exotic fruit crop with growing demand in Kenya? 🌱

Star fruit, also known as Carambola (Averrhoa carambola), is a unique tropical fruit famous for its beautiful five-point star shape when sliced. It has a sweet-to-mildly tart taste and is becoming increasingly popular among consumers looking for healthy and unusual fruits.

For farmers, star fruit offers an opportunity to diversify into specialty fruit production, with potential markets in fresh fruit, hospitality, juice processing and value addition. 🌿📈

🌱 𝗤𝗨𝗜𝗖𝗞 𝗙𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗦

🌟 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗼𝗻 𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘀: Star Fruit, Carambola
🌿 𝗦𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰 𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲: Averrhoa carambola
🥭 𝗧𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲: Sweet to mildly tart, juicy and crunchy
💪 𝗡𝘂𝘁𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲: Vitamin C, antioxidants and fiber
🌳 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗵𝗮𝗯𝗶𝘁: Tropical/subtropical fruit tree
📅 𝗙𝗿𝘂𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴: Can produce multiple crops under suitable conditions

🌿 𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗔𝗟 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗗𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦

Star fruit performs best in warm areas with adequate moisture.

🌡️ 𝗧𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲: 20–32°C
🌧️ 𝗥𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗮𝗹𝗹: 1,200–2,000 mm annually
⛰️ 𝗔𝗹𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲: Up to about 1,200 metres
🌱 𝗦𝗼𝗶𝗹𝘀: Deep, fertile and well-drained loamy soils
⚗️ 𝗦𝗼𝗶𝗹 𝗽𝗛: Approximately 5.5–6.5

Irrigation is recommended in areas where rainfall is unreliable, especially during prolonged dry periods.

📍 𝗣𝗢𝗧𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗔𝗟 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗔𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗦 𝗜𝗡 𝗞𝗘𝗡𝗬𝗔

Star fruit can perform well in several warm regions, including:

📌 𝗖𝗼𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗞𝗲𝗻𝘆𝗮: Kilifi, Kwale, Lamu and Mombasa
📌 𝗪𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗞𝗲𝗻𝘆𝗮: Kakamega, Bungoma and Kisumu
📌 𝗟𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗼𝗻: Homa Bay, Migori and parts of Siaya
📌 𝗟𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗘𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻: Makueni, Machakos and Kitui with irrigation
📌 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗞𝗲𝗻𝘆𝗮: Warmer parts of Murang’a and Kirinyaga

However, always assess your soil, water availability and local climate before establishing a commercial orchard.

🌱 𝗙𝗔𝗥𝗠𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗣𝗥𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗖𝗘𝗦

🌿 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹: Seedlings can be raised from seed, while grafted or budded plants can offer earlier and more uniform production.

📐 𝗦𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴: About 5m × 5m or 6m × 6m, depending on the production system and farm conditions.

💧 𝗜𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Important during dry periods.

✂️ 𝗣𝗿𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴: Helps maintain tree shape, improve light penetration and encourage productive growth.

🐛 𝗣𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁: Monitor for fruit flies, aphids and diseases such as leaf spot. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) should be used where necessary.

🥭 𝗙𝗥𝗨𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 & 𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗩𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚

🌳 Grafted trees can begin producing in approximately 3–4 years, depending on management and growing conditions.

🥭 Mature trees can produce significant quantities of fruit under good management.

🌟 Fruits develop their characteristic yellow colour as they mature and can be harvested at the appropriate maturity stage depending on the target market.

🛍️ 𝗠𝗔𝗥𝗞𝗘𝗧 𝗢𝗣𝗣𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗨𝗡𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗘𝗦

Star fruit can be marketed through:

🛒 Supermarkets and fresh fruit outlets
🏨 Hotels, restaurants and hospitality businesses
🥤 Juice and beverage companies
🍹 Fresh juice businesses
🌱 Health-conscious and specialty fruit markets
🌍 Potential export markets
🍯 Value-added products such as juices, jams and dried fruit

The key is to identify your market before planting on a large scale. A beautiful fruit is great, but a buyer waiting at the other end is even better! 😄

💡 𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗥 𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗥 𝗙𝗥𝗨𝗜𝗧 𝗙𝗔𝗥𝗠𝗜𝗡𝗚?

✅ Exotic and visually attractive fruit
✅ Growing interest in healthy and specialty fruits
✅ Can diversify your farm income
✅ Suitable for fresh consumption and value addition
✅ Potential for local, hospitality and export markets
✅ Can perform well in suitable warm Kenyan regions

⚠️ 𝗜𝗠𝗣𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗔𝗡𝗧: Star fruit contains oxalic acid and may be unsafe for people with kidney problems. Consumers with kidney disease should avoid it unless advised otherwise by a qualified healthcare professional.

text:
HOME BANCSHARES $HOMB KEEPS MORE OF EVERY DOLLAR THAN ANY BANK ON THE GROWTH LEN5. IT STILL BOUGHT THE GROWTH:

Home BancShares at $29.97, Friday's close, +$0.20 / +0.67% from Thursday's $29.77 close - tenth of thirty on the Growth Len5 watch. The Conway, Arkansas company, 2,543 employees, runs Centennial Bank, lending to businesses and developers across Arkansas, Florida, Texas, Alabama and now Tennessee.

The verdict: one of the most profitable banks in the country, and almost none of last quarter's growth came from its own customers. The loan book grew $1.49B. Its borrowers accounted for about $24M of it.

July 15, for the three months to June 30:

- Total revenue a record $295.1M, +10.6% on the three months before
- Net interest income, what a bank earns on loans after paying its depositors: $241.6M, +7.9%, on a 4.51% margin - a 7.00% average yield on loans against 2.39% paid on deposits
- Adjusted profit, meaning profit with one-off items set aside, $0.64 a share against $0.58 a year earlier; counted the ordinary way, $0.59
- Loans $17.13B from $15.63B; assets $24.71B

Then the number that decides how to read all of it. Of that $1.49B of new loans, $1.47B arrived in a box: Mountain Commerce Bancorp, a Tennessee bank bought during the quarter for $12.7M in deal costs. The existing franchise wrote $46.4M of new lending in the community branches, less a $22.6M decline at Centennial CFG, its commercial finance arm. Net, roughly $24M on a book that started at $15.63B - about 0.6% if that pace held for a year.

A purchase is not a shortcut to that margin, though. It is where the margin gets applied. Home BancShares spends about 40 cents to bring in each dollar of revenue, an adjusted efficiency ratio of 40.46%, and has been stripping costs out of acquired banks since founder and chairman John Allison started it in 1989. Mountain Commerce is that method working exactly as designed. It is also that method being necessary.

Ameris Bancorp, ticker ABCB, at $84.66, Friday's close, +$0.04 / +0.05% from Thursday's $84.62 close, is the same idea run the other way. The Atlanta company bought nothing last quarter: its July 23 report put loan growth at 6.4% annualized, all of it written by its own lenders - roughly ten times the pace Home BancShares managed unaided. It keeps less of it, on a 3.88% margin and a 1.53% return on assets against 2.09% here, profit measured against everything the bank owns. Reported profit was $0.77 a share against $1.60 adjusted, after an $82.5M accrual for a jury verdict in a California employment case - a courtroom, not a credit problem. It sits eighth of thirty on this same Growth Len5, with the growth arriving from customers.

One name, six Len5es:

- GROWTH - STRONG, and the Len5 watching it, tenth of thirty. Wants profit growth the price has not already charged for. Adjusted profit per share went $0.58 to $0.64 in a year, +10.3%, against about 12.4 times the last year of earnings and 1.32 times book value - what owners would keep after paying every debt. Not a price that assumes much. CHANGE IT: mid-single-digit loan growth written by its own lenders, no bank purchased.

- QUALITY-VALUE - PARTIAL. Wants a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought for less than it is worth. Price is on offer at 1.32 times book. The rebuild half splits: anyone with capital can open a bank, and plenty do, but very few run one this lean for this long. CHANGE IT: that 40.46% holding through a year when deposits get dearer - the discipline is the part nobody can buy.

- DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - PARTIAL, the near miss. Wants settled earning power bought cheaply, no credit taken for the balance sheet, usually with a dated event attached. Settled and cheap are both here; the event already closed. And loans where the borrower has fallen behind ran 1.08% of the book at June 30, against $328.4M set aside - a cushion, not an alarm, but this style will not look past it. CHANGE IT: that 1.08% back under 1%, no new deal alongside it.

- INCOME - PARTIAL. Wants cash reaching owners that the business itself funds. On July 22 the dividend went to $0.23 from $0.21, +9.5%, a ninth straight yearly rise, plus 1.5M shares bought back for $40.5M. That is $0.92 a year, about 3.1% here, on near 38 cents of every profit dollar - covered, and modest next to what this style watches. The same capital buys the next bank. CHANGE IT: both growing in a year when nothing is acquired.

- MOMENTUM - NOT A FIT. Wants a price near the top of its one-year range with the recent climb and the longer one agreeing. Near the high is arguable, 5.5% under July 29's $31.70. Agreement is absent: up 5.9% across twelve months, peaking the day after the July report and sideways since. On September 8 Hovde Group's Edward Najarian started coverage at Outperform, $34 target; the shares went nowhere on it. CHANGE IT: a close above $31.70.

- HYPERGROWTH - NOT A FIT, furthest off. Wants a business early as well as fast. Founded 1989, 2,543 employees, $24.71B of assets, and the fastest thing it did last quarter was sign a purchase agreement. CHANGE IT: nothing a quarter can do.

WATCH the organic lending line rather than the total - $46.4M against $1.47B is the whole argument. WHEN: third-quarter results are tentatively Wednesday, October 14, after the close, $0.63 a share carried against the $0.64 just earned. The nearer date belongs to somebody else: the Federal Reserve announces Wednesday, September 16 at 2:00pm ET, target range 3.50%-3.75%, three of its twelve voters having pushed for an increase in July. That sets the rate a borrower in Conway or Tampa has to sign for. RISK: a bank this good at absorbing other banks has an obvious way to produce next quarter's growth, and it does not involve lending to anyone new.

There is nothing wrong with buying a bank, and Home BancShares is plainly better at it than most. But a purchase is the company's decision and a loan is the customer's, and only the second says anything about the towns it lends in. Last quarter the customers stayed home.

Not investment advice.

text:
SpaceX is paying for its newest 444 acres in drinking water. Brownsville agreed to release the land after SpaceX put an investment on the table that could roughly double the region's potable water capacity, a trade no other company in America is even positioned to offer a city.

That vote happened August 28.

On September 16, the city of Starbase votes to absorb the same parcel, and getting there required some genuinely creative lawyering. Texas only lets a city annex land it touches, and this tract sits miles from Starbase near the Brownsville ship channel. The solution was to extend Starbase's jurisdiction down the Highway 4 right of way, with TxDOT signing off, so that the city legally touches the field. Starbase has to annex the highway before it can annex the land. The paperwork calls the maneuver Project Quantum.

Meanwhile the drone footage shows graders, excavators, and dump truck convoys working the full tract on September 11, five days before the annexation vote. The dirt work started before the land even had a city.

SpaceX says this site supports operations near the Port of Brownsville rather than launches, and a separate petition would take Starbase from 927 acres to nearly 8,000. The launches get the cameras, but Starship's flight rate is getting built in county records and water deals like this one, months before any hardware shows up.

text:
SWEDEN ON A KNIFE-EDGE: THE SMILES DO NOT TELL THE WHOLE STORY

Letters from Stockholm — 14 September 2026

Many white Swedes have assured me that they would never vote for the far right. Yet the morning after the election, Sweden remains bitterly divided.

The centre-left bloc has held a provisional one-seat lead, with late and overseas ballots still capable of changing the outcome. I think a change of government is coming, but nobody can honestly declare victory yet. 

Election coverage.

The Sweden Democrats spent four years supporting the government and influencing its direction. Their origins in neo-Nazi and white supremacist circles are documented. Putting on a suit does not make that history disappear. Reuters.

After thirty years here, I have become wary of polite assurances. A smile tells you very little about what somebody believes—or what they do in the privacy of a polling booth.

But I also believe Sweden’s leaders made serious mistakes over immigration. They admitted people faster than they could provide effective integration, suitable housing and functioning community support. Ordinary residents have had to live with the consequences.

In the early hours of Sunday, I watched six teenagers fighting and screaming outside a hotel, waking the neighbourhood. Their behaviour was disgraceful. Whatever their background, residents deserved peace and the young people involved deserved to be held accountable.

Such scenes give the far right material for its campaigns. But six teenagers cannot stand as representatives of every African, refugee or immigrant in Sweden. 

Responsibility belongs to the individuals involved.
Anyone offered safety in another country has a duty to respect its laws and the people around them. Equally, nobody should have to accept racism as the price of living there.

The political climate has hardened. Sweden now offers eligible adults SEK 350,000 to return voluntarily to their countries of origin. That is a conditional repatriation grant, not an offer to every foreign-born resident. Swedish Migration Agency.

Proposals affecting refugees’ permanent residence are also deeply consequential. But saying every refugee’s permanent residence has already been cancelled would be inaccurate. European Commission overview.

I did not vote. I felt politically exhausted and unconvinced by the choices before me. That was my decision, and I accept that abstaining meant surrendering my voice in an exceptionally close contest.
I know the way back to the airport through which I arrived. But many people have built their entire lives here: children, careers, families and homes. Their future deserves more than election slogans and collective suspicion.

Sweden needs order, honest immigration policy and individual accountability. It also needs to confront racism without pretending that every concern about integration is racist.

The count is unfinished. So is the argument about what kind of country Sweden wants to be.

text:
#vss365 #sanguine #bionicanadian #bravewrite

She walks alone through corridors of grey
Where silence wears the face of yesterday
No footstep answers
No soft voice draws near 
Only the hollow echo of her fear
Emptiness curls like smoke inside her chest
A nothingness that offers no rest 
Loneliness, a cold and nameless sea
Drowns every hope she dared to see

Then she slips into Dostoevsky’s White Nights
In Petersburg’s pale, unending lights
Where streetlamps bleed a ghostly gleam
And life seems deserted, bleak, a dream
A vacuum where no warmth is known
An abyss without a single stone 
A tunnel lost in dreamless deep 
Where shattered mirrors secrets keep
No destination calls one’s name
No hearth awaits, no familiar flame
She walks as destiny decrees
Through misty squares & whispering trees
 
Next, she steps to Browning’s My Last Duchess
Where kindness is a crime the Duke must punish
She’s the Duchess who smiled at all like sunlight on leaf & stone
Words she rode, a cherry bough she’d own
Her thanks, as free as breath, to great & small
“ She had a heart… too soon made glad,” she made the duke said
Eventually all her smiles were dead
Now mute she stands in paint, so calm, so mild
He keeps her kindness caged, and calls it “style”
 
Now Frost’s The Road Not Taken splits her mind
Two silences lay equal, both unkind
And sorry she could not inhabit both
She stood a long while, hollow and unguessed
Two roads diverged in yellow wood
And she, too weary to choose good
Took the one that seemed less worn
Though both were thorned, & both forlorn
She shall be telling this with a sigh 
Somewhere ages and ages hence
Did her choice make a difference? 
 
Then Shakespeare’s Hamlet whispers in her ear
“To be, or not to be” the question clear
Whether ’tis nobler in the mind to bear 
The slings and arrows of outrageous sorrow
Or to take arms against a sea of troubles
And by opposing, end them
She stands upon the threshold of her soul
Where conscience makes a coward of the whole
 
At last, she hears young Kipling’s steady voice in If
If you can walk through rooms where vanished echoes stay 
And wear the dusk like rosy pout, though no tears will show
If every love becomes a shadow before the day
And silence is the only name your mirrors know
Then you have learned the mystic art of being none
A moon without a sky, a night without a sun
Then you have known the fate that shadows her days
To bloom unseen in darkness & fade without a trace

She walks on, still melancholy’s guest
But now  wind down and with courage in her chest
The poets lent their lamps to light her way 
Through emptiness, she finds a sanguine day

text:
I've been thinking at length about a comment I made on trading recently. "Lather, Rinse, Repeat." - "The directions for trading are on the shampoo bottle." That's true, but I've been thinking about the journey from the beginning, to he point I read the instrucitons. And, yes, that's literally how it happened. I grabbed a new bottle of shampoo one morning and wondered what was in it. When I turned it around I noticed the directions, which I had seen, but that time it hit different, and I knew.

There's nothing unique and what I do. Some look at it and think it's crazy, some are interested, some think it's old school, and whatever. That's fine. None of what I do, or share online is anything other than information. I'm no guru, or anything of the kind. I literally just do what I do. And for me it works. No more needs to be said about that.

Mostly I think about when I first started to lern about trading. I say it that way, because most of the time we loosely say :when I started trading", but that implies we had some knowledge and understanding, stepped up to the machine and went to work. I knew absolutely nothing about trading, and the same thing was true when I opened my first chart. I noticed that when the candles went up, so did the price, and when candles went down, so did the price. LOL.....truth! 

There were no real materials, videos, influencers, or anything at the time. the FOREX Market had just gone public on the internet and I was determined to be a participant. And, I'd never seen a live shart before!! My limited understanding or anything markets can from the Sunday Omaha World Herald, and the Sioux City Journal. Literally paper charts and quotes mixed with some news and findementals, all which meant nothing to me at the time.

The only thing I was sure about, well certain about was that I would loose money. I was exactly right about that too! But the one thing I had right was an assumption that turned out to be true. I remember sitting down with myself and talking and thinking through how I had to approach this as a business. That was exactly correct as well. I have a business head by nature. 

I won't go into the journey from candles sticks to the futures market today again. But really the first time I put an SMA on the Forex chart and then later the Gator indicator my journey really began. And as silly as it might sound when I found EMA things changed. I put the 11 EMA on a chart one day and I just say everything different that I had before. I noticed how it followed trend, and how price stair stepped up the 11 EMA.

What I learned, well I learned many things, but the first thing I learned was something I wanted to understand was right in front of me. I didn't really even understand trend until I saw that 11 EMA on the chart. As soon as that became clear I realized that was my path to goal. 

My goal? To determine better entry points and be able to hold longer, extracting more profit. Though I didn't fully understand the difference I also knew I was cut out to be a Technical Trader. Nothing wrong with Fundementals, they just don't do for me, what Technicals do. And to be fair, I was in the process of learning many more things, I just didn't know it at the time. 

Why did I pick FOREX? Well I was always interested in currency exchange and it seemed interesting. LOL. I also opened a Scottrade account shortly after it became available on the web. I knew I needed more visual tools that Scottrade offered at the time, so I went FOREX. But, yeah, I placed a few stock trades as well just trying to get a feel for stock trading. It was all baptism by fire for me. I didn't even know anybody who traded. LOL so it was just me, the water, and the fire and occasionally there wasn't enough water to manage the fire!! LOL

Back to the point. I failed miserably a few times. Did stupid things. Cussed, screamed, kicked things, all of that! LOL....if you know, you know. You will learn trading is an emotionally draining activity. All the Guru's ranting that you need to keep your emotions out of trading are only right in the sense that you need to be balanced. 

Past that we are human. And if you aren't going to get emotionally charged on the downside and failures, then you can't celebrate the wins and victories either! Yes, think about that! While that's a subject for another time, and in a small sense it is favorable advice, it is not the end-all.

There were some breaks in the 90's and 2000's to regroup, for sanity, and for just need. Trading and Learning to Trade are completely different and there are growing pains along the way. And through those time I began to learn that trading was NOT about the money. Putting money at the forefront only has disastrous endings. That's the biggest trap. Or at least it was for me back then, and still would be if I let it.

When I made it about the skill and the trade again I noticed my life was better and I realized that trading had taken first place. Trading is greedy like that! You life, health, relationships, family, and even employment in some cases, comes first!

There was a question on X the other day about bad habits and trading, and what bad habits are tied to. My response was they were all tied to one thing. Greed. 

Whether we want to admit it nor not, that's the biggest single trait that drives bad trading habits. Greed is way bigger than just being greedy. Greed forces you to play the same game this system plays. The system is greedy by nature and if you apply greed to battle the greedy, you will loose! It's that simple. The market scales always tip to the greedy side. 

Even if you don't see it, or understand it, it's greedy. And your own greed will suck you in. Get a handle on your greed and keep you life first place and let trading compliment, or enhance, your life as a tool, not a financial, or set of financial actions. You are not depositing to withdraw. 

You are working to mitigate risk and extract profit from a greed filled system. (and no I am not bashing any market, form, broker or anything. It's just fact. markets are greedy and fickle. Truth!) And most all traders have gotten caught up in it, especially starting out. I clearly remember thinking early on "the quicker I get this down pat, the quicker I learn, the bigger and better trades I can make and make." That's greed. Perhaps naive greed, but greed nonetheless.

The journey from learning to FOREX, to the OTC, to the Big Boards, To Futures didn't always come easy or without sacrifice, or failure. But that's how a trader paves the way you success! You absolutely have to put the work in to garner the reward.

And to be honest, you don't really need a lot of skill to be a trader, you need a good skillset, and skill is secondary to that. You need the skillset that keeps your life, health, well-being, and relationships first place as it should be that also includes the trading skillset.

I quit worrying about success rates and all the things some think are so important in valuing you performance as a trader a long time ago. For the most part that's bunk. You can win 85% of your trades and still blow an account, or lose all your money and go broke, so forget those measurements as far as I am concerned. Just learn to be good and build on that! And keep it SIMPLE!

There are some good folks who trade on X and they don't know it.......lol......but help remind me from time to time of where I came from and what matters. So for the edition of "me" and in a roundabout way reminding me of "my journey" (and failures) 😂.......................

I have to say a thanks for the posts the last few days that have, unknowingly to them, spurred me to reflect and my keep my perspective in-check to: @linzy_long_hold @cdntradegrljenn @iamJMinx and @paxtrader777  @traderchicago7 @BlueHogFutures

Anyway, rant over, perspective in check, and for me that's "Lather, Rinse, and Repeat." It doesn't matter the brand of the shampoo in the bottle, they are all designed to do the same thing. Just follow the directions!

Trading can be ridiculously funny, a wonderful life, and amazingly disappointing, because, well, it's trading!!

Tomorrow morning it's early morning grains and then hit the hogs.....unless they hit back, which hogs do sometimes! 🤣🤣

Happy Trading!!

text:
Kevin Garnett says he fired his agent after learning he rejected Minnesota’s $122,000,000 offer while on vacation. KG later signed an NBA record $126,000,000 contract

“I’m in Jamaica, and I’ll never forget this. I got the USA Today, I pop it open, the first joint says, ‘Garnett denies $122 million.’ And I’m like, ‘What the fuck.’ I had a bowl of fruit in my lap and I remember it spilled. I tapped shorty, ‘We gotta go.’ And I zoomed home”

“The problem was I never got to deny anything. The agent did. So the first thing I checked him about was, ‘Don’t be speaking for me.’ He was like, ‘This is how it goes. This is the process.’ And I was like, ‘Nah.’ I didn’t really like that so I fired him”

“Because my movement and me being able to speak for myself was huge for me. I didn’t want somebody speaking for me. I’m right here. I can say it. I probably would’ve taken the $122 million. But he was pushing me and really teaching me the business of how basketball works”

“He was like, ‘These are the incentives. What’s the vision you have for yourself. This is what we’re going to implement right here. Those things you just named. We’re going to put in flight time. We’re going to put in private charters. We’re going to put in the vacation’”

“We were making a wish list and then implementing it. I’ll say out of ten things, I got eight of them just because I asked for them. I had the leverage, on top of getting what I wanted. I actually wanted to be the one to say that I knew my worth and I went for it”

(via @KnuckleheadsPod ft. @KevinGarnett5KG)

text:
You leave a £150k job to build a startup. Then you pay yourself £40k while working twice as hard. Hopefully it will all be worthwhile on an exit. Or will it?

The first question that comes up is at the start is: can you pay yourself with dividends instead of a salary? That sounds much more tax-effective. It doesn't work. Watch the video for why.

Then, if things are going well and a chunky exit is on the horizon, how do you minimise tax on that? Should you leave the country? Should you do the Delaware flip and incorporate the company to the US? Can you move your shares into a trust?

I spoke with exit planning expert Naila Mirza about something founders leave far too late: how to get value out of the company you’re building.
In the early days, that means thinking about salary vs. dividends, pension contributions and the most tax-efficient way to pay yourself.

Then there’s the exit. The mistake is waiting until you have an offer on the table before thinking about tax, residency and how you’ll realise the value you’ve spent years creating. Exit planning shouldn’t start when you’re exiting, it should start years earlier.
 
A few years ago with Entrepreneur Relief, you paid just 10% capital gains tax on the first £10M you made selling your shares. But that's now whittled down to just £1M and 18% capital gains tax - a huge UK founder advantage, gone.

With the UK tax landscape becoming increasingly uncertain and periodic government talk of exit taxes, you need to start your exit planning way, way sooner.

Note that none of this is tax advice, and neither of us are tax specialists.

text:
Report of @HumanRightsCtte  into Human Rights and the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Is Published Today.

My last act as Chair of @UKParliament JCHR was to oversee the Inquiry and Report into Human Rights and the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence. This Report could not be more timely or important.

The unanimously agreed Report is published today and may be read at https://t.co/VPJCgV8hAK 

I was especially grateful to the Committee's team of clerks and advisers and for for the advice and help of ourSpecial Advisor Special Adviser, Professor Karen Yeung https://t.co/LmM1UzYPJA

Having served on the Committee since 2023 and, as chair since 2024, chairing over 60 sessions and meetings of the JCHR I have now stepped down as chair and from the Committee with @Alexsobel elected as the new chair. A new Crossbench Peer will be appointed to the Committee in October. It has been an honour to serve Parliament in this capacity.
---
Background:

We launched our inquiry in July 2025 in the context of wide public debate and concern about the growth and diversification of Artificial Intelligence (‘AI’). Our aim was to investigate the extent to which existing law and regulation was sufficient to protect human rights in the UK in the context of AI.

Important work has been undertaken or is being carried out in related fields by other Committees, including the House of Lords Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, the House of Lords Justice and Home Affairs Committee, the House of Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, the House of Lords AI Weapons Committee, and others. 

All touch on human rights impacts and have raised important issues. Because AI is a general purpose technology, we felt that our Committee, with its cross-cutting remit, was especially well placed to consider the wide-ranging impact of AI on human rights.

We received over 70 pieces of written evidence, and are grateful to all those who took the time to share their views, experiences and expertise with us. Over the course of ten oral evidence sessions we heard from senior academics, researchers, science communicators, civil society campaigners, policy bodies, legal experts, technology specialists and entrepreneurs, major technology firms, regulators charged with overseeing elements of AI use, and the Minister for AI. 

We are especially grateful to our Special Adviser, Professor Karen Yeung, Interdisciplinary Professorial Fellow in Law, Ethics and Informatics in the Birmingham Law School and the School for Computer Science at the University of Birmingham, for her advice and guidance.

In order to clearly set out the case for change, this report starts by explaining what artificial intelligence is and why we believe it raises vital human rights issues. We then discuss the existing legal and regulatory protections, and explain why we consider they are seriously lacking. Finally, we set out our proposals for comprehensive, tailored law and regulation to address these risks and protect human rights.

As our inquiry drew to a close, a new Prime Minister took office. The new administration acted immediately to make clear the importance it places on AI. Kanishka Narayan MP was appointed Minister of State (Minister for Artificial Intelligence) jointly in the Cabinet Office and the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade on 20 July 2026, having previously been Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State at the then Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, and Minister for AI Opportunities. He will attend Cabinet.1

The Committee considers that this increased prominence of AI within government offers an opportunity to drive economic growth while respecting rights, and makes our report timely. The continuity in this key portfolio also encourages us to believe that the evidence we took, and the conclusions we drew from it, remain relevant and useful to policy-making and public debate. We look forward to continuing to work with the Minister in his expanded role.

Finally, since our inquiry finished taking evidence, there have been many high-profile developments which illustrate the importance of the issues we examined. No report can keep pace with the accelerating change created by AI in our economy and society, and the Committee may revisit this area in future.
@andyburnham @KemiBadenoch @EdwardJDavey @Nigel_Farage @TimClementJone1 @LordSpeaker @CommonsSpeaker @UKHouseofLords @HouseofCommons

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, warns that swarms of rogue AI agents could take over the internet within the next six months, and cause hundreds of billions worth of damage. The JCHR Report is timely and its reciommendations require an urgenbt response.

text:
Technology gives precision. But beauty? It still flows through the sculptor’s touch.

Meet Viraj Khatavkar, a third-generation sculptor from Pune carrying his family’s 70-year legacy forward.

His grandfather was the first to craft a fiberglass Ganesh idol at Tulshibaug in 1975, after decades of handmaking Utsav Murtis as tall as 14 feet.

When asked to recreate Honaji Tarun Mandal’s 125-year-old Ganesh idol — a rare 21-inch piece showing the deity in a tilted wrestling pose.

Viraj knew precision by hand alone would be near impossible.

So he earned his Master’s in 3D Modelling & Reverse Engineering. Using scanners, software, and robotic carving, he turned the original into a stunning 3-foot Utsav Murti.

What usually takes 2.5 months by hand was finished in 1 month, without losing the intricate artistry.

“This smart work and technology offer maximum accuracy,” says Viraj.

And his journey goes beyond idols—on March 8, 2025, Viraj helped craft the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj statue unveiled in Tokyo—a proud Indo-Japan cultural milestone.

If you could preserve one tradition with new-age tech, what would it be? Share in the comments.

text:
Anguilla at a Glance

Anguilla is a small British Overseas Territory in the northeastern Caribbean, known for powder-white sand beaches, turquoise water, luxury resorts, and an unusually strong culinary reputation. It lies in the northern Lesser Antilles, directly north of Saint Martin/Sint Maarten and east of Puerto Rico.

📍 Location
Region: Eastern Caribbean, Leeward Islands
Size: About 35 square miles (91 km²)
Capital: The Valley
Population: Approximately 16,000 residents
Language: English
Currency: Eastern Caribbean Dollar (XCD), though U.S. dollars are widely accepted.
History

Anguilla was first settled by Indigenous peoples from South America thousands of years ago. The Amerindian inhabitants called the island Malliouhana, meaning "Sea Serpent."

Key periods include:

Indigenous settlement dating to roughly 2000 BC.
English colonization beginning in 1650.
Development of plantation agriculture, including cotton, tobacco, and sugar, with enslaved Africans providing much of the labor.
Emancipation of enslaved people in 1834.
The Anguilla Revolution in 1967, when residents resisted administration from St. Kitts-Nevis.
Anguilla became a separate British Overseas Territory in 1980.
People and Culture

Most Anguillians are of African descent, with cultural influences from African, British, and broader Caribbean traditions.

Cultural Highlights
Traditional sailboat racing is the national sport and a major point of pride.
Music includes reggae, calypso, soca, and local folk styles.
The annual Summer Festival features parades, races, concerts, and cultural celebrations.
The atmosphere is generally relaxed, upscale, and less crowded than destinations such as Aruba, Jamaica, or the Bahamas.
Cuisine

Anguilla is frequently called the**"Culinary Capital of the Caribbean."**

Must-Try Foods
Grilled spiny lobster
Conch fritters
Fresh snapper, mahi-mahi, and grouper
Goat dishes
Johnny cakes
Pigeon peas and rice
Seafood soups and stews
Rum-based drinks and local cocktails

The island has over 100 restaurants ranging from beach shacks to world-class fine dining.

Beaches: How Do They Rank?

Anguilla's beaches consistently appear among the best in the Caribbean and the world.

Recent Recognition
Shoal Bay East was ranked**#6 beach worldwide** and**#1 beach in North America and the Caribbean** in the 2026 World's 50 Best Beaches rankings.
Meads Bay and Rendezvous Bay also appeared among top Caribbean beaches.
USA Today's 10Best Awards have repeatedly ranked Anguilla beaches among the Caribbean's best.
Notable Beaches
Shoal Bay East
Meads Bay
Rendezvous Bay
Maundays Bay
Cove Bay

Many travel experts consider Anguilla's beaches the finest overall collection of beaches on a single Caribbean island.

Cost of a One-Week Vacation

These are realistic 2026-style estimates for a 7-night trip, excluding airfare unless noted.

Couple
Travel Style Approximate TotalBudget $2,500-$3,500
Mid-range $4,500-$7,000
Luxury $8,000-$20,000+

Typical mid-range breakdown:

Hotel: $250-$500/night
Food: $100-$200/day for two
Rental car/taxis: $300-$600/week
Activities: $200-$800
Family of 4
Travel Style Approximate TotalBudget $4,000-$6,000
Mid-range $7,500-$12,000
Luxury $12,000-$30,000+

Families often choose villas or condo-style accommodations, which can provide better value than multiple hotel rooms.

Airfare from the Continental U.S.

Prices vary by season, but these are typical round-trip ranges per person.

Departure Area Economy Premium Economy Business/FirstMiami/Fort Lauderdale $400-$800 $900-$1,400 $1,500-$3,000
New York/Boston $500-$1,000 $1,200-$2,000 $2,000-$5,000
Chicago/Dallas $600-$1,100 $1,300-$2,200 $2,200-$5,500
West Coast $700-$1,300 $1,600-$2,600 $3,000-$7,000

Travel during Christmas, New Year's, Presidents' Day, and spring break can increase prices substantially.

How Easy Is It to Get There?
Option 1: Fly Direct to Anguilla (Easiest)

Some U.S. cities have direct or near-direct service into Clayton J. Lloyd International Airport (AXA), though options are limited.

Pros

No ferry
Simplest arrival

Cons

Fewer flights
Usually more expensive
Option 2: Fly to St. Maarten (Most Common)

Most American visitors fly into Princess Juliana Airport (SXM) in Sint Maarten and then continue to Anguilla.

You then choose:

Ferry
Ferry crossing: approximately 20-25 minutes
Taxi required between airport and ferry terminal
Usually the lowest-cost option.
Private Boat Transfer
Departs near the airport
Faster and more convenient
More expensive.
Regional Flight
8-10 minute flight from SXM to AXA
Most seamless option after flying into Sint Maarten
More expensive than the ferry.
Bottom Line

For many travelers, Anguilla is one of the Caribbean's most beautiful islands, with:

Some of the world's highest-rated beaches
Excellent restaurants
Very safe, relaxed atmosphere
Less crowding than many Caribbean destinations
Strong luxury accommodation selection

The tradeoff is that it is more expensive and slightly harder to reach than destinations such as Cancun, Punta Cana, Aruba, or Jamaica. Most U.S. visitors either fly directly into Anguilla or connect through Sint Maarten via ferry or a short regional flight.

For a comfortable week-long vacation, I'd recommend budgeting approximately $5,500-$8,000 for a couple and $8,000-$14,000 for a family of four, including airfare from most U.S. cities.

As this week marks a "Super Central Bank Week," overall market sentiment remains cautious.

A pivotal Federal Reserve interest rate decision is scheduled for Wednesday. Until this major event unfolds, most asset classes are likely to remain range-bound with choppy price action as traders await a clear direction; directional momentum is currently limited.

Trading strategies should focus on range-based swings, patiently waiting for the data release to trigger a breakout and define the trend.

The US Dollar Index opened the week by extending its corrective upward trend, briefly breaking above last week's highs. While the dollar is showing short-term bullish corrective strength, the sustainability of this rise is questionable given the proximity of the policy decision.

For intraday trading, the priority is to monitor the resistance level around 99.3; failure to break through suggests a likely return to range-bound oscillation. If the 98.9 support level holds, the short-term bullish bias remains intact while awaiting data guidance.

Gold opened lower this morning and traded weakly; after a brief rally to near $4,355, the price faced resistance and pulled back. Short-term bullish momentum appears exhausted, and the market is exhibiting a typical range-bound consolidation pattern.

Attention is currently focused on the $4,320–$4,310 support zone; if this holds, the price will likely oscillate within the $4,310–$4,360 range for the time being.

A decisive break below $4,310 would extend the short-term weakness, potentially leading to a retest of Friday's lows; however, stabilizing at lower levels would still offer opportunities for a corrective rebound trade.

If the price re-establishes itself above the $4,355 level, the short-term bearish pattern would end, opening up further upside potential toward the $4,380–$4,400 resistance zone.

After stalling at highs, the market has returned to a pattern of range-bound consolidation.

Overall, gold has entered a quiet, range-bound phase ahead of the data release, characterized by poor momentum continuity for both bulls and bears. Traders should avoid chasing rallies or panic-selling, instead focusing on range-based trading anchored to key high and low points.

Special pujas, abhishekams, floral decorations and other rituals were performed at the temple, with devotees standing in long queues for darshan.

text:
THE DIVINE CONNECTIONS IN THE PATTERN OF TRUTH

In the doctrine, The Element Called Faith, we learned about the main divine connections we are looking for when observing Christ in the pattern He set for our faith.

These connections each hold a pattern or model for faith we are to follow:

1)  R/W - The Record and the Witness - God set this pattern for our faith through Jesus Christ. The record is the blueprint of truth (the doctrine of Christ), which is being set in your heart through the stewardship of a living apostle. The witness speaks of the Father sending the Holy Spirit to enter into the record and into your heart to bear witness to Christ in you. God set this pattern in Christ, the Firstborn. If we observe Christ in the Record and the Witness, God beholds His Son in us and says, “This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased,” and our faith is accepted of God because God accepts Jesus Christ. Our faith is perfect because Christ is perfect.
 
2)  The three R’s - Revelation, Resistance, and Reward - God set this pattern for the cycles of our growth. While on earth Jesus demonstrated this path for our faith; He set the example as the Firstborn. If we observe Christ in this pattern, God beholds His Son in us and says, “This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased,” and our faith is accepted of God because God accepts Jesus Christ. Our faith is perfect because Christ is perfect.
 
3)  V.H.P. - Vulnerability, Humiliation, and Pain - God set this pattern first in Jesus who restricted the expression of His divinity in that He did not use His divine power to please Himself. He suffered the contradiction of sinners against Himself and endured the pain of the cross. If we observe Christ in this pattern and also endure the contradiction according to faith, God beholds His Son in us and says, “This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased,” and our faith is accepted of God because God accepts Jesus Christ. Our faith is perfect because Christ is perfect.
 
4)  D/R - The Death and Resurrection of Jesus Christ - Jesus willingly laid down His life that He might take it up again according to the promise of life that is in God the Father (Jn.10:17). We do the same through our cycles of growth, following the example of the Firstborn, enduring the death of the old man and embracing the divine life according to the power of Christ. If we observe Christ in this pattern, God beholds His Son in us and says, “This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased,” and our faith is accepted of God because God accepts Jesus Christ. Our faith is perfect because Christ is perfect.
 
5)  Holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens - Heb.7:26, “For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens.” Jesus Christ set this pattern for us to follow. If we observe Christ in this pattern, God beholds His Son in us and says, “This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased,” and our faith is accepted of God because God accepts Jesus Christ. Our faith is perfect because Christ is perfect.
 
6)  The Priesthood - Heb.7:17, “For he testifieth, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec.” Jesus Christ set a pattern for our priesthood that is not according to Levi, but by selection outside of Moses (through Melchisedec). If we observe Christ in His priesthood, we will offer the spiritual sacrifices at His new altar, in His new temple, worshipping God in Spirit and in truth. God beholds His Son in us and says, “This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased,” and our faith is accepted of God because God accepts Jesus Christ. Our faith is perfect because Christ is perfect.
Through reflection on this pattern set in the doctrine of Christ, we can then exercise our faith in God; we are following “the faith” (the doctrine of Christ) and following Jesus through His example, pleasing God.

We can take to covenant the following things by recognizing the pattern Jesus set in Himself for faith: 
👉 the scriptures (Bible and other writings) 
👉 dream symbolisms (and other manifold graces)
👉 allegories in nature 
👉 allegories in the knowledge of civilization and things constructed from the knowledge of civilization

God inspired/created these things and put them in this dimension making earth a reflection-stimulating environment for His children.

For today's activity, identify the pattern set in Jesus in the allegories around you. What does the window symbolize? Can you see the hidden pattern in Christ? What secret does the tree hold? 

In the following activities we will learn to identify the pattern in the Bible and in dream symbolisms.

text:
We will be honest about jurisdiction. Rivers State does not control every port, petroleum asset, federal regulator or private concessionaire. We will use our own powers fully and cooperate lawfully where others must act.

This is therefore the covenant I offer you, an administration that can be judged by what works, what reaches the people and whether government tells you the truth about its progress.

Our manifesto is not a catalogue of wishes. Every Local Government Area has a productive role to play. Our statewide systems, power, logistics, skills, food and fisheries, digital services, environmental protection and accountable government must connect communities to the larger Rivers economy. Women, young people, persons with disabilities and people outside political networks must be able to see fairer routes into work, enterprise and public services.

We will use public money with discipline.

The State budget should provide essential public services, prepare serious projects and build infrastructures that enables production. Government should not pretend that ownership is the only path to progress when a commercial project can attract private development financing and professional operatorship.

Useful inherited projects and lawful obligations will be judged on evidence, not on who started them.

We will also treat environmental protection as part of the core duty of government. From riverine communities facing pollution and coastal risk to urban communities facing flooding, unsafe water and failing drainage systems. Our people deserve credible information, faster response and practical protection.

Development that destroys the conditions for life and livelihood is not transformation.

I do not ask for a blank cheque. I ask for the opportunity to serve and be judged by the evidence we publish and the difference our people can see in their lives and communities.

At the end of our tenure, ask whether politics is safer; institutions are more trusted; priority projects have moved beyond announcement; whether small and medium scale enterprises work better in supported areas; whether tourism, the creative sector and blue economy have been given their proper places; whether more people have moved from training into real work; whether environmental monitoring and response are stronger; and whether government tells you clearly what succeeded, what failed and what must be corrected.

I am not asking you merely to support Dumo Lulu-Briggs. I am asking you to join us to return political power to service. Let us choose purpose over capture, work over noise, competence over permanent conflict and prosperity over poverty. Let us build a Rivers State in which every community can say: the State sees us, hears us, respects us and works for us.

Together, by the grace of God, we can Reset Rivers State.

I have set my sights on where our collective strides can take us.

I ask for your trust, and I pledge myself to your service.

Yours ceaselessly,

@DumoLuluBrigg
NDC Governorship Candidate for Rivers State | 2027

text:
9/

Large universities run a related pipeline, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭.

The Day-1 CPT model — hybrid master’s, work authorized from the beginning, minimal campus time, recruiter-driven enrollment — is concentrated in the smaller schools discussed above.

NYU, Columbia, Northeastern, USC, ASU, Illinois, Purdue, Michigan and the major Texas publics generally do not sell that package.

Students there usually attend conventional degree programs. Northeastern’s CPT-heavy co-op model, for example, is a longstanding academic design used by domestic students too.

𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞-𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐩𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐢𝐬𝐧’𝐭 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 “𝐬𝐜𝐡𝐨𝐨𝐥, 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐚 𝐣𝐨𝐛” 𝐞𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫.

F-1 graduates get 𝟏𝟐 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐎𝐏𝐓. A qualifying STEM degree adds 𝟐𝟒 more.

That means up to 𝟑 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝐅-𝟏 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐬 before H-1B.

For F-1 workers still treated as nonresident aliens for tax purposes, practical-training wages are generally exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes. During that period, both worker and employer avoid those payroll taxes.

𝐒𝐓𝐄𝐌 𝐎𝐏𝐓 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐬𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐲 “𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐬𝐭𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞.”

It depends on the CIP code assigned to the degree and whether that code appears on DHS’s STEM list.

Beyond core engineering, biology, math and physical science, the list now includes Business Analytics, Financial Analytics, Data Analytics, I-O Psychology, Landscape Architecture, Institutional Research and Environmental/Natural Resource Economics.

After the 2023 update, DHS received 𝟏𝟑𝟑 nominations covering 68 fields for addition — and 𝐳𝐞𝐫𝐨 for removal.

That changes the product:

𝐧𝐨𝐧-𝐒𝐓𝐄𝐌 → 𝟏𝟐 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬 𝐎𝐏𝐓
𝐒𝐓𝐄𝐌 → 𝐮𝐩 𝐭𝐨 𝟑𝟔 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬

So the CIP classification can add 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 to the value of a degree.

Universities therefore have an incentive to offer and market STEM-designated professional master’s programs. The curriculum can be legitimate and rigorous; the immigration value is still part of what is being sold.

In ICE’s 2024 data, master’s students were roughly 𝟒𝟔.𝟓% 𝐨𝐟 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐧 𝐬𝐭𝐮𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 — larger than the bachelor’s share.

A famous university can have an extremely selective undergraduate college while operating much larger professional master’s programs with different admissions economics.

UNT and UT Arlington are useful boundary cases: huge international graduate populations and OPT footprints, without being Day-1 CPT schools.

A qualifying U.S. master’s also gives access to the separate 𝟐𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎-𝐩𝐞𝐫-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐇-𝟏𝐁 𝐚𝐝𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐝-𝐝𝐞𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧.

So the degree can carry both a longer OPT runway 𝐚𝐧𝐝 another H-1B selection opportunity.

Two different products:

𝐃𝐚𝐲-𝟏 𝐂𝐏𝐓: 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 → 𝐡𝐲𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐝 𝐦𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫’𝐬 → 𝐂𝐏𝐓 → 𝐎𝐏𝐓 → 𝐇-𝟏𝐁

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐲: 𝐦𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫’𝐬 → 𝐎𝐏𝐓 / 𝐒𝐓𝐄𝐌 𝐎𝐏𝐓 → 𝐇-𝟏𝐁

A Purdue or Columbia graduate who attended classes and earned a real degree is 𝐧𝐨𝐭 equivalent to someone enrolling at a satellite center principally to maintain work authorization.

But “meritocratic” still flattens three different questions:

𝟏. 𝐀𝐜𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐢𝐜 𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐭 — did the student earn the degree?
𝟐. 𝐀𝐝𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 — how selective is that particular master’s program?
𝟑. 𝐋𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐫-𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐫𝐮𝐥𝐞𝐬 — OPT length, STEM-CIP status, payroll-tax treatment and the H-1B master’s cap.

A student can be talented and legitimately earn a difficult degree 𝐚𝐧𝐝 still enter a labor market whose rules give that degree immigration value beyond the education itself.

𝐒𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐫-𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐢𝐭.
𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐜𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐢𝐜 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭.
𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐢𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐢𝐧 𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐡.
