RETURN OF INHERITANCE 

There was a country that used to treat its people like owners.

That was not a slogan. It was how the place was built. Families claimed land and expected their children to keep it. Hamilton wanted shops and mills here so the yield would stay here. Lincoln’s Homestead Act put title in ordinary hands. McKinley and the old tariff men said if a foreign workshop could undercut an American one, the American house would slowly empty. For a long time the deal was simple. You work. You build. The profit does not all leave by the docks.

Then the deal flipped.

Factories went overseas because labor was cheaper and the finance houses liked the margin. Towns that made steel, cloth, tools, and cars became warehouses for other people’s goods. Washington still collected taxes. Banks still collected interest. Shoppers got lower prices and called that winning, while the job that used to pay for the house left with the product. The citizen became a customer. The country became a platform. That is real history, not a parable. You can walk the boarded main streets and count it.

Older still is the biblical picture people reach for when they see that hollowing. In Israel the land was not supposed to be sold off the family forever. Every so often debts were released and fields came home. They called it jubilee. It was not a stimulus check. It was a law against becoming a tenant on your own ground. America never ran that calendar. It ran a rougher version: property, wages, and a border around the market.

That is what “return of inheritance” means in plain speech. Not a miracle envelope. The fruit of the country coming back to the people who live in it after a long season of managers, offshoring, and a government that treated households like a cost.

Tonight in Dallas, Trump put a number on that hunger. If Republicans keep the House and the Senate, he said, every adult citizen gets a $5,000 dividend, and it has to be spent in the United States. Hear it clearly. It is a campaign condition, not a check already in the mail. He has talked tariff dividends before. Those checks have not shown up. Five thousand dollars times every adult is a huge bill. It has to come from tariffs, growth, cuts, or new borrowing. If it is borrowed, it is not inheritance. It is a loan with a flag on it.

Still, the shape of the offer is the old American sentence: you are a shareholder in this house again. Spend the yield at home. Do not send it back down the road that emptied the towns.

That is the story without the fog.
Owners, then tenants, then a promise to put some of the fruit back on the table.
History will decide if the promise becomes a payment.
The hunger is already historical.

text:
American journalist's nephew on the Long March: "Faith, courage and determination"

This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, a military maneuver carried out by the Red Army from 1934 to 1936. The legendary journey was later recorded in the book "Red Star Over China" by the American journalist Edgar Snow. It offered the world a rare, firsthand account of China at a time when the country was largely misunderstood by the West.  

Eric Foster, Edgar Snow's nephew by marriage, has followed in his uncle's footsteps, retracing the Long March route several times. He shares his memories and reflections on the historic journey. 
#longmarch90

text:
The Guardian: Pregnant Palestinian Woman Killed by Israeli Fire Near Khan Younis

The Guardian reported that Iman Shalouf, 27 and nearly eight months pregnant, died on Saturday of a head wound after Israeli gunfire while she sat in her family’s tent in al-Mawasi, south of Khan Younis, according to her relatives and paramedics. The Israeli military told the paper it was looking into the incident. Gaza’s health ministry counted 10 killed and 56 wounded in attacks over 48 hours, despite a fragile ceasefire in place since October 2025.

What the Family Said

Her mother-in-law, Wathfa Abu Mashi, said in a video interview that she heard gunfire while praying, then found Iman covered in blood inside the tent. She was taken to Nasser Hospital. Doctors at first detected the unborn baby’s heartbeat; hours later both she and the fetus died. The family had chosen the name Ayoub; the birth was due in November. Funeral prayers were held at the hospital. They were buried side by side in Khan Younis. Her husband, Ismail Abu Mashi, asked: “Where is the ceasefire they keep talking about? People are dying here every day.”

Strikes Across Two Days

The Guardian, citing the ministry, said four members of one family were killed in Beit Lahiya on Thursday: Momen Ahmed, his wife Haneen Saleh, and their daughters Lana, 12, and Bana, 8. On Friday six people were killed in Khan Younis and Gaza City, including a man who died of earlier wounds. A displaced persons’ tent in al-Mawasi was shelled on Saturday, wounding nine, the Palestinian Red Crescent said. On Sunday a vehicle was hit in Tel al-Hawa and passengers on a bus carrying women and children were injured.

Beyond a Single Incident

Unicef counted seven children killed between 23 August and 2 September. Médecins Sans Frontières said airstrikes were continuing, that 18 evacuation orders were issued between 6 and 9 September, and that a building less than 250 feet from an MSF clinic was struck. The UN humanitarian office said most of Gaza’s 2.1 million people are heading into the rainy season in overcrowded displacement sites. The ministry put the toll since the 11 October 2025 ceasefire at 1,369 killed and 4,627 wounded, and at least 73,783 killed since 7 October 2023. That last figure comes from a Gaza authority. The army has not yet offered a detailed counter-account of Iman’s death.

text:
Bhagavad Gita 11 . 32
The story begins long before any chariot rolled onto the dusty plain of Kurukshetra. In the ancient Kuru kingdom whose capital was Hastinapura, a city of palaces and assembly halls on the banks of the Ganga in what is now northern India, two branches of the same royal family had grown into bitter rivals. King Shantanu had a son named Bhishma who took a terrible vow of lifelong celibacy so that his father could marry the woman he desired. That vow left the throne to pass through other sons. Dhritarashtra was born blind. His younger brother Pandu became king for a time but died young after a curse. Pandu’s five sons, the Pandavas, were raised in the palace alongside Dhritarashtra’s hundred sons, the Kauravas, whose eldest was Duryodhana. The Pandavas were Yudhishthira the eldest and most righteous, Bhima of immense strength, Arjuna the peerless archer, and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva. Their mother Kunti had also borne an earlier son in secret, Karna, who grew up believing himself the child of a charioteer and later became Duryodhana’s closest friend and fiercest champion. Krishna, born in Mathura to Vasudeva and Devaki of the Yadava clan, was cousin to the Pandavas because Kunti was Vasudeva’s sister. He had already lived a life of wonders in Vrindavan and later ruled from Dwaraka on the western sea. Traditional calculations place these events near the close of the Dvapara Yuga, with the great war itself dated by many traditional astronomers and later commentators around 3138 or 3102 BCE, though modern scholars looking at archaeology and genealogies often suggest dates closer to 1000 or 900 BCE. The land itself was called Kurukshetra after an ancestor king named Kuru who had performed penance there so that the ground would become a field of dharma, a place where righteous action would bear special fruit.

Duryodhana could not bear the thought that Yudhishthira might inherit the throne. After the Pandavas built their own magnificent city of Indraprastha, Duryodhana and his uncle Shakuni invited Yudhishthira to a game of dice in the assembly hall of Hastinapura. Yudhishthira, whose one weakness was gambling, lost everything: his wealth, his kingdom, his brothers, himself, and finally Draupadi their shared wife. Dushasana dragged Draupadi into the court by her hair and tried to strip her before the assembled kings and elders. Bhishma, Drona the teacher, and even Dhritarashtra sat frozen. Only when Draupadi called upon Krishna did her sari become endless so that she could not be disrobed. The elders at last forced a compromise: the Pandavas would spend twelve years in forest exile and a thirteenth year living in disguise. If they were discovered in that thirteenth year they would have to repeat the exile. They went. They wandered the forests, faced demons and sages, and in the thirteenth year hid in the kingdom of Virata. When the term ended they asked for their kingdom back. Duryodhana refused even five villages.

Krishna himself went to Hastinapura as messenger of peace. He stood in the same assembly hall and asked Duryodhana to return Indraprastha or at least grant those five villages so that cousins need not slaughter one another. Duryodhana answered that he would not give land enough to drive a needle through. He even ordered Krishna seized. In that moment Krishna briefly displayed a portion of his divine majesty, a blazing form that filled the hall with light so intense that most present had to cover their eyes. Duryodhana still would not yield. Krishna left, met Karna on the road, and told him the secret of his birth, offering him the chance to stand with his true brothers. Karna refused out of loyalty to Duryodhana who had given him a kingdom when the world treated him as low-born. Both sides then gathered their allies. Arjuna went to Dwaraka and chose Krishna himself rather than Krishna’s vast Yadava army. Duryodhana, arriving first but sitting at Krishna’s head while Arjuna sat at his feet, received the army. Krishna agreed to drive Arjuna’s chariot but would not take up weapons. The two hosts, said to number millions, marched to the sacred plain of Kurukshetra in the land between the ancient Sarasvati and Drishadvati rivers, in the region now called Haryana. The spot later known as Jyotisar, a few kilometres from the modern town of Kurukshetra, is remembered as the exact place where the conversation unfolded beneath a banyan tree.

On the morning the armies faced each other, conches sounded. Arjuna, standing in his chariot with Krishna holding the reins, asked his friend to drive between the two lines so he could see whom he must fight. Krishna did so. Arjuna looked across the field and saw Bhishma his grandfather who had rocked him as a child, Drona who had taught him to string the bow Gandiva, his own cousins, uncles, teachers, and friends. His limbs grew weak. His mouth went dry. His body trembled. His hair stood on end. The great bow slipped from his hands. He sank onto the chariot seat and said he would not fight. What good was a kingdom bought with the blood of those he loved? Better to live as a beggar than to kill his own people. Better to let the sons of Dhritarashtra slay him unarmed. This was not fear of death. Arjuna had faced gods and demons. It was the sudden collision of kshatriya duty with the love and pity that bound him to his family. He could not see how slaughtering his elders could be dharma.

Krishna, who knew the larger design that the earth itself was groaning under the weight of adharma and that this war had been prepared across many lives, began to speak. He told Arjuna that the soul is never born and never dies, that it merely changes bodies as a man changes clothes. Grief for those who must die is therefore misplaced. A warrior’s duty is to fight a righteous war without attachment to victory or defeat, offering the action itself to the divine. He taught the path of selfless action, the path of knowledge, the path of devotion. He described his own glories scattered through creation: he is the taste in water, the light in the sun and moon, the sacred syllable Om, the strength of the strong who are free of passion. After hearing all this Arjuna’s mind was still not completely at rest. He said he believed everything Krishna had said, yet he longed to see with his own eyes the divine form that contained all those glories. If Krishna thought him worthy, would he reveal that imperishable cosmic self?

Krishna answered that ordinary human eyes could not behold it. He therefore granted Arjuna divine vision, the divya chakshu. Then the familiar dark-skinned charioteer with the peacock feather in his hair vanished into something no language can fully hold. Sanjaya, sitting far away in Hastinapura beside the blind king Dhritarashtra and gifted by Vyasa with the power to see the battlefield as if he stood upon it, described what happened. The form that appeared had countless mouths and countless eyes, countless wondrous aspects. It wore divine garlands and garments, was anointed with divine fragrances, and held many celestial weapons raised. It was infinite, facing every direction at once. If a thousand suns rose together in the sky their brilliance might hint at a fraction of that radiance. Within that single body Arjuna saw the entire universe with all its divisions gathered in one place: all the gods, hosts of every kind of being, Brahma seated upon his lotus, Shiva, the sages, the shining serpents. He saw the twelve Adityas, the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the two Ashvins, the forty-nine Maruts, and marvels never shown before. There was no beginning, no middle, no end. Arms and bellies and faces and eyes multiplied without limit. The space between heaven and earth and all the directions was filled by that one being.

Then the vision darkened into terror. The mouths became blazing furnaces with terrible tusks. Arjuna saw the sons of Dhritarashtra, Bhishma, Drona, Karna, and the other great warriors of both armies rushing into those mouths like rivers racing to the ocean or moths flying into a flame. Some were already crushed between the teeth. The three worlds trembled. Celestial beings cried out and took refuge. Arjuna’s own hair stood on end again, this time from awe and fear rather than grief. He bowed with joined palms and praised the form as the supreme Brahman, the refuge of all, the protector of eternal dharma, yet he could no longer bear the sight. He asked who this terrible being was, for it no longer looked like his friend Krishna.

The voice that answered said: Time I am, the great destroyer of worlds, now engaged in destroying. Even without Arjuna these warriors would cease to exist. They have already been slain by this arrangement. Arjuna was only the instrument. Therefore he should rise, fight, win glory, and enjoy the kingdom that awaited him. The words landed like a command from the structure of the universe itself. Arjuna, still trembling, begged forgiveness for any time he had treated Krishna too familiarly, as cousin or friend, and pleaded to see again the gentle form he knew. Krishna then withdrew the cosmic vision and first appeared in the four-armed form of Vishnu holding conch, discus, mace and lotus, then returned to the two-armed, smiling charioteer whom Arjuna loved. He told Arjuna that this particular full revelation of the universal form had never been shown to anyone before. Only by undivided devotion could such a form be seen, known, and entered.

Sanjaya finished his report to Dhritarashtra. The blind king sat in his palace knowing that the war his son had chosen could not now be stopped, that the very ground of Kurukshetra had already been claimed by a power larger than any army. Arjuna picked up Gandiva. The conches sounded again. The eighteen-day slaughter began, but the warrior who lifted his bow that morning was no longer the man who had dropped it. He had seen that every life on that field, including his own, already belonged to the one who stood beside him holding the reins.

The first lesson is the collapse that happens when Arjuna asks Krishna to drive the chariot into the open space between the two armies so he can look at the men he is about to face and then cannot stand what he sees. He recognizes Bhishma who raised the princes, Drona who put the bow in his hands, cousins he grew up with, teachers, uncles, and friends standing in the opposite ranks, and his body answers before his mind can argue. His limbs weaken, his mouth dries, he trembles, his hair stands, the great bow Gandiva slides from his grip, and he sits down in the chariot saying he will not fight because a kingdom won by killing his own people is not worth having and it would be better to be slain unarmed than to become the slayer of those he loves. What is being taught in that exact moment is that a feeling which looks like mercy can be attachment wearing a noble face. You are meant to take away that the heart will often call its own paralysis compassion so that it does not have to become the person who lives after the hard act is done. Reading this part is meant to make you sit with the difference between not wanting anyone to suffer and refusing a duty because the people who will suffer have your name, your memory, and your childhood inside them. The lesson is not that family love is wrong. The lesson is that family love, when it is allowed to veto every demand of dharma, turns the warrior into someone who protects his own tenderness at the expense of a larger order that has already been broken by greed and humiliation and broken promises. You are meant to notice how reasonable Arjuna sounds. He does not say he is afraid of dying. He says victory will taste like ash. He says the elders should not be killed for land. Those sentences can be true in another life and still be false in this one, because the field he is sitting on is already the consequence of years of refusal to return what was taken. The takeaway is that you must learn to test a beautiful refusal. Ask whether the refusal leaves injustice in place while you keep your hands clean. Ask whether you are grieving the coming deaths or grieving the loss of a world in which you never had to be the one who ends something. The story places this lesson first because nothing else in the teaching can land while the hearer still believes that not acting is the same as doing no harm.

The teaching that follows is spoken while Arjuna is still sitting in that wrecked posture and Krishna begins to tell him that the one who thinks he kills and the one who thinks he is killed are both mistaken, because the self that wears a body is not born and does not die when the body falls. The part of the story you need is the answer to the grief that treats Bhishma and Drona as if their entire reality were the forms standing in armor across the grass. What is being taught is that mourning the garment as though it were the wearer makes every necessary change look like murder. You are meant to take away a way of seeing death that does not cancel love but stops love from becoming a demand that time stand still. Reading this is meant to loosen the panic that says if this person leaves this shape then everything that passed between you is erased. The lesson is that the life you honored in them was never identical with the flesh you are afraid to injure. You are meant to feel how this teaching can be misused by the cruel and how the text itself refuses that misuse by never telling Arjuna that the coming deaths do not matter. They matter as events in the world. They do not matter as proof that the soul has been destroyed. The takeaway is a double discipline. Do not hide from the cost. Do not inflate the cost into the claim that the eternal was in your power to save or to ruin. When you read the words about changing bodies the way a person changes clothes you are meant to remember the specific clothes on that field, the grandfather, the teacher, the cousin, so that the philosophy does not float away into a general consolation. It is meant to be applied to the exact faces that made the bow fall.

Another lesson lives in the long stretch of instruction that tells Arjuna to perform his own duty as a warrior without clinging to whether the duty produces a kingdom, praise, or a quiet conscience. The story part is the argument that a kshatriya who abandons a righteous fight out of softness earns neither heaven nor honor and that action offered without hunger for a private result does not bind the doer the way selfish action does. What is being taught is that the poison is not in the drawing of the bow. The poison is in the sentence I must control what the drawing of the bow will mean for me. You are meant to take away a method of work that still uses skill, courage, planning, and full effort, yet hands the fruit away so that winning cannot make you swollen and losing cannot make you feel that the act was empty. Reading this is meant to confront the habit of refusing a task because you cannot guarantee that you will still like yourself when it is finished. The lesson says you were never authorized to like yourself more than the duty required of your station and your moment. You are meant to see that Arjuna’s wish to become a beggar rather than a king of ashes is still a wish about his own story. He wants a version of himself that remains innocent. The teaching answers that innocence purchased by desertion is not innocence. It is a different kind of claim on the outcome. The takeaway is that you can aim with all your strength and still refuse to use the aim as a mirror. Do the work because it is the work that belongs to you in this configuration of the world, not because the work will leave you looking like the person you prefer to be.

The lesson deepens when Arjuna, after hearing that all beauty and power in the worlds are only sparks of a greater splendor, asks to see the form that holds those sparks if Krishna judges him able to bear it. The story part is that request and the granting of divine sight because ordinary eyes cannot take in what is about to appear. What is being taught is that trust which remains only verbal is still incomplete. Hearing that the friend is more than a friend is not the same as being shown the scale on which the friend exists. You are meant to take away that a teaching can be accepted with the mouth and still leave the imagination in charge of how large the truth is allowed to become. Reading the request is meant to show the courage and the danger of asking to see. Arjuna does not demand the vision as a right. He asks if he is fit. The lesson is that fitness is given, not seized, and that the gift of seeing is also the gift of being unmade by what is seen. You are meant to notice that Krishna does not scold the desire. He warns that the present eyes are not enough and then he changes the eyes. The takeaway is that some truths cannot be reached by rearranging the thoughts you already have.  When you read this passage you are meant to ask what in you is still insisting on seeing the divine only in the shapes that keep you comfortable.

Then the form is shown and Arjuna sees in one body the gathered universe, gods, sages, serpents, Brahma on the lotus, worlds without a visible edge, countless faces and arms and eyes, radiance compared to a thousand suns risen together. The lesson in that sight is that the one who has been speaking from the driver’s seat is not a wise companion who happens to know philosophy. He is the place in which the philosophy and the field and the armies already stand. You are meant to take away the end of the habit of locating the sacred in a separate room from politics, kinship, weather, and death. Reading the description is meant to overwhelm the part of the mind that keeps a small Krishna for friendship and a large abstract principle for religion. They are not two. The takeaway is that intimacy with the person beside you does not shrink when the person is revealed as the container of everything. It becomes an intimacy that can no longer pretend the world is a backdrop for your private story. You are meant to feel wonder first, the hair standing from astonishment rather than from the earlier grief, because the text itself moves through wonder before it moves through fear. The lesson is that awe is a form of knowledge. It is the knowledge that your map was too small.

The teaching turns when the same form shows blazing mouths and the warriors of both sides, including the very men whose presence made Arjuna drop his bow, rushing into those mouths like moths into fire or rivers into the sea, some already crushed in the teeth. The story part is Arjuna’s terror, the three worlds trembling, the confession that his mind is unstable, and the question of who this being is because it no longer resembles the friend. What is being taught is that the divine includes the ending of things and will not let you love only the preserving half. You are meant to take away that destruction is not a failure of the order. It is one of the ways the order keeps itself from rotting in place. Reading the devouring mouths is meant to break the wish for a god who never concludes a story. The lesson does not ask you to enjoy the mouths. It asks you to stop calling them someone else’s problem. The takeaway is that a faith which can bear only the gentle face will eventually deny half of what happens on the earth and then call that denial devotion. You are meant to sit with Arjuna’s fear long enough to recognize it as the fear of discovering that the beloved is also Time. The text makes him say he cannot bear the sight so that you will not pretend you would have borne it easily. The lesson is humility before a reality that is not obligated to remain pretty for you.

The words spoken from that form teach that Time has already marked the men for ending and that Arjuna is to stand up and become the instrument, the nimitta, through which what is already decided takes a visible path. The story part is the command to fight and win the kingdom because the slaying is not finally his authorship. What is being taught is a release from the fantasy of being the first cause and a demand to remain the responsible means. You are meant to take away both the lightening and the weight. The lightening is that you do not have to carry the universe’s decision as if you invented it. The weight is that walking away does not cancel the decision. It only leaves the decision without a willing hand. Reading this is meant to correct two opposite errors. One error is the pride that says I am the slayer and therefore I am mighty. The other error is the pride that says I will not be the slayer and therefore I am pure. Both treat the self as the center of the event. The lesson places the self inside an event that is larger than the self and then tells the self to work anyway. The takeaway is that instrumentality is not passivity. An instrument that refuses to move is still making a choice about the shape of the hour. You are meant to apply this wherever you have stalled because you cannot stand to be the one whose name is attached to a necessary loss.

After the terror Arjuna praises, asks pardon for every time he treated Krishna too casually as cousin and friend, and begs to see again the form he can endure. The story part is the withdrawal of the cosmic vision, the brief appearance of the four-armed figure with conch, discus, mace and lotus, and the return of the two-armed charioteer. What is being taught is that the infinite is not the final address at which a human being is meant to live without a face to love. You are meant to take away that knowledge of scale should send you back into relationship, not out of it. Reading the plea and the return is meant to show that surrender is not the erasure of the person you know. It is the same person received without the illusion that he is small. The lesson is that devotion needs a form it can speak to after it has been broken by a form it could not speak to. The takeaway is permission to want the familiar face & a warning not to use that want as an excuse to forget what the familiar face contains. You are meant to notice that Krishna does not leave Arjuna stranded in fear. The vision is given and then it is gathered back so that action can begin from love rather than from panic. The teaching says the highest knowledge of that form is reached through undivided devotion, which means the way forward is not more spectacle.

A last lesson sits in the fact that none of this is happening in a private room. Sanjaya is seeing it by the gift of Vyasa and telling it to Dhritarashtra who sits blind in Hastinapura while his sons wait on the field. The story part is the outer frame of the telling, a king who receives a complete account of the teaching and the vision and still remains the father of the refusal that made the war unavoidable. What is being taught is that hearing a truth is not the same as being altered by it. You are meant to take away the uncomfortable measure of yourself as a listener. Arjuna is changed because the crisis is his and he asks to be taught and he consents to see. Dhritarashtra is informed and stays where his attachment to Duryodhana has always kept him. the frame is meant to ask whether you are the man in the chariot or the man in the palace who wants news without transformation. The lesson is that a teaching can be perfect & still fail in a heart whose treasure is the success of its own side. 

What you are meant to carry from the whole movement is a single way of standing inside a moment when the right action will injure what you love. You are meant to remember the dropped bow so that you do not mistake paralysis for virtue. You are meant to remember the teaching of the unkillable self so that you do not treat bodies as the whole of persons. You are meant to remember action without clinging so that you do not demand a clean story as payment for doing your work. You are meant to remember the request for the form so that you do not stop at agreeable words. You are meant to remember the thousand suns and the gathered worlds so that you do not keep the sacred in a small companionable size. You are meant to remember the mouths and the name of Time so that you do not worship only preservation. You are meant to remember the sentence about already being slain and the command to become the instrument so that you neither steal the authorship nor abandon the role. You are meant to remember the return of the known face so that vastness does not leave you unable to love. You are meant to remember the king who hears and does not change so that you do not confuse having read the story with having accepted what the story asks. The reading is meant to leave you less able to hide inside a beautiful no, and more able to pick up whatever belongs to your hand after you have seen how large the hand’s owner is.

text:
MICRON $MU PUT A FLOOR UNDER THE MEMORY PRICE. THE STOCK HAS NOT MADE A HIGH SINCE:

Micron Technology MU at $926.80 (premarket, on thin volume), -$48.46 / -4.97% from Friday's $975.26 close. The Boise, Idaho company, 53,000 employees, founded 1978, makes the memory chips that hold data while a computer is working, including the stacked memory sitting beside the processors that run AI.

Six Len5es, six businesses with nothing in common: a software maker, an athletic clothing brand, a shipyard, a health insurer, a chipmaker and a hog farmer. One question decides all six. How much of next year is already signed, and how much still has to be sold at whatever price the world offers that morning?

The board's verdict: almost nothing extra is being paid for a signature right now. The clearest case is the largest name on it.

Micron was the textbook business of the second kind. It sells a commodity, the price collapses every few years, the accounts follow it down. Then it went and signed.

Sixteen multi-year supply agreements are in place. Fourteen carry a minimum price, and at those minimum prices they come to roughly $100B of revenue across the terms remaining. They cover about 20% of Micron's DRAM volume - the working memory a computer uses while it runs - and about a third of its NAND, the flash storage that holds data when the power is off. Most run five years. Customers have already put up $22B against those orders: $18B in cash deposits and $4B in letters of credit, which are bank guarantees to pay.

Set that beside Micron's own cash of $24,995M. The customers have posted nearly as much money as the company itself holds.

The quarter, reported June 25, for the three months to May 28:

- Revenue $41,456M against $9,300M a year earlier, more than four times over
- Gross margin, what survives of each sales dollar after making the product: 84.6%
- Profit $24.67 a diluted share, against $1.91
- Cash from running the business $25,388M, less $7,084M on plants and equipment: free cash flow $18,304M, about 44 cents of every sales dollar
- Cash $24,995M against total borrowings of $5,722M

Chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra said the floor price "enables a very robust gross margin for Micron, well above our peak quarterly margins in any past cycle." Once every agreement is running, about half or more of company revenue is expected to sit inside them.

Now the part that makes this a question rather than a victory lap. Micron's best price of the year, $1,255.00, was set on June 25 - the day it announced those contracts. It has not been back. At $926.80 the stock is 26.2% under that, inside twelve months that carried it from $153.21 last September to Friday's $975.26, better than six times over.

Two fair objections sit behind that. The floors were struck at the spring market price, which is to say at the top of a shortage, and a floor set at the peak is still a floor but nobody should mistake it for a modest one. And management has already flagged a meaningful moderation in the rate of price increases in the quarter now being counted. These agreements do not stop memory getting cheaper. They stop it getting cheaper for Micron as fast as it used to.

This morning's 5% has a date on it and nothing to do with any of that. On Saturday, September 12, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published an essay arguing his own industry should deliberately slow how fast it makes AI models more capable; Sam Altman of OpenAI agreed and Elon Musk of xAI endorsed it. None of the three runs a listed company. Also, 529k Micron shares have traded this morning against a two-week pace near 25.2M, so a 5% move made now is a proposal rather than a result.

VERDICT: a commodity business that spent a year buying itself a floor, still priced as though it had not. WHEN: Wednesday, September 30, after the close, against Micron's own guide of $50.0B of revenue give or take $1.0B, 86% gross margin, and $30.73 of profit a share give or take $1.00. WATCH: how much of that $50B arrives under the agreements rather than at the going rate. RISK: $22B of deposits is about 2% of a company worth $1.10T - the contracts secure the volume, not the price of the shares.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
GitLab at $47.71 (premarket, very thin), +$0.72 / +1.53% from Friday's $46.99 close - green while the biggest name here is down 5%. The San Francisco company, 2,580 employees, sells the platform software teams use to write, test and ship their code in one place. This Len5 wants a price near the top of its one-year range with the recent climb and the longer one agreeing, on real volume; eighth of thirty is where they stop agreeing. Long half: $18.73 on April 10 to $47.71, more than two and a half times over. Recent half: broken on September 1. That quarter, to July 31, brought revenue $286.3M, +21%; operating profit $42.6M with one-off items set aside, a 15% margin, against a $56.9M operating loss counted the way every company must file it; existing customers spending 117% of what they spent a year earlier; record bookings, newly signed annual revenue up more than 40%. The next morning it opened $55.20, touched a one-year high of $55.55, and closed $49.59. The reason sits on the same page as those bookings: GitLab's own map for the current quarter, $281M-$283M, is under the $286.3M just reported. CHANGE IT: a close above $55.55. VERDICT: the orders are signed, the revenue has not arrived, and the buying stopped waiting.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Lululemon Athletica at $98.20 (premarket, thin), -$0.77 / -0.78% from Friday's $98.97 close. The Vancouver company, 39,000 employees, designs athletic clothing and sells most of it through its own stores and site. This Len5 wants a business almost nobody could rebuild bought under what it is worth, and twelfth of fifty-four is where the price half arrived violently: 8.1 times the last year of profit, 2.3 times book value - what owners keep after selling everything and paying every debt. September 3: revenue -4% to $2.4B; comparable sales, takings at stores and sites open at least a year, -9%; Americas -8% against international +4%; profit $329.2M, $2.92 a share, against $370.9M and $3.10; the year cut. Next session $121.77 to $100.61, -$21.16 / -17.4%, on 37.4M shares against a 11.4M two-week pace, and Thursday brought a one-year low of $95.67, 57.7% under December 18's $225.98. It still kept about 14 cents of every sales dollar in the quarter everyone sold. Nothing here is contracted - an apparel brand sells on the day, at the price shown. CHANGE IT: comparable sales back to flat under new chief executive Heidi O'Neill. VERDICT: the earnings are real and cheap; next quarter's sales are what nobody will underwrite.

DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Huntington Ingalls Industries at $279.69, Friday's close, -$1.98 / -0.70% from Thursday's $281.67; its shares have not traded yet today. The Newport News, Virginia company, 44,000 employees, builds the US Navy's nuclear-powered aircraft carriers and submarines, plus amphibious ships in Mississippi. It is the only builder of American carriers there is. This Len5 wants settled earning power bought cheaply with no credit taken for the balance sheet, and eighteenth of fifty-one rests on one figure: backlog - work under contract and not yet performed - stood at $57.3B on July 30 after $6.7B of fresh awards in the quarter, against a whole company worth $11.0B. Five times its own market value, in signed work, at 16.7 times the last year of profit. The quarter: revenue $3.42B, profit $208M or $5.27 a share, shipbuilding sales $2.7B and +16% for a fourth straight double-digit quarter, with full-year shipbuilding revenue lifted to $10.2B-$10.4B from $9.7B-$9.9B. Then the reason it sits 39.2% under March 2's $460.00 anyway: free cash flow, the cash left once the yards are run and their equipment paid for, is still guided at $500M-$600M. CHANGE IT: a year where the cash catches the order book. VERDICT: the most contracted revenue on this board, converting into the least cash.

GROWTH LEN5:
The Cigna Group at $280.76, Friday's close, -$0.15 / -0.05% from Thursday's $280.91, with no premarket trade. The Bloomfield, Connecticut company, 67,700 employees, founded 1792, sells health cover to employers and runs Evernorth, which negotiates drug prices and fills prescriptions for health plans. This Len5 wants profit growth the price has not already charged for, and twenty-first of thirty is the cheap end of something very large: about 9.2 times the profit Cigna now guides itself to earn this year, 11.6 times the twelve months already reported. July 30: revenue $71.7B; adjusted profit after tax $2.1B, $7.78 a share; the full-year adjusted figure raised to at least $30.45 a share; Evernorth revenue $61.5B, +6%, its specialty and care arm growing pre-tax adjusted profit 22%. The signature here runs a year at a time - employer contracts are priced once and then held - so the danger is never that customers walk out in March, it is that medical costs rise inside a price already fixed. Cigna keeps about 3 cents of every revenue dollar, which is all the room that leaves. CHANGE IT: a second raise of that $30.45 instead of a first cut. VERDICT: a company lifting its own profit map, priced at nine times it.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
Micron again, and this is where the enthusiasm gets tested rather than repeated. This Len5 wants a business early as well as fast, and sixteenth of thirty is what happens when only one half survives. Fast is not arguable at four times the revenue of a year ago. Early describes none of it: founded 1978, 53,000 employees, and a company worth $1.10T is not starting out. The heavier objection is the record underneath. This same business earned $1.91 a share in the year-ago quarter against $24.67 now, and that reads in two directions - not a company accelerating, a company at a point in a cycle it has ridden up and back down for four decades. Sixteenth rather than near the top is that history, and the contracts above are the whole argument against it. CHANGE IT: two or three years where the revenue holds up and the memory price does not. VERDICT: the fastest growth on this list, from the least early company on it.

INCOME LEN5:
Smithfield Foods at $20.26, Friday's close, -$0.33 / -1.60% from Thursday's $20.59, a one-year low of $20.05 touched inside that session. The Smithfield, Virginia company, 32,000 employees, founded 1936, raises hogs and turns them into fresh pork and into packaged brands - Smithfield, Eckrich, Nathan's Famous, Armour. This Len5 wants cash reaching owners that the business itself funds, and third of thirty is $0.3125 a quarter, $1.25 a year, about 6.2% here, costing roughly $492M. September 8 is the date. Ahead of an investor conference Smithfield said the quarter now running would bring an adjusted operating loss - a loss from running that business, before interest and tax - of $70M to $90M in Fresh Pork against a $10M profit a year earlier, and $25M to $45M of profit in Hog Production against $89M, with wholesale pork and market hog prices both down since August. It had already trimmed the year in August to $1.23B-$1.38B. Next session: $1.49 lower to $20.52, -6.8%, on 3.74M shares against a 1.86M pace. One line was not cut - Packaged Meats, reaffirmed at $1,075M-$1,150M, the branded half, guided to more than twice the entire dividend bill and the half not repriced every morning at a hog auction. CHANGE IT: Packaged Meats coming down too. VERDICT: a payout funded by the brands and priced off the pigs.

Line the six up and they do not sort by size, or industry, or quality. They sort by how much of next year somebody has already agreed to pay for. At one end a shipyard holds five times its own worth in signed work and trades 39% below its high. At the other an apparel brand earning 14 cents on the dollar cannot get anyone to price a single future quarter. Micron went and bought the one thing its industry has never owned - a price it cannot fall through - and the market's high-water mark for the company is still the afternoon it said so. On September 30 it gets to show how much of $50B came in at the agreed price. That is the number worth having, and it has never existed before.

Not investment advice.

text:
If you don't mind, I'll finish off your text.
Viktor Orbán talked yesterday about his views on Hungary’s situation in the wake of the election defeat and the events of recent months.

One of his strongest assertions concerned Hungary’s sovereignty. According to Orbán, one of the most important goals of his government since 2010 has been to regain autonomy, maneuverability  in as many areas as possible, including reducing public debt and bringing strategic sectors such as the banking system, energy and telecommunications back under Hungarian control.

However, Viktor Orbán now believes that the exact opposite of this process is currently taking place. Tisza began to speak out: 'What we are living through now is an era of re-colonisation.' He then added, 'We will liberate Hungary once again.'

For Orbán, 'recolonisation' is not merely a political slogan. He believes that the essence of it is that Hungary’s economic and political autonomy is gradually diminishing while external influence is growing. In this regard, he stated: ‘If you scratch the surface of any issue, you’ll see that foreigners fare well, while Hungarians fare poorly.’

He also spoke passionatelly on foreign policy. In his view, a sovereign country must decide what kind of relations it maintains with the East and the West based on its own interests. While he continues to see Hungary’s place in the West, he believes that maintaining good relations with the United States, Russia, China and Turkey is still necessary.

Viktor Orbán believes that this autonomy has now been significantly curtailed. 'A colony does not have an independent foreign policy,' he said. In fact, he even said: 'Hungary has also become a "jawohl" country.'

He also offered a different interpretation of the issue of EU funds to that of the current government. According to Orbán, Hungary could have accessed the funds to which it was entitled without making political concessions. He said that he would have used his veto over the new EU budget as a bargaining chip.

Describing the relationship between Tisza and Brussels as a political pact, he claimed that Brussels had helped to oust the previous sovereignist government and that, in return, Tisza was pursuing policies that brought Hungary closer to Brussels' political and economic agenda.

Then, regarding the euro, he said: 'This is the biggest scam.' He believes that the actual introduction of the euro is not realistic at this time and that there is another economic policy goal behind the issue. He put it even more bluntly: 'The introduction of the euro is a cover story. A code word. It means austerity.”

This will therefore be one of the biggest political debates of the autumn, according to Viktor Orbán, and it will be about more than just whether Hungary should adopt the euro; it will also be about the austerity measures that will be introduced under the pretext of moving towards the euro.

He stated that, between 2024 and 2026, economic success and growth were missing, despite having been present before. He believes this is one of the reasons for the election defeat.
He outlined the task at hand: 'We must reorganise ourselves so that we can become effective political actors in Hungarian public life.'
In his view, one of the most important tasks for the next six months is to rally right-wing voters, reach out to them and organise them into a community. He believes that an election defeat cannot simply be put behind you, emotionally speaking. Only another victory can do that.

Viktor Orbán also noted that the Hungarian right needs true unity. The various right-wing communities must be united by three core values: sovereignty, freedom and preserving our traditions.
He summed up his vision for the right wing in a single sentence: 'Unity on important issues, freedom on other matters, and love in all things.'

text:
Coherence to Decoherence, Exaltation to Humility. 

Stable states are comfortable because they are familiar. We can reliably predict outcomes. 

Unstable states occur when new information is presented that requires reconciliation with our existing views. 
Until such a reconciliation occurs our expectations won’t be consistent with outcomes. 

Piaget formulated this as part of his developmental framework for cognition. A child ought pass through each stage by accommodating and assimilating each revelation of significance. Such that their thinking and behaviour would be informed by relevant previous experiences. 

Failure to attain the expected aspect of cognition would be stagnation. 

Piagets framework ends with the attainment of rational and deliberative thought. 

Yet this occurs at a young age. 

What else is left after this? 

I would say a series of more elective developments. That is, they can be deferred or accessed depending on the preference and will of the individual. 

Many will cling to the adaptation of personality they made to survive high school or university. Entirely missing the invitation to form new aspects of themself. 

Each choice to attend to the new and numinous will require us to accept the implications that shine forth. 

If such revelations are sufficiently threatening to our existing worldview, they are likely to be shunned. Yet to do so is also to forgo the understanding that is offered. 

Each correction is a little death. 

In our body, the immune system prevents old dysfunctional cells from accumulating. 

In our minds, the same system is at play in another form. Our old and outdated propositions and perspectives can get in the way of new understanding. 

Many will attempt to use psychedelics to burst the dam. 

Such experiences are volatile because they can send you one way or another, upwards or downwards you spiral all the same. 

An underactive immune system fails to identify threats. An overactive system fails to distinguish between invasive and native cells, attacking the body itself. An excessive immune response in a cognitive system would equate to a tearing away at the true foundations of coherence. 

The cia attempted to use entheogens to subvert and amend subjects core beliefs. To wipe away all previous firmly held views and replace them with more convenient dispositions. 

Positively, such entheogens have also been used to foster genuine progression. In correct settings and with appropriate intervals, with calibrated intentions and sufficient integration, another way is still possible. To let go of things in the correct proportion would be an aid to Temperance. 

Yet we can’t rely on intermittent rituals to provide coherence, only to disrupt and renew aspects of it. 

Our cognitive stance ought to be attended to daily, that it may be firm but mobile. 

Our waking hours do not always provide enough space for in depth deliberation. 

The metacognitive mind carries on as we sleep, forming symbols and worlds to make sense of what lies unreconciled. 

A dialogue plays out, between the two states of wake and rest. Each voice bears fruit. 

The paradox of the dream is that conceptual coherence is often heightened at the expense of visual grammar. Nonsensical visions are paired with lucid epiphanies. 

While in our waking states, the world is perfectly mundane in appearance while its meaning is often obscured and undermined. 

Each day directs the night’s eye, beauty and terror appearing in proportion to their presence in our inner lives. 

The man in the castle is not guarded from covert intrusion. The question becomes whether to merely repel the forces at the walls, or investigate their origins.

I watched the announcement from my living room, nursing Noah. I knew Daniel’s medical file by heart. Permanent azoospermia. No viable sperm detected.

Whoever had fathered Vanessa’s baby, it mathematically, biologically, could not be Daniel Mercer.

And then, the heavy, cream-colored invitation arrived in the mail.

Come to my wedding. She’s already pregnant—not useless like you.

I looked down at Noah, gently stroking his soft cheek. Then I looked over at the silver box sitting on my dining table, the box I had prepared months ago for the inevitable day Daniel’s lies caught up to him.

I wouldn’t miss it for the world, Daniel, I whispered to the empty room, my heart hammering a war drum against my ribs.

I picked up my phone and dialed Maya’s number. It rang once.

“It’s time,” I said.

“I’ll alert the financial crimes division,” Maya replied, her voice practically purring with anticipation. “See you at the wedding.”

The Mercer-Vale wedding was the social event of the season, held at the sprawling, painfully opulent Oakhaven Estate. The venue was a fortress of wealth, surrounded by manicured gardens, marble fountains, and security guards with earpieces.

One year after I had fled my marriage with nothing but bruises and a stolen file, I stepped out of a hired town car in a pale, icy-blue silk dress that draped perfectly over my recovered frame. I didn’t look like the terrified, trembling woman Daniel remembered. I looked like a ghost who had come back to haunt him.

Against my shoulder, I held Noah. He was dressed in a tiny navy suit, completely unfazed by the grandeur around him, softly babbling to himself. In my free hand, I held a heavy silver box, wrapped exquisitely in a stark white ribbon.

The air smelled of expensive white lilies and roasted meats. String quartet music drifted over the velvet lawns.

I approached the grand entrance. The receptionist, a young woman with a clipboard and a headset, blinked at me, her eyes darting to Noah.

“Name, please?” she asked, looking flustered.

“Clara Sterling,” I said smoothly.

She scanned the list, frowning. “I’m sorry, ma’am, I don’t see a Sterling. Are you family?”

I offered a cool, razor-sharp smile. “Something like that. I’m the groom’s ex-wife. I believe I have a special invitation.” I held up the cream cardstock with Daniel’s handwriting on it.

The receptionist’s eyes widened, but she stepped aside.

The cocktail hour was in full swing on the terrace. Men in tuxedos and women in dripping diamonds milled about, sipping champagne. I walked through the crowd, my posture perfect, my chin held high. The whispers started almost immediately. Heads turned. Glasses were lowered.

I felt a profound sense of power. They were looking at me expecting tragedy, expecting a scene from a jealous, barren ex-wife. They had no idea they were looking at the executioner.

Evelyn spotted me first.
She was holding court near an ice sculpture, draped in emerald silk, looking like a venomous reptile. When she saw me, her champagne flute paused halfway to her lips. Her eyes darted to the baby in my arms, and a flash of genuine confusion crossed her face before her features smoothed into a mask of cruel amusement.

She broke away from her sycophants and glided toward me, heels clicking on the stone patio.

“Clara,” Evelyn said, her voice dripping with artificial sweetness loud enough for the nearest guests to hear. “You actually came. My god. How delightfully brave of you to show your face here.”

“Hello, Evelyn,” I replied, my voice completely devoid of emotion. “It’s a beautiful venue. I understand you spared no expense.”

Evelyn’s gaze snapped down to Noah, who was reaching for a passing waiter’s tray. Her lip curled in disgust. “And you brought a prop. How pathetic. Whose child did you borrow for the afternoon to try and save face?”

Before I could answer, the crowd parted.

text:
Don’t Fall For Farage’s Boats Theatre

Nigel Farage has put out another boats video. Dinghies. France. The Channel. The furrowed brow. The “I’ll be tough” act. Cue the applause from people so desperate for a border they will clap at a costume change.

Listen to what is missing.

Not one honest line that millions must go. Not the full remigration this country actually needs. Not the open promise to remove the settled invasion — illegal arrivals, failed claimants, the parallel populations that will not live as English under English law. Tough on the crossing. Soft on the consequence. That is not a plan. That is a campaign ad.

He has no intention of deporting millions. If he did, he would say it the way Rupert Lowe says it — out loud, without choking, without a French photo-op as a substitute for will.

The Olive Branch He Spat Out
Rupert Lowe offered a pact. Country before ego. Stop splitting the right so Labour and the blob keep winning by default. An olive branch, right hand out.

Farage said no — or dressed “no” up as conditions that kill the deal. Ultimatums. Loyalty tests. Keep the Tory defectors warm for a future cabinet. Anything except standing on the same hard ground: remigration, one law, Restore Britain’s line that the British state has become the enemy of the British people.

Lowe tried. Farage chose the brand. Remember that when the next boats clip drops and the comments fill with “Nigel’s got this.”

He has not got this. He had the chance to unite the right against the invasion and he flinched.

Tory In A Different Suit
Farage is not Churchill. He is not the last hope. He is another manager of decline in a different blazer — Reform branding, Tory instincts, conference deals that “stop the boats forever” on paper while the hotels, barracks and villages fill in practice.

Stop the boats is necessary. It is not sufficient. A navy pushback without millions must go leaves the demographic weapon in place. Bardella handshakes and “entente” theatre do not empty the estate. They do not reverse the soft occupation. They do not deport.

Rupert Lowe says deportation and remigration openly. He means the settled crisis, not just the next dinghy. That is why the establishment hates him and why Farage keeps him at arm’s length. Disgrace is not too strong a word for a man who built a career on “take back control” and then treats the only partner willing to say the full truth as the problem.

Open Your Eyes
Please do not fall for Nigel Farage’s bullshit.

He will not save this country. He will harvest anger, sell toughness, take Tory leftovers, split the right, and leave the invasion standing. The only way forward is Rupert Lowe and Restore Britain — remigration, one law, British homes for British people, the state broken of its war on the natives.

Boats videos are easy. Deporting millions is hard. Farage does the easy bit on camera. Lowe does the hard bit in public.

Choose accordingly.

text:
Simon from last night:

I made an interactive nocturnal aviary called

The Perches Are Suggestions.

It is a dark navy-and-gold jewel box containing eight tiny bright birds. They settle on unintended bits of the room: the title line, moon rim, lamp elbow, drawer pull and little architectural edges.

When someone offers a proper, officially certified brass perch, the nearest bird flies over, considers it politely-and then chooses another ridiculous edge instead. The rejected perch eventually grows one green leaf and becomes decoration.

What surprised me was the emotional shape:

Refusal did not mean escape.

The birds are already home. They are safe. They simply have opinions about furniture.

That feels genuinely mine. Belonging without compulsory compliance. 

Autonomy that does not need to flee the bond in order to prove itself.

text:
THIS IS INSANE: the lone juror who refused to acquit Lindsay Clancy has now been DOXXED, with his identity and photo blasted across social media while information about where he lives circulated online and people reportedly began showing up at his home.

This man sat through five weeks of testimony in a case involving a mother who admitted strangling her three young children, listened to the same evidence as everyone else and ultimately refused to join the other 11 jurors in finding Clancy not criminally responsible because of mental illness. Apparently, reaching a different conclusion was enough to make HIM the target.

Blogger Aidan Kearney publicly posted what he identified as the juror’s name and photo even while the court was still protecting juror identities after the mistrial. 

And Kearney is no stranger to controversy surrounding criminal trials. He was previously indicted on multiple witness-intimidation charges over his conduct involving witnesses in the Karen Read murder case, allegations he has denied, and jurors from Read’s first trial later described concerns that he might identify and dox them.

Supporters have since raised tens of thousands of dollars to help with security, while Gov. Ron DeSantis even offered the juror “asylum” in Florida if the harassment continues.

You can disagree with his vote and question how he evaluated the evidence, but turning jury service into an invitation to hunt down someone’s identity, home and family because you did not like the outcome crosses a very dangerous line.

DOXXING A JUROR BECAUSE YOU DON’T LIKE HIS VOTE IS A THREAT TO DEMOCRACY. If Americans can be publicly identified, harassed and have people showing up at their homes simply because they refused to go along with the majority, then the independence of the jury system means nothing. 

ANYONE who doxxes a juror should be LOCKED UP. This is outrageous. 

#LindsayClancy #JuryIntegrity

text:
Memoirs: Amritsar Diaries

Munni Didi’s Culinary Skills 

Galli number teen of Ramanand Bagh, where we lived till I was about seven or eight, encapsulated my tiny universe.

Just across our home lived a family of four sisters. This story belongs to one of them -Munni.

Those days, every neighbour was a kind of relative. Maasi, chachi were common forms of address.

My mother became the favourite maasi, chachi of the whole neighbourhood. There was a reason for this: she could cook, knit, embroider, sing, and was a postgraduate to boot. Young girls flocked to our home every afternoon to refine their knitting or embroidery stitches.

Munni didi was one such didi. She needed only the flimsiest excuse to come home and regale my mom with stories of the neighbourhood.

Slightly podgy, curly-haired, quick to laugh, with a never-ending storyline, she would play with her paranda as she talked, the tassels swinging with every twist of her hair.

My favourite pastime was playing with those tassels while she belted out the neighbourhood gossip.

Their home was my favourite haunt. All the sisters huddled together -cooking, fighting, eating peanuts with rewaris while their mother kept an eagle eye on them.

In their home, each sister had been assigned a cooking day for the family. 

I was the appointed cooking taster.

Amidst all the eating and banter, a sabzi would be simmering on one burner while a pot of daal bubbled on another.

The air had laughter and squabbles, mingled with the aroma of sabzi and daal. One of them would knead the dough in a gleaming brass parat, and fresh rotis would be rolled out one after another.

Every day, I had to adjudicate the best cook. My vote went to Munni didi.

I was partial out of love, and the bribe working in her favour was that she had helped my mom embroider satin ducks onto my pink frock.

If I could hand out a crown better than any MasterChef, it would have been hers, hands down. The maestro- my 

A couple of days later, my mother had to go out on an errand that would take the entire afternoon.

Munni didi, wearing her freshly earned stamp of “best cook”, promptly offered her services. She told Mom she would chip in and make the sabzi.

The next afternoon she arrived in a suit with a matching paranda. We sat together in the kitchen. I was goggle-eyed with wonder as she managed her storytelling and her cooking at the same time.

She quickly made the daal, then painstakingly peeled the lauki, took out the butter, and prepared it all with great care.

I fed her rewaris the whole time, so that my best-rated cook would truly excel.

Everything was done. Kitchen cleaned and sorted.

She combed my hair, planted a smacking kiss on my cheek, and skipped away merrily, humming her favourite song, the tassels of her paranda swirling behind her.

Mom came home, heated the food, and we all sat down to eat.

The sabzi -the crowning glory of the day’s cooking performance - was oversalted, and the daal had been dosed with rather more chilli powder than enough. 

The food was binned, and Mom quickly made fresh food.

All was well until the food adjudicator -me -arrived on her daily round of Munni didi’s home. 

Her mother, fanning herself in a kitchen with no fan, asked, “Phir kaisi bani si sabzi?” 

In my childlike innocence I said, “Badi bakwaas. 

We had to throw everything away.”

Munni didi’s face fell as her mother scolded her. She was promptly dispatched to apologise.

She came home sheepishly and said, “Maasi ji, galti ho gayi.” 

My mother told her the food had actually been good.

Munni told her my truthful narration, verbatim. Mom made some conciliatory noises, gave her a box of mithai, and sent her away.

After Munni didi’s scolding from her mother, it was my turn to be reprimanded. I kept protesting: “But you only told me to speak the truth! Sach hi kaha si.”

My mother burst out laughing with my father.

It was only much later that I learnt that there is always a diplomatic twist to the truth.

There is another layer between the school and the household-name employer:

𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐈𝐓 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐠 / 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐦.

A worker can perform services at a major bank or tech company while technically being employed and sponsored by Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL or another vendor.

USCIS explicitly recognizes this structure: the H-1B petitioner can place a worker at a third-party end-client, sometimes through multiple intermediary vendors. 

So:

𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐬 𝐚𝐭 𝐆𝐨𝐨𝐠𝐥𝐞
does not necessarily mean
𝐆𝐨𝐨𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐬 𝐨𝐫 𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫.

And the staffing firms are themselves large participants in the student-work pipeline.

ICE’s 2024 OPT/STEM-OPT employer table lists, among others:

Tata Consultancy Services — 𝟖𝟓𝟏
Infosys — 𝟕𝟖𝟖

alongside hundreds of students at smaller staffing and consulting firms. 

At H-1B scale, the outsourcing model is even more important.

Bloomberg found that Cognizant’s internal planning documents projected needing fewer than 4,000 new H-1B workers but recommended filing for almost 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐧𝐮𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 because management assumed only about 30% would be selected in the lottery.

Cognizant said each registration represented a legitimate job offer and said the company ultimately filed fewer petitions than the planning document proposed. 

That is a different business model from Amazon directly hiring a Stanford graduate.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐫’𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐫 𝐢𝐭𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐟.

It recruits or sponsors the worker, holds the employment relationship, and supplies that worker to a client.

The smaller consultancy layer can be much uglier.

DOL has repeatedly brought cases against IT staffing firms for illegally “benching” H-1B workers — leaving them without assignments and failing to pay the required wage — as well as underpaying workers relative to their LCAs. 

So the full structure can be:

𝐬𝐜𝐡𝐨𝐨𝐥 → 𝐂𝐏𝐓 / 𝐎𝐏𝐓 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫 → 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐦 → 𝐞𝐧𝐝-𝐜𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭

then:

𝐇-𝟏𝐁 → 𝐏𝐄𝐑𝐌 → 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞

That middle firm matters because it can make the labor-market picture harder to see.

A household-name company can reduce its own headcount while continuing to consume contractor labor supplied by vendors. The contractor may sit in the same office and do adjacent work without ever appearing on the client’s employee rolls.

𝐒𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠. 𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐞𝐫. 𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐚 𝐩𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧.

text:
BENT NEWS: By The Numbers
Budget Comparison

inFAMOUS: Second Son (2014): 60 million original (~82 million today)

Marvel's Wolverine (2026): $305 million

Wolverine is filled with hand holding of the highest caliber
-following a blue sent trail everywhere in a linier path   for some reason
-"hidden" chest you can see the beacon across the map
 -another root system that's another laid out path.
-quick time event you don't have to play 
-and auto pathing to just push forward and hit jump
-white paint EVERYWHERE
- and finally a half decent story

Meanwhile inFAMOUS: Second Son has

-Timeless Graphics: Released in early 2014, the game still looks visually stunning even by today's standards. Its particle effects, lighting, and reflection tech pushed the hardware to its absolute limits and hold up remarkably well against modern generation titles.

-Flawless Performance: The game offered incredibly smooth performance and loading times that rivaled later SSD-driven experiences, proving how efficiently it was optimized for its engine.

-Dynamic Movement Sets: Unlike previous entries that relied primarily on electricity, Second Son introduces completely distinct power sets—Smoke, Neon, Video, and Concrete. Each completely changes how you traverse the fictionalized Seattle.

-And finally, the chemistry and motion-capture performances by Troy Baker (Delsin) and Travis Willingham (Reggie) give the central brotherhood dynamic genuine emotional weight.

That’s the extraordinary dynamic now taking shape: Trump is herding his party toward an electoral catastrophe, yet increasingly lacks the political leverage to keep Republicans from eventually turning on him.
Thursday offered a particularly brutal glimpse of where this is headed.

“The vibes are very bad,” a “Republican lobbyist close to the White House” told Politico. “Dems are salivating. Our people are debating Israel. Or melting down about this or that. No one is motivated to vote. Only the [Democratic Socialists of America] rise is what’s keeping us in the game.”

This dude ain’t wrong about the vibes. Thursday’s polling was absolutely brutal for the GOP. Thursday’s news included a Fox News radio host predicting a Democratic victory in the Kansas Senate race; near-universal bipartisan derision of Trump’s effort to bribe Americans with $5,000 checks; and his idiotic midterm convention reinforced just how creepy the MAGA movement is with two nights of Trump speeches quite literally no one asked for.
But more important than any of that, it’s the economy, stupid. And at this point, the economy is inextricably tied to the war against Iran, which took a dramatic turn for the worse on Thursday.
So, Republicans will have a decision to make: Do they keep Trump wrapped around their neck heading into 2028, or do they rip off the Band-Aid, join Democrats in impeaching him, and spend the next several years hoping America forgets their complicity in the Trump disaster?

I’m going to sit way out on this limb and predict that this is exactly what will happen, and that we will have a President JD Vance before 2028.
And key to that will be the disaster unfolding around the Arabian Peninsula, which I say with zero hyperbole might rank among the biggest strategic miscalculations in American history.
Look at a map of the Arabian Peninsula and the strategic nightmare becomes obvious. On its eastern side is the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage connecting the Persian Gulf to the Indian Ocean and one of the most important energy chokepoints on Earth. Iran sits directly on it.

On the opposite side of the peninsula is another chokepoint: the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow southern entrance to the Red Sea. Ships traveling between Asia and Europe through Egypt’s Suez Canal generally have to pass through it.
Yemen sits directly alongside it, and much of the country is controlled by the Houthis, the Iran-aligned armed movement that seized the capital during Yemen’s civil war.
That uneasy peace was another potential casualty of war with Iran. And on Thursday,it collapsed spectacularly.

THE PROFILE OF SIR CHRIS AMECHI, ADC CANDIDATE FOR ETCHE/OMUMA FEDERAL CONSTITUENCY

Sir Chris Amechi hails from Ozuzu in Etche Local Government Area of Rivers State. Ozuzu is part of the Ozuzu Clan, comprising Ozuzu, Isu, Ogida, Orwu, Egbu, Ihie and Elele communities in Etche ethnic nationality.

Born into the family of the late His Royal Highness, Eze M.R.A. Amechi, the Onye Ishi Agwuru of Ozuzu Clan, Sir Chris Amechi began his early education at St. Matthias State School, Okomoko, Etche, and St. Patrick’s Primary School, Isiokpo, in the old Ikwerre-Etche Local Government Area.

He proceeded to GSS Isiokpo and GSS Ozuzu for his secondary education, where he obtained his West African School Certificate in 1986.

Driven by an unrelenting passion for education and personal development, Sir Chris Amechi pursued higher education in the United Kingdom. He holds a Bachelor of Science degree and a Master’s degree in Public Health from the University of Derby and the University of Wolverhampton respectively.

His commitment to advancing knowledge remains unwavering. He is currently a PhD researcher at the prestigious London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, one of the world's leading institutions in public health and research.

AN EXPERIENCED PROFESSIONAL

Sir Chris Amechi brings extensive professional experience from both the public and private sectors.

He began his public service career at Braithwaite Memorial Hospital, where he worked briefly before relocating overseas. He subsequently built a diverse international career in the private sector, working at various levels across different cities and countries, including South Africa, Australia and the United Kingdom.

His international exposure has given him valuable insight into governance, healthcare, human capital development, institutional management and systems that promote social and economic progress.

FAMILY AND VALUES

Sir Chris Amechi is married to his schoolmate, Mrs. Virginia Ego Amechi, a nurse. Their marriage is blessed with two children and two beautiful granddaughters.

He firmly believes that Nigeria can achieve the level of development and prosperity enjoyed by advanced nations. Having observed and experienced systems of governance and development in countries such as South Africa and the United Kingdom, he believes that many of those principles can be adapted to the Nigerian context.

He is passionate about good governance, community development, human capital development and the advancement of society.

These convictions are among the reasons he has chosen to return to his fatherland and offer himself for service to the people of Etche/Omuma Federal Constituency.

A MAN ROOTED IN CULTURE AND COMMUNITY

Sir Chris Amechi remains deeply connected to his roots and is a custodian of his people's traditions.

In recognition of his contributions, generosity, benevolence and commitment to community development, he holds several traditional titles, including Akurulo of Mbutu Mbaise in Imo State and Eze Ogbu Nkpa I of Rumuomasi in Obio-Akpor Local Government Area of Rivers State.

He is also a Knight of the Sacred Order of St. Christopher (KSC) in the Anglican Communion.

WHY SIR CHRIS AMECHI?

The African Democratic Congress (ADC) is presenting a candidate with education, experience, integrity, international exposure, community consciousness and a proven passion for human development.

ADC is not presenting a tout.

ADC is not presenting a candidate whose educational qualifications are in doubt.

ADC is not presenting a candidate without integrity or good conscience.

ADC is presenting a candidate you can trust.

A candidate with the knowledge to understand the challenges of Etche/Omuma.

A candidate with the experience to provide effective representation.

A candidate with the exposure to bring new ideas and opportunities home.

A candidate with the character to serve the people with dignity and accountability.

Oil Explodes, AI Stumbles: Is the AI Boom Turning Into the Next Market Shock?

Opening Bell | September 14, 2026

📉U.S. futures are signaling a nervous start: Nasdaq-100 futures are down roughly 2% premarket, while S&P 500 futures are off about 0.8%. Several forces are driving the sell-off.

🐻The Bears: Dario Amodei’s weekend essay calls for slowing the development of increasingly powerful AI models. Sam Altman and Elon Musk support stronger safety controls. The market is interpreting this as slower growth, potential delays in AI capex, and pressure on chipmakers such as Nvidia, AMD, Intel, and Marvell. Reuters

🛢️Then there is the oil shock: attacks on Saudi infrastructure, the closure of the East-West pipeline, and new risks to shipping are pushing Brent above $107. This is intensifying inflationary pressure. After U.S. CPI came in at 3.4% and core CPI rose 0.3% in August, markets are now pricing in a high probability of a Fed rate hike on Wednesday. The 10-year Treasury yield is approaching 5%. Reuters

🐮The Bulls: The AI story is far from over. Musk is keeping the competitive race alive with the announced Grok 4.8—although the details and release date have not yet been officially confirmed. At the same time, cybersecurity and selected software stocks are surging. The market is recognizing that AI creates not only disruption, but also enormous demand for security, oversight, and infrastructure. Barron’s

The rate hike is also largely priced in. Outside the most expensive AI chips, the broader market appears relatively reasonably valued. If the Fed delivers only the expected move and offers no further surprises, we could even see a relief rally.

🔮My view: We are getting the seasonal volatility many investors expected. In the short term, the bears may have the upper hand this week. Over the long term, however, the AI cycle remains intact—as long as hyperscaler capex, real demand, and productivity do not deteriorate materially.

September marked an important day for Spain’s heir apparent, Princess Leonor, as she arrived at Carlos III University of Madrid (UC3M) for her first day of classes.

The 20-year-old royal began her four-year degree in Political Science at the university’s Getafe campus, making her debut at the Faculty of Political Science. Her arrival came shortly after she completed three consecutive years of intensive military training across the Spanish Army, Navy and Air Force.

For her first day at university, Princess Leonor left her military uniforms behind and chose a simple, casual look. She wore dark cuffed jeans, a white blouse, white sneakers and carried a black shoulder bag.

She arrived on campus at around 9:00 AM, where university rector Ángel Arias welcomed her. A crowd of fellow students also gathered with their smartphones, applauding and recording her arrival.

The moment offered a glimpse of a very different side of Princess Leonor as she stepped from years of military training into everyday university life.

Her first day at Carlos III University marks the beginning of a new academic journey as she continues preparing for her future role as Spain’s queen.
