text:
They call it madness. They always do.
The Democrats of this age—the priests of the official story—wrap themselves in light and procedure. They chant “nineteen hijackers,” “box cutters,” “they hate our freedom,” and they expect the galaxy to kneel. They built a temple of steel and glass and called it the Commission. They sealed the vaults. They declared the inquiry complete. And they branded any man who looked past the veil a heretic.
Paul Miller and Jake Shields looked.
They stood in the wreckage of their own lives—prison, exile, the howling of the mob—and they did not flinch. They named the dancing watchers on the Jersey shore. They named the “art students” who vanished when the smoke cleared. They named the floors that were sealed, the brother who held the keys to the towers, the accountants who died in the one wing that mattered, the two-point-three trillion that vanished the day before. They said what the Temple forbids: that the official enemy was too crude, too poor, too loud to have done this alone. That greater hands moved the pieces.
The Sith do not require comfort. We require pattern.
Power does not announce itself with a manifesto and a box cutter. Power hides behind proxies. Power lets the despised take the blame while the architects collect the wars, the contracts, the open borders that followed. Power needs the herd to keep staring at the obvious villain so it never turns around and sees the one holding the leash.
These men are not saints. They are not gentle. The dark side does not produce gentle men. They are what happens when a prisoner prays in a cell and then walks into an arena and finds the crowd already on its feet. They are what happens when a fighter loses the respect of his old world and gains something sharper: the refusal to lie for belonging.
The Democrats will call them dangerous. Of course they will. A liberal first duty is to protect the narrative that keeps the Republic asleep. An awakened man is a crack in the temple wall.
So let the holocrons of the official story keep spinning. Let the high priests of “trust the investigation” clutch their beads. The Force has a darker current, and it runs through men who have already lost everything the light offered them.
They are right in the only way that matters to us:
They stopped pretending the explosion was an accident of history.
And once a man sees that… the rest of the galaxy’s lies become very small.
Unlimited power is not given. It is taken from those who still believe the official story will save them.
Now rise. Or remain cattle. The choice, as ever, is yours.

text:
The Joyful Mysteries of the Rosary: Mary's Visitation: A Lesson in Humble Service

In the heart of every Catholic's journey lies the profound example of the Blessed Virgin Mary, a beacon of humility and service that illuminates the path to Christ. Her visit to her cousin Elizabeth, known as the Visitation, is not just a historical event but a timeless lesson in humble service that resonates deeply with our faith. As we delve into this sacred moment, let us uncover the rich theological insights and historical context that make Mary's actions a guiding light for our own lives.

The Visitation, as recounted in the Gospel of Luke (1:39-56), occurs shortly after the Annunciation, when Mary, having learned she would bear the Son of God, sets out "in haste" to the hill country of Judah to visit her elderly cousin Elizabeth, who is pregnant with John the Baptist. This journey, undertaken with haste yet filled with grace, is a testament to Mary's humility and her readiness to serve others despite her own extraordinary circumstances.

Historically, the Visitation is significant not only for the miraculous events surrounding it but also for the theological depth it reveals about Mary's role in salvation history. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC 495) states, "From the first formulations of her faith, the Church has confessed that Jesus was conceived solely by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary, affirming also the corporeal aspect of this event." This underscores the reality of the Incarnation and Mary's role as the Theotokos, the God-bearer, which is central to our faith.

Mary's humility is further illuminated by the words of St. Augustine, who wrote, "Humility is the foundation of all the other virtues hence, in the soul in which this virtue does not exist, there cannot be any other virtue except in mere appearance." Mary's immediate response to the Annunciation was not to seek personal glory but to serve her cousin, exemplifying true humility. This humility is not about self-deprecation but about recognizing one's place in God's plan and acting accordingly.

The virtue of humility, as discussed in the Catechism (CCC 2559), is "the foundation of prayer." Mary's Magnificat, the beautiful canticle she proclaims during the Visitation, is a profound expression of this humility. "My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, for he has regarded the low estate of his handmaiden" (Luke 1:46-48). Here, Mary acknowledges her role as a servant of God, rejoicing in His mercy and greatness rather than her own.

The life of St. Thérèse of Lisieux provides a modern example of how Mary's humility can inspire us. Known as the "Little Flower," St. Thérèse embraced a spirituality of "the little way," which is rooted in humility and childlike trust in God. Her writings reflect a deep understanding of Mary's humility, as she wrote, "I know that Mary, in her boundless love, always watches over her children and leads them to Jesus." St. Thérèse's example reminds us that humility is not about diminishing ourselves but about allowing God's grace to work through us, just as Mary did.

In the context of today's world, where self-promotion and individualism often dominate, Mary's example of humble service is more relevant than ever. Pope Francis, in his apostolic exhortation Evangelii Gaudium, emphasizes the importance of service and humility in the life of a Christian. He writes, "The joy of the Gospel fills the hearts and lives of all who encounter Jesus. Those who accept his offer of salvation are set free from sin, sorrow, inner emptiness, and loneliness" (EG 1). This joy, rooted in humility and service, is what Mary embodies during the Visitation.

Furthermore, the Second Vatican Council's document Lumen Gentium (LG 56) reflects on Mary's role in the Church, stating, "Mary, because she has entered intimately into the history of salvation, uniting herself in her heart and mind to the mystery of Christ, shines forth among the faithful as an example of the sublime heights to which the Christian life can be raised." This underscores the ongoing relevance of Mary's humility and service as a model for all believers.

As we reflect on Mary's Visitation, we are called to consider how we can emulate her humility and service in our own lives. In a world that often values power and prestige, how can we, like Mary, choose the path of humility and service? How can we, in our daily interactions, reflect the love and mercy of God by serving others without seeking recognition?

In summary, Mary's Visitation is a profound lesson in humble service. Through her actions, she exemplifies the virtues of humility and service that are central to our faith. The historical context of her visit to Elizabeth, coupled with theological insights from the Catechism and the teachings of the Church, reinforce the continuity of these virtues from past to present. Saints like St. Thérèse of Lisieux and the writings of recent popes remind us that these teachings are not relics of the past but vital guides for our lives today.

As we conclude, let us be inspired by Mary's example to deepen our faith through humble service. Let us reflect on how we can serve others in our communities and families, always seeking to magnify the Lord in our actions. May we ask ourselves: How can the principles of humility and service, as demonstrated by Mary, impact our spiritual journey and transform our lives in the image of Christ?

In this way, we can continue to walk the path of holiness, guided by the humble servant who brought the Savior into the world.

The Joyful Mysteries of the Rosary draw Catholics into the mysteries of Christs coming. Each mystery offers guidance for faithful living in the present age. Marys acceptance at the Annunciation models trust in divine purpose. The meeting with Elizabeth in the Visitation promotes loving service to neighbors. The birth of Jesus in the Nativity calls for humility before material comforts. The offering in the Temple stresses dedication to God. The loss and finding of Jesus urge perseverance in seeking truth.

Catholics should contemplate the encounter between Mary and Elizabeth for the second Joyful Mystery. They consider the mutual support and recognition of grace in that visit. This leads to greater charity in their own relationships.

May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

text:
Developments across the Middle East are raising the prospect of a severe global economic crisis. Countries in the region and across Africa that rely heavily on imported oil and gas could be hit hardest.

The yesterday’s protests in Syria are part of this development. They should be a wake-up call for countries in the region to honour their promises and offer meaningful support to a nation emerging from 13 years of devastating war.

They also make one thing clear: a country like Syria cannot rebuild its economy on pledges made at high-profile fundraising events. Several Syrian officials have said that most of those who made such promises have failed to deliver.

Syria also needs economic policies that reflect the realities of life after war. For now, it cannot afford to throw its markets wide open to trade with larger, more stable economies.

Israel has played a major part in making the crisis worse. Its repeated strikes and incursions into southern Syria, along with its support for a separatist project in Suwayda, have frightened off investors and delayed projects across the country.

I recently read a compelling analysis suggesting that Turkish business leaders are now less inclined to invest in major projects in Damascus because of Israel’s repeated strikes and expansionist ambitions. Instead, they are likely to focus on Aleppo and other northern cities, which are closer to Türkiye and seen as more stable.

May God protect Syria and its beloved people, and help them through this crisis soon…!

GAME PREDICTION

Kansas City Chiefs vs Denver Broncos
NFL · Sep 14 · 8:15 PM ET

Expert AI commentary
Denver rides an impressive preseason trajectory into Arrowhead, having torched Minnesota 34–6 last week and dominated Atlanta 27–7 earlier. Sam Ehlinger logged 3 TDs across preseason games, showing crisp accuracy and decisiveness that Kansas City's secondary, in transition, may struggle to contain early. Justin Joly (105 receiving yards, 1 TD) provides a reliable target underneath, while Cody Schrader's dual-threat profile keeps defenses honest. Kansas City, conversely, limped through the preseason: losses to the Rams (12–20) and Buccaneers (15–16), plus a 9–9 tie with Seattle suggest offensive timing issues and defensive vulnerability. Garrett Nussmeier has seen limited volume (370 yards, 0 TDs in three games), and the receiver room—Andrew Armstrong, Jake Briningstool—has been quiet. Brashard Smith (130 rushing yards) offers some ground game competence, but Kansas City's preseason offensive line play was spotty.

The passing matchup tilts Denver: Ehlinger's composure and arm talent versus a KC secondary missing continuity is a mismatch Denver can exploit. Denver's edge rushers—supported by a stout front—will apply pressure that forces Nussmeier into uncomfortable windows. Conversely, Brashard Smith and Emmett Johnson represent KC's best avenue to control tempo and keep Denver's offense off the field. Home field and tradition favor Kansas City, but preseason form, recent head-to-head momentum (Denver 20–13 at home in Week 17, 22–19 in Denver in November), and Ehlinger's hot hand suggest Denver walks out with a win. Expect a close, grinding affair with Denver stealing a low-scoring victory in a season opener defined by rust and field position battles.

text:
USDA Nebraska Weekly Livestock Auction Summary for the week ending September 12, 2026

For The Week
The Nebraska livestock market caught a strong second wind through the week ending September 12 as buyers returned to the ringside with aggressive conviction. Following two consecutive weeks of downward corrections, the market rebounded sharply, fueled by active local backgrounder participation, expanding internet bidding, and a larger than normal crowd of order buyers. 

Total auction receipts moderated, with yearlings coming off summer grass and out of grow yards making up the dominant share (95% of feeder volume over 600 lbs). 

Demand rated good to very good across all classes. Yearling steers 650 to 950 lbs posted powerful gains, surging $5.00 to $15.00 higher, while yearling heifers 650 to 1000 lbs traded steady to $15.00 higher compared to recent tests. Meanwhile, direct negotiated feedlot trade stabilized after early month drops, with live sales clearing from $218.00 to $223.00/cwt and dressed trade holding steady around $345.00/cwt.

Price Trends by Class
Feeder Steers
Light calves and short yearlings were offered in limited packages but commanded strong eye appeal, while heavy yearlings found outstanding buyer competition to erase recent losses.

400 to 500 lbs: Light packages and unweaned calves traded from $452.00 to $500.00/cwt.
650 to 700 lbs: Advanced sharply, clearing actively from $387.00 to $393.00/cwt.

700 to 800 lbs: Swept through the rings in a broad, high demand $341.00 to $352.00/cwt baseline.
800 to 900 lbs: Solid volume load lots rebounded to sell between $322.00 and $330.50/cwt.

900 to 1000 lbs: Heavy backgrounded yearlings liquidating in large drafts cleared from $303.50 to $319.50/cwt, with fleshy packages discounted to $284.00/cwt.

Feeder Heifers
Heifer classes saw robust demand, with yearlings matching the steer rally to print gains up to $15.00 higher on open and spayed drafts.

400 to 500 lbs: Light drafts cleared from $410.00 to $495.00/cwt.
550 to 600 lbs: Yearling grow-yard packages averaged $381.00/cwt.
650 to 700 lbs: Maintained strong footing, trading from $334.00 to $357.00/cwt.

700 to 800 lbs: Spayed and open load lots locked down firm lines from $321.00 to $352.00/cwt.
800 to 900 lbs: Cleared from $291.00 to $329.00/cwt.

Over 1000 lbs: Heavy 1005-lb fleshy heifers brought $285.00/cwt.

Slaughter and Negotiated Cash
The direct cash cattle arena leveled off after recent declines, as feedlot managers defended cash lines against further packer pullbacks.

Live Sales: Cleared steady to firm on the week, liquidating the bulk of northern transactions from $218.00 to $223.00/cwt.

Dressed Sales: Held a uniform, steady baseline across northern yards, settling bulk delivered trade at $345.00/cwt.

Weekly Market Tops and Barn Highlights
Feeder Steer: $625.00 /cwt 335 lbs, Crawford Livestock
Feeder Steer: $500.00 /cwt 445 lbs, Crawford Livestock
Feeder Steer: $393.00 /cwt 672 lbs, Ericson Livestock
Feeder Steer: $352.00 /cwt 746 lbs, Ericson Livestock
Feeder Steer: $319.50 /cwt 906 lbs, Ericson Livestock
Feeder Heifer: $525.00 /cwt 330 lbs, Crawford Livestock
Feeder Heifer: $495.00 /cwt 429 lbs, Crawford Livestock
Feeder Heifer: $381.00 /cwt 573 lbs, Ericson Livestock
Feeder Heifer: $352.00 /cwt 775 lbs (Spayed), Ericson Livestock
Bred Cows (Young): $3,300.00 /head 2-4 yr old T1 Stage (~1,301 lbs), Ericson Livestock
Bred Cows (Mid-Age): $3,300.00 /head 5-8 yr old T1 Stage (~1,390 lbs), Ericson Livestock
Bred Heifers: $3,200.00 /head <2 yr old T1 Stage (~898 lbs), Ericson Livestock

Regional Analysis
The Yearling Rebound: Yearling feeder volume dominated auction blocks (representing 95% of feeder cattle over 600 lbs). Order buyers aggressively stepped up to fill late summer and early-autumn backgrounder pens, driving double digit price recoveries across 650 to 950lb classes.

Replacement Interest: Replacement females accounted for 4% of total auction receipts. Demand for young and mid age T1 bred cows remained stable, topping at $3,300.00 per head, while young bred heifers under two years old commanded $3,200.00 per unit.

Supply Distribution: Total auction receipts comprised 88% feeder cattle (59% steers, 41% heifers), 8% slaughter cattle, and 4% replacement cattle.

Looking Ahead
The sharp physical cash rally demonstrates strong underlying feeder demand despite ongoing board fluctuations. USDA's updated national production forecasts have trimmed 2026 red meat expectations down to 24.877 billion pounds due to slower slaughter paces and lighter dressed weights. With feed grain costs remaining somewhat stable, feedlot operators are showing renewed willingness to bid up for green, high performing yearlings, though overall entry breakevens remain tightly tethered to the $218.00–$223.00 live cash anchor.

Buyer’s Analysis
Renewed Aggression: Bidders discarded previous caution, moving away from slow fractional bidding to push yearling weights $5.00 to $15.00 higher across major regional ring sales.

Condition & Health Focus: Green, thin-fleshed yearlings off summer grass commanded prime dollars, whereas drafts carrying heavy feedlot flesh (e.g., 947 to 994lb steers at $284.00–$287.00/cwt) faced severe, multi-dollar discounts.

Upcoming Sales
Valentine Livestock Auction: Thursday September 17, Special Feeder Sale.
Ogallala Livestock Auction Market: Thursday September 17, Regular Feeder Sale.
Burwell Livestock Market: Friday September 18, Special Calf and Feeder Auction. Weighups at 9 AM, regular auction at 11:30 AM.
Lexington Livestock Market: Friday September 18, Special Calf and Feeder Auction.

text:
Individual breakdowns from the @NextUpRecruits camp.

Woodford County SG Rylan Maples. 
(NXN Top 20 All Star) (@Rylanmaples2029) 

Woodford County’s 2029 SG Rylan Maples is now one of the most intriguing prospects in the entire state of Kentucky after moving in from Florida. While watching his film it was obvious he was a deadly 3P Shooter especially off the catch, but he brought and showed off much more of his game at the NextUpRecruits camp on Saturday. 

Game 1 he made his presence known on both sides of the court. Immediately called as the shooter he faced extended individual defense right off the bat. He was able to get a couple buckets at the rim while utilizing high IQ cuts within the available spacing. Being a legitimate 6’5, I was impressed with his defensive IQ and versatility. He switched 1-5, he hard hedged ball screens, and not only played great individual permitter defense, but he also played great help defense and continued to contest shots at the rim. He got his first 3 ball soon after coming off a deep catch, a one step pivot to create space and drained it from near NBA range. 

Game 2 featured some great wings on the other side who matched Rylan’s positional size. Rylan’s jumper wasn’t falling initially this game, but it didn’t stop him from continuing to play hard defense, and rebounding at a high level this game. What he did show off this game is a really tight and advanced ball handle from his film and it was quite clear. On 2 separate occasions he broke down defenders 1 on 1 while going to his left side/hand. The first going between the legs twice, before hard stepping right, spinning back to his left, and hitting a one handed runner. The second was from the top of the key, going left with a power dribble he enters a hop step, and turns and fades from just inside the FT line. He hit multiple mid range fadeaways during this camp and looked on balanced each time. Again his IQ and knowing when to cut also gave him multiple buckets at the rim. Like I said, even without the 3p falling he effects every game. 

Game 3 is where he finally found his touch. Rylan went off and exploded with 27 Points and 7 made 3P’s. Showing off his ability to not only be a standstill catch-shoot guy, he created space with his handle and knocked down multiple 3’s to show off another level of his game. As far as I know that is the most 3’s made in a game at the entire camp. 

Overall, Rylan exceeded my expectations and really proved he’s been working everywhere to become an elite overall player, and a dangerous scorer. His ball handling ability is noticeably better than what it has been, and he’s worked on using that advantage to create space and knockdown shots at a high level. This is a future 25-30 PPG scorer in his high school career. The entire game is coming together at exactly the right time and with exceptional positional size he has all the advantages to be one of the most dangerous scorers in Kentucky this season, regardless of class. 

I got the awesome opportunity to interview Rylan while at the NextUpRecruits Camp, he continues to work hard everyday on his game and his main goal remains the same with some big dream offers in mind! 

Coaches, make sure you follow Rylan Maples and keep up with his progression.

text:
With No Assimilation, Migrants Threaten Europe

Victor Davis Hanson, August 30, 2025: August 30, 2025

Almost weekly in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France, and Germany, a sensational assault committed by an illegal migrant—often enjoying some sort of state support or with prior arrests for the same crime—surfaces.

Until recently, European politicians and the media sought to either ignore such news or accuse those who clamored for tighter borders, more police protection, and stiffer penalties of being “racists” or “xenophobes.”

Until recently, that is.

Mass protests are now common in Britain against the Labour Party’s open borders policies and generous welfare entitlements for immigrants who arrive illegally and without authentic “political refugee” status.

Greek officials, also swamped by illegal immigration, now cite President Donald Trump’s secure border policies as new models for their own.

The majority of European immigrants now come from majority-Muslim countries in the Middle East and North Africa. Yet many arrivals seem angrier at their newfound liberal hosts than at the dictatorships they fled back home.

Europe’s immigration policies will not work in a multi-ethnic democracy.

Too many immigrants are arriving too quickly, without sufficient diversity, language fluency, skills, or familiarity with the customs and culture of their host nations. They often enter with separatist religious and cultural values antithetical to the very place they seek refuge.

Yet, there is no European plan of civic education to assimilate immigrants and teach them the rules, laws, and culture of their hosts.

It is then no surprise that what follows is ghettoization, resentment, and loud attacks on the very nation in which they seek sanctuary, denouncing it as decadent and godless.

In the past, Europe’s anemic military budgets, reliance on borrowed money, socialism, and a once-strong economy papered over these existential challenges of illegal immigration.

Or, as left-wing former German chancellor Angela Merkel once inanely said of massive illegal influxes into Europe, “Wir schaffen das” (“We can do this”).

But, of course, Merkel could not.

She offered zero plans on how to integrate, assimilate, and acculturate millions of Europe’s illegal aliens. Now, some 15% of Germany’s population are foreign nationals.

Unfortunately, the statist economies of high-cost Europe are stagnating.

Massive welfare outlays, coupled with a shrinking and aging native population—with a birth rate sinking below 1.4—are finally slowing economic growth.

Current German Chancellor Friedrich Merz put the dilemma bluntly: “The welfare state as we have it today can no longer be financed with what we can economically afford.”

Yet the more socialism ossifies, the more popular culture still demands free benefits that a shrinking number of taxpayers can no longer provide.

The United States is finally taking the opposite approach of cracking down on illegal immigration, deregulating the economy, and unleashing high technology to fast-track new frontiers of artificial intelligence, robotics, cryptocurrency, and genetic engineering.

Often, Europe’s best and brightest—and frustrated—are migrating to greater opportunities and freedom in the U.S., further hampering European research and development.

Europe foolishly adopted a self-defeating energy policy to achieve net-zero emissions by subsidizing inefficient wind and solar power while ignoring or shutting down far cheaper natural gas, nuclear, and coal-powered electrical generation.

Meanwhile, China, grinning like a Cheshire cat and caring little about its carbon footprint, is eagerly exporting wind and solar systems to the suicidal West.

Yet China itself is busy building about two massive coal-fired plants a month, and the largest and most environmentally disruptive hydroelectric projects in the world.

No wonder average European electricity costs are even steeper than those in failing California. European consumers often cannot afford to turn their heaters and air conditioners on, while businesses cannot compete with industries abroad that enjoy far cheaper power.

Trump has declared that the 80-year postwar order is calcified and that the U.S. will no longer run huge trading deficits with European Union nations. Instead, it will demand symmetrical tariffs, further challenging past European mercantile profitability.

The days of Europe disarming and relying on the United States for defense are also over, given that Russian leader Vladimir Putin, for the third time in 15 years, invaded a neighboring country.
Yet Ukraine is not Chechnya or Georgia, but instead on the doorstep of Europe.

So in panic, a perennially delinquent NATO is not only promising to spend the required 2% of gross domestic product on defense but also increasing arms budgets to 5% of GDP, a higher rate even than that of the U.S.

No one knows how Europeans will afford such massive rearmament.

To do so would require opening up their economies, adopting far more flexible and traditional energy policies, securing their borders, ending illegal immigration, pruning the welfare state, increasing their fertility rates, and dropping the diversity, equity, and inclusion salad bowl while re-embracing the melting pot of integration and acculturation.

We will soon see whether Europeans can adopt such needed reforms, or find the necessary medicine worse than their current crippling continental disease.

text:
COMPANY-SPECIFIC IMPLICATIONS

Valero has a strong operational fit with a diesel-led export-margin thesis because of its large refining platform and access to U.S. and international fuel markets. Its 2Q 2026 disclosure reported approximately 3.0 million b/d of refining throughput and $4.4 billion of adjusted refining operating income. The investment implication is incremental upside on an already highly profitable operating base, not a transition from depressed margins to normal profitability. Diamond Green Diesel adds separate exposure to renewable transportation fuels, but its economics also depend on feedstock costs and other segment-specific factors. Valero’s operating leverage is attractive only to the extent that realized petroleum margins improve beyond the substantial profitability already achieved. Valero Energy

Marathon Petroleum also has substantial exposure through its Gulf Coast, Midcontinent, and West Coast system. It reported approximately 2.9 million b/d of throughput and $6.655 billion of refining and marketing adjusted EBITDA in 2Q 2026. Its geographic breadth creates several potential channels of benefit, including export-linked Gulf Coast pricing and stronger inland product values. However, the consolidated investment is not a pure refining-margin exposure because the midstream business contributes materially to earnings and valuation. Valero and Marathon are strong operational candidates for the thesis, but the distinction between physical suitability and attractive share-price entry remains essential. PR Newswire

Phillips 66 should also benefit from stronger realized transportation-fuel margins, but its consolidated earnings exposure is diversified across refining, midstream, chemicals, marketing, and renewable fuels. The company reported 96% crude utilization, an 86% clean-product yield, and $3.307 billion of refining adjusted EBITDA in 2Q 2026. Those operating metrics support meaningful product-market exposure, but they do not establish its incremental diesel yield or the amount of September margin expansion it will capture. Chemical feedstock costs, commercial positions, geographic exposure, and the contribution of other businesses can make its equity response differ from that of a more refining-concentrated company. Phillips 66 Investors

PBF Energy offers potentially significant exposure to tighter coastal product markets, but operating reliability and actual crude costs are particularly important. Its current baseline must incorporate the completion of the Martinez restart in May 2026; treating Martinez as still unavailable would materially misstate the company’s operating position. PBF also reported reducing gross debt by more than $1 billion during 2Q 2026. The potential upside should therefore be assessed against a restored operating footprint and changed balance sheet, while separating recurring refining earnings from insurance receipts and other special items. Strong regional product prices are valuable only while the company can manufacture the products it is committed to supply. PBF Energy Investor Relations

HF Sinclair is a more geographically differentiated exposure. Its refineries are located in Kansas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Wyoming, Washington, and Utah, with product markets concentrated in the Southwest, Rockies, Pacific Northwest, and neighboring Plains states. Much of its benefit would be transmitted through regional pricing and replacement economics rather than a direct Gulf Coast export channel. Inland supply access can be advantageous, but the realized result depends on local inventories, transportation constraints, feedstock differentials, and regional demand. It should not be modeled as a smaller version of a predominantly export-oriented Gulf Coast system. HF Sinclair Investor Relations

Among smaller refiners, Delek’s Texas, Arkansas, and Louisiana footprint and CVR Energy’s Midcontinent refining exposure create different regional sensitivities. Par Pacific adds Hawaii, Washington, Wyoming, and Montana exposure, making Pacific product availability and individual refinery economics particularly relevant. These companies may have substantial equity sensitivity to margin changes, but smaller corporate size does not establish superior exposure to Saudi diesel displacement. Regional basis, operating concentration, financing requirements, and the mix of nonrefining businesses can dominate the response. Delek US Holdings

Capacity changes must also be reflected accurately. Phillips 66 identifies its Los Angeles refinery as idled, while Valero’s Benicia plan involved phased idling in 2026 and continued supply through inventories and imports. Higher California product prices should not be applied as manufacturing-margin upside to inactive capacity. Remaining operating facilities may benefit from regional scarcity, while businesses with contractual supply obligations but insufficient production may instead face expensive replacement purchases. Phillips 66

Integrated producers require a different framework. ExxonMobil owns 50% of SAMREF through its subsidiary, so a SAMREF production loss would directly offset part of any benefit from stronger margins elsewhere. Upstream operations, other refining assets, chemicals, and trading further complicate the net exposure. Integrated oil companies should not be treated as interchangeable substitutes for independent U.S. refiners in a Saudi refinery-feedstock disruption thesis. Samref

QUANTIFYING THE EARNINGS AND CASH-FLOW SENSITIVITY

A useful illustrative calculation begins with actual product exposure rather than total crude capacity. For a hypothetical refinery processing 300,000 b/d with a 35% diesel yield, a $10/bbl improvement in the realized diesel crack would add approximately $1.05 million per day, or $31.5 million over 30 days, before offsets. The benefit is not $10 multiplied by all 300,000 b/d because diesel represents only part of the refinery’s output.

Assume the same refinery has a 45% gasoline yield and gasoline cracks weaken by $3/bbl. That would offset approximately $12.15 million over 30 days. If 40% of crude throughput also incurs a $3/bbl deterioration in its acquisition differential, another $10.8 million would be lost. The remaining benefit would be approximately $8.55 million over 30 days before other cost changes. These are illustrative assumptions, not forecasts, but they show how a favorable diesel headline can translate into a much smaller improvement in total refinery profitability.

At the corporate level, every $1/bbl improvement in realized margin across 1 million b/d of throughput produces approximately $30 million of incremental pretax earnings over 30 days, assuming unchanged throughput and other costs. A sustained $5/bbl improvement would produce approximately $150 million over 30 days or $450 million over 90 days. The relevant variable is the captured margin after crude and product basis effects, not the largest quoted benchmark crack.

The timing is important. A disruption beginning in mid-September affects only part of 3Q, and a multieweek event can distribute its earnings impact across 3Q and 4Q. Applying a full-quarter sensitivity to the September event would overstate the immediate quarterly contribution unless comparable margin strength was already present earlier in the quarter. Conversely, product prices can respond before refinery runs actually decline, so earnings recognition does not begin only when the first Saudi unit reduces throughput.

Higher earnings also need not produce an identical contemporaneous increase in cash. For an illustrative 1 million b/d business with 20 days of net inventory-related exposure, a $20/bbl increase in value could require approximately $400 million of additional working capital before offsets from supplier credit, financing, or hedging. Inventory accounting, cash settlement of hedges, receivable timing, and replacement-product purchases can create substantial differences between headline margins, reported earnings, and cash available for debt repayment or shareholder distributions.

DURATION AND SEVERITY SCENARIOS

In a rapid-restoration scenario, sufficient pipeline flow resumes before local inventories become binding. Saudi refinery production and product loadings remain largely intact, although some deliveries may be delayed. Product risk premiums would then have scope to reverse. Crude prices or sour-grade premiums could remain elevated if export capacity recovers more slowly than refinery feedstock supply. This is the clearest scenario in which a continuing pipeline impairment can coexist with limited refining-margin upside or even margin pressure.

In an intermediate scenario, inventories and partial restoration support some facilities, but actual incremental refinery runs fall by an illustrative 600,000 b/d for 30 days. Assuming a 50% diesel/gasoil yield and 25% gasoline yield, that would remove approximately 300,000 b/d of diesel/gasoil and 150,000 b/d of gasoline: 9 million barrels and 4.5 million barrels, respectively, over the month. These yield assumptions are deliberately illustrative rather than plant-specific estimates. The net international shortage would be smaller to the extent that inventories, alternative production, imports, or consumption reductions compensate.

In a severe scenario, prolonged feedstock interruption, additional infrastructure damage, and shipping constraints cause much larger incremental run reductions. An assumed 1.5–1.8 million b/d loss at a 50% diesel/gasoil yield would imply approximately 750,000–900,000 b/d of missing diesel/gasoil production. That is a stress case, not an established loss, and requires evidence that the affected throughput was actually operating before the event. Under those conditions, prompt product pricing could become highly nonlinear, with competition for immediately available cargoes and forced consumption adjustment more important than normal refining-margin relationships.

The transition between these scenarios need not be smooth. Local inventories can conceal the physical effect initially, followed by a rapid reduction in operations when usable stocks approach minimum levels. Partial restoration can then sharply reduce the expected shortage before the entire pipeline is repaired. A single repair-duration headline therefore provides less information than the joint path of restored flow, refinery rates, usable inventories, and product loading commitments.

VALUATION, DEMAND DESTRUCTION, AND POLICY RISK

The principal valuation error would be capitalizing a temporary scarcity premium as permanent earnings. A refinery generating an incremental $150 million of pretax profit during a 30-day event has earned an event-specific cash-flow benefit, subject to taxes and working capital. It has not necessarily acquired a permanently higher annual earnings capacity. Longer-term value depends on whether the event changes normalized industry utilization, operating costs, required inventories, capital spending, or the expected frequency of disruption.

There is also a substantial distinction between good operating exposure and an attractive trade. U.S. refiners were already reporting strong earnings before this attack. The relevant comparison is therefore incremental realized profitability versus the expectations embedded in share prices, consensus forecasts, and the product forward curve. A physically bullish development can produce poor equity returns if a more severe or longer disruption was already priced. Conversely, sustained margins beyond the currently assumed restoration window could create earnings upside even without a further rise in spot cracks.

Demand destruction is not merely a remote downside scenario. The September IEA report forecast a 2.5 million b/d decline in global oil demand during 2026, with weakness concentrated in middle distillates and petrochemical feedstocks, particularly in Asia. Further product-price escalation could support near-term scarcity margins while reducing the volume of fuel ultimately consumed. Refiners can therefore benefit from the initial shortage and subsequently face weaker demand and margin normalization. IEA

Government intervention represents another uncertainty. Reuters reported on September 11 that the White House was considering use of the Defense Production Act to expand U.S. refining capacity, without a final decision. Capacity expansion or efficiency projects would not constitute an immediate replacement for a multieweek product shortfall. Any separate intervention affecting exports, product specifications, inventory releases, or industry economics would need to be evaluated on its actual terms rather than assumed in advance. Reuters

Crude-stock releases can alleviate feedstock scarcity where crude is the binding constraint, but they do not directly supply diesel. When distillation, hydroprocessing, hydrogen, or product logistics are already constrained, additional crude cannot be converted instantly into the required finished fuels. Similarly, unusually high market margins increase the opportunity cost of an outage but do not eliminate maintenance requirements or justify assuming that every U.S. refinery can operate continuously through the event.

WHAT WOULD CONFIRM OR WEAKEN THE INVESTMENT THESIS

The strongest confirmation would be documented incremental run cuts at previously operating Saudi refineries, sustained reductions in product-loading programs, and strengthening freight-adjusted U.S. export netbacks. Rising diesel futures alone would be less conclusive. A stronger thesis requires evidence that product realizations are improving faster than actual crude acquisition costs and that the U.S. facilities expected to capture the opportunity remain operational.

The most important disconfirming evidence would be restoration of enough pipeline flow to protect refinery feedstock, continued Saudi product exports supported by inventories, alternative crude receipts, or weaker foreign product demand. Another adverse combination would be rising medium- and heavy-sour crude costs without corresponding improvements in the U.S. product basket. Company-specific unplanned outages could also turn an apparent beneficiary into a purchaser of expensive replacement fuel.

Monitoring should distinguish prompt stress from persistent earnings improvement. The relevant indicators include confirmed pipeline throughput, refinery operating rates, product cargo cancellations, physical diesel premiums, the shape of the diesel forward curve, actual sour-crude differentials, and export prices after freight. An hourly exception-based alert focused on confirmed changes in those variables would be more useful than indiscriminate alerts for additional attack headlines.

The overall implication is selectively positive for U.S. refiners and most clearly bullish for diesel and gasoil availability, conditional on actual incremental Saudi production losses. Jet fuel also faces upside risk, while gasoline, naphtha, and residual products require more differentiated treatment. Valero and Marathon have strong operational alignment with an export-linked refining thesis; Phillips 66, PBF, HF Sinclair, and smaller refiners offer materially different combinations of geographic exposure, feedstock economics, operating concentration, and corporate diversification.

The decisive distinction is between an impaired crude-transport system and an impaired finished-product supply system. A prolonged shutdown that removes Saudi refinery output while U.S. plants retain feedstock and operating availability would materially strengthen U.S. refining economics. A partial restart that protects Saudi refineries but leaves international crude supply constrained could deliver a much smaller benefit. The approximately 1.8 million b/d headline identifies the potential scale of exposure; actual refinery operations, inventories, and realized product-versus-feedstock margins determine the investable earnings consequence.

text:
Six Strangers, One Rope of Hands: The Night a Drowning Dog Refused to Let a Flooded Canal Win

Nobody on that bridge planned to become part of a rescue chain that night. They were just passersby — a woman walking home, two teenagers filming a swollen river for their story, a man on his way to buy bread. And then, in the space of about twenty seconds, an ordinary evening turned into one of those moments that separates people who watch from people who act.

Below them, a concrete spillway roared. Rainwater had turned a normally tame urban channel into something closer to a wild river: brown, frothing, and fast enough to swallow anything that fell into it without so much as a splash to mark the loss. And right at the edge of that churn, paddling for its life against a current that outmatched it in every way, was a small black dog.

This is the story of what happened next — and why a shaky, vertical phone video of it has now been watched by more people than will ever read a headline about the weather event that caused it in the first place.

A City Built Around Water, and the Storm That Turned On It

Cities that grow up around rivers, canals, and drainage channels make a quiet bargain with the water. Most days, the arrangement barely registers. The channel is a pleasant strip of blue-grey, maybe lined with a walking path, a few benches, a low railing where people lean to watch ducks or throw in bread. Kids ride bikes along it. Dogs get walked along it. It is, for 350-something days a year, furniture.

Then a storm arrives that the drainage system wasn't built for, and the bargain gets renegotiated without anyone's permission.

That's what had happened here. Heavy rain upstream had pushed the water level up the concrete banks until the current went from "background noise" to "genuinely dangerous" in the space of an afternoon. The spillway — a long, sloped concrete apron built specifically to manage overflow during exactly this kind of event — was doing its job, sheeting a fast, shallow torrent of muddy water down into the main channel below. It's an engineered feature, designed to protect the city from flooding. It was never designed with a small dog in mind.

Somewhere along that stretch, whether it slipped near the edge, was startled by the noise and force of the rushing water, or simply misjudged how strong the current had become, the dog went in.

The Moment Everything Changes

There's a particular kind of silence that falls over a crowd right before someone decides to move. It's not literal silence — people are still talking, some are already shouting, phones are already being pulled out — but there's a beat, a held breath, where everyone is doing the same math: how bad is this, really?

For the small black dog fighting the current at the base of the spillway, the math was brutal. The water wasn't just fast; it was relentless, the kind of current that doesn't let up for a second to let a swimmer catch their bearing. Every few moments a fresh surge would push against the dog's body, dragging it sideways, spinning it, testing whether four paddling legs could out-muscle physics. They couldn't, not for long. The dog was being pinned against the base of the sloped wall — close enough to solid ground to look almost within reach, and yet completely unable to climb the wet, slick concrete on its own.

That's the cruelest kind of danger: visible safety, inches away, entirely unreachable.

Above, on the pedestrian bridge and the railed walkway that ran along the top of the spillway, a crowd had already begun to gather. Someone had spotted the dog. Then someone else. Within moments there were a dozen people lined up along the railing, phones raised, voices rising over each other — not idle gawking, but the particular urgency of people watching a life hang by a thread and realizing that watching alone wasn't going to save it.

Somebody Has to Go Down There

Here is the part of the story that video footage captures with a bluntness that words struggle to match: the moment a man swings his legs over the railing.

He isn't wearing rescue gear. He isn't a firefighter, or at least there's nothing in his appearance that marks him as one. He's dressed like someone who left the house an hour earlier expecting a normal evening — casual clothes, ordinary shoes, nothing built for grip on wet concrete. And yet, without a visible pause for deliberation, he goes over the barrier and starts moving down the steep, slick face of the spillway toward the water.

It should be said plainly: this is an extraordinarily risky thing to do. Wet, angled concrete is one of the most unforgiving surfaces a human body can try to stand on. A fast-moving flood channel is not a swimming pool; if a person's footing goes, the same current dragging the dog around like a leaf could just as easily take a grown adult. Rescue professionals train for years to do controlled water rescues precisely because untrained attempts go wrong with sobering frequency. Nothing about this article is meant to suggest that climbing down a flooded spillway after an animal is the "correct" way to handle this kind of emergency — in almost every version of this story that doesn't end well, it starts exactly like this one did.

But intention and risk assessment are not always in the driver's seat when someone is watching a small, terrified creature drown twenty feet below them. Instinct got there first.

Building a Chain, One Grip at a Time

What happens next is the part of the video people replay.

The first man doesn't try to walk all the way down to the water alone and haul the dog up single-handedly — not because it's a considered strategy so much as because the slope is too steep and too slick for any one person to hold their footing that far down while also managing a panicked, soaked animal. Instead, almost spontaneously, a second person follows him over the railing. Then a third. Within moments, what began as one impulsive decision becomes something that looks almost choreographed: a human chain, each person gripping the hand, wrist, or jacket of the one above them, extending down the concrete slope toward the water like a rope made of people.

It's worth pausing on how fragile that chain actually is. Every link is a person standing on a wet, angled surface with nothing to hold onto but another person. If any one of them loses footing, the physics of the slope means they don't just fall — they could easily take the people below them down too, sliding toward the same current that's already fighting the dog. There's no safety harness, no rope tied to the railing, no coordinated rescue plan called in over a radio. There is only trust: trust that the hand above you will hold, trust that your own grip will hold the person below.

And yet they keep extending it. One more person climbs over. Then another. The chain reaches further down the slope, closer to where the dog is being tossed against the base of the wall by the current.

The Reach

The final man in the chain — the one closest to the water, braced as best he can be on the wet concrete with the others holding his weight from behind — leans out toward the dog.

This is the moment the whole rescue turns on. The dog has to be within reach, which it barely is, thanks to the current periodically shoving it up against the concrete base rather than sweeping it further downstream. And the dog has to be grabbable — not biting in panic, not thrashing in a way that makes a firm grip impossible, not swept away by a surge in the exact half-second the hand reaches out.

None of that is guaranteed. Panicked animals in the water are unpredictable; fear can make even the gentlest dog snap at anything that touches it, and a current can undo a rescue attempt in less time than it takes to describe. But this time, the hand connects. Fingers close around the scruff of the dog's neck and the loose skin along its back — not gently, because gentle doesn't work in that kind of current, but firmly enough to fight the water's pull.

And then the chain reverses.

Passing a Life Up a Wall of Concrete

What follows is, in its own way, more impressive than the initial reach. Pulling a soaked, thirty-some-pound dog against a current up a steep, slippery slope is not a one-person job, and the men on the spillway seem to understand that instinctively. The dog is passed — hand to hand, grip to grip — up the human chain, each person taking hold for just long enough to move it one link higher before passing it to the person above.

It's not smooth. The dog struggles. Feet scrabble for purchase on concrete that offers none. At one point the animal appears to twist half-free, caught only by a fistful of fur and the quick reflexes of whoever's holding on. Down below, the water keeps rushing past, indifferent, ready to reclaim anything that slips.

But link by link, the dog moves upward. Away from the current. Away from the base of the wall. Toward the railing, toward the crowd, toward solid ground.

By the time the dog reaches the top of the slope, there are hands from multiple directions all reaching for it at once — the original chain of rescuers, plus people who'd stayed at the railing now leaning over as far as they can to help finish the job. Someone gets a proper hold under the dog's front legs. Someone else steadies its back half. And then, in one final motion, the dog is lifted bodily up and over the railing, back onto the walkway, back onto ground that isn't trying to sweep it away.

What the Crowd Sounds Like When It Works

Video from the scene captures something that's easy to overlook amid the drama of the rescue itself: the sound of the crowd the moment the dog clears the railing. It's not a single reaction — it's overlapping voices, a ragged mix of relief and something close to disbelief, the sound of a dozen people who'd been silently rehearsing the worst-case outcome suddenly not needing to.

That sound matters, because it's a reminder of what was actually being risked here, and by whom. Every person who climbed over that railing to form the chain was, in a very real sense, gambling their own safety on a stranger's dog. None of them knew whose pet it was, whether it had an owner searching for it somewhere nearby, or whether it was a stray that had simply been in the wrong place when the storm hit. It didn't matter. The animal was in trouble, and that was reason enough.

Why We Can't Look Away From Videos Like This

There's a reason clips like this one spread the way they do — shared, re-shared, captioned in a dozen languages, watched by people who will never set foot anywhere near the city where it happened. It isn't just that the footage is dramatic, though it certainly is. It's that it compresses something people want to believe about human nature into twenty-odd seconds of unedited, unscripted, entirely unglamorous footage.

Nobody involved is a professional. Nobody is wearing a uniform. Nobody had time to think about how this would look on camera, whether they'd be praised or criticized, whether the risk was "worth it" by any rational calculation. A group of strangers looked at a small animal in mortal danger and, almost without discussion, decided that letting it drown while they watched from safety was simply not an option they were willing to live with.

That instinct — the one that makes a person climb over a railing toward a flooded channel for an animal they've never met — isn't something you can train into existence. Either it's there, waiting for the right (or wrong) moment to surface, or it isn't. Videos like this one are, in a strange way, proof that it's there far more often than cynicism would suggest.

The Part of the Story That Deserves a Warning Label

It would be irresponsible to tell this story without being honest about how easily it could have gone differently.

Fast-moving floodwater is one of the most underestimated hazards in any city. It doesn't need to be deep to be lethal — knee-height water moving at speed can knock an adult off their feet, and once you're down, the same current that swept a dog off its feet will do the same to a person, except a person weighs more, has less natural swimming instinct in a panic, and is often wearing clothes and shoes that work against them rather than for them. Concrete spillways like the one in this video are frequently coated in a thin biological film — algae, silt, the residue of countless overflow events — that makes them treacherously slick even when they look merely damp.

Every safety agency that deals with water rescue says some version of the same thing: don't enter fast water to save an animal. Call trained responders. Throw something that floats. Use a pole, a branch, anything that extends your reach without requiring you to enter the current yourself. This isn't advice offered to diminish what happened in this video — the men who went over that railing did something genuinely brave, and it worked. It's advice offered because "it worked this time" is not the same as "it was safe," and the difference between the two has ended tragically for rescuers, human and canine both, more times than anyone likes to count.

The honest, slightly uncomfortable truth sitting underneath this feel-good story is that it's also a story about how narrow the margin was between a viral rescue video and a very different kind of headline.

What Happens to a Dog After a Rescue Like This

Video footage rarely follows a story past its most dramatic frame, and this one is no exception — the clip ends with the dog back on solid ground, shaking off water, clearly exhausted and disoriented but alive. What happens in the minutes, hours, and days after is, in cases like this, usually a quieter story that plays out away from any camera.

Dogs pulled from cold, fast-moving water are typically checked over for injuries sustained while being tumbled against concrete or debris, for signs of exhaustion or shock, and for secondary complications like aspiration of contaminated floodwater into the lungs, which can cause problems hours or even a day or two after the initial event even when the animal seems fine in the immediate aftermath. Anyone in a similar situation — pulling any animal from floodwater, whether it's a beloved family pet or a stray nobody recognizes — is generally well advised to have it looked over by a vet, even if it seems to walk away unscathed, precisely because some of the real dangers of near-drowning don't announce themselves immediately.

Whether this particular dog belonged to someone in the crowd, someone nearby who'd been searching for it, or no one at all, one thing was already true the moment it cleared that railing: on that stretch of flooded channel, on that particular evening, its survival stopped being a matter of luck and became a matter of a half-dozen strangers deciding it would be.

The Chain That Didn't Need a Plan

If there's a single image from this story worth holding onto, it isn't the dog paddling in the current, dramatic as that moment is. It's the chain — six, seven, maybe more people, none of whom had met each other twenty minutes earlier, linking hands down a slope none of them had any business standing on, because somewhere in that chain was a shared, wordless agreement that a life was worth the risk.

Nobody organized it. Nobody was in charge. There was no whistle, no countdown, no plan beyond the most basic version of one person reaching toward danger and everyone else, instinctively, making sure that person didn't have to reach alone.

That's the whole story, really, stripped of its adrenaline and its warnings and its viral-video packaging: a dog fell into water that wanted to keep it, and a handful of strangers on a bridge decided, individually and then collectively, that they weren't going to let it.

The current lost. That's rare enough, in stories like this, to be worth telling.

Not the First Dog, Not the Last Flood

Anyone who spends time around rescue services, animal shelters, or simply the darker corners of the internet's video archive knows this story isn't unique in its shape, even if every version of it feels singular in the moment. Flooded drainage channels, engineered to move stormwater quickly and efficiently out of populated areas, are quietly one of the more dangerous features of modern cities precisely because they're designed to be invisible on ordinary days. A channel that's ankle-deep and lazy in July can become a genuine hazard within an hour of sustained rainfall, and animals — off-leash dogs chasing a scent, cats exploring somewhere they shouldn't, even livestock in more rural versions of this story — have no way of reading a weather forecast or understanding why the "safe" strip of water they know is suddenly behaving like something else entirely.

Search through enough local news archives and you'll find versions of this story from cities on nearly every continent: a dog swept into a canal during a storm, a crowd gathering, someone going in after it, sometimes successfully, sometimes not. Fire departments in flood-prone regions increasingly train specifically for animal rescues in exactly these conditions, because the pattern is common enough to justify dedicated equipment — throw ropes, animal rescue slings, even small inflatable rafts kept on standby during storm season. That kind of institutional response, when it arrives in time, is unambiguously safer than a chain of untrained bystanders on wet concrete. The trouble is timing. Professional responders, however well-equipped, usually need minutes to arrive that a struggling animal in fast water often doesn't have. That gap — between when help is needed and when trained help can physically get there — is exactly the gap that bystanders in stories like this one end up filling, for better and, sometimes, for worse.

What makes this particular video stand out isn't the premise, then, so much as the execution: the sheer number of people willing to extend the human chain, the speed with which the plan (if it can even be called that) assembled itself, and the clean, complete success of the outcome. Plenty of similar rescue attempts end with an animal saved but a rescuer injured, or with the crowd unable to reach the animal in time despite trying. This one, by whatever combination of luck, grip strength, and concrete texture, worked all the way through.

What the Comment Sections Looked Like

Once footage like this leaves the original crowd's phones and starts circulating more widely, it tends to pick up the same handful of reactions in comment sections and shares, translated into whatever language it lands in next. There's the wave of pure relief — people who clearly watched with their hand over their mouth and needed to say something the second the dog cleared the railing. There's the practical contingent, the ones pointing out, correctly, that untrained water rescues carry real risk and that professional responders exist for a reason — a point worth taking seriously even amid the celebration. And there's a smaller, quieter thread of comments from people who've been on the other side of a moment like this themselves: the ones who've climbed over a railing, or waded into water they probably shouldn't have, for a dog, a cat, a stranger's kid, because in the moment it didn't feel like a decision so much as a reflex.

That last group tends to say the same thing, in different words: you don't decide to do it. You just find yourself already doing it, and sort out whether it was a good idea afterward.

How to Actually Help, If You're Ever the One Watching

For anyone who watches a video like this and wonders what they'd do in the same position, there's a version of "helping" that doesn't require climbing over a railing into fast-moving water, and it's worth knowing before the moment arrives rather than during it.

The first and most effective thing most people can do is call for professional help immediately — fire and rescue services in most cities are equipped and trained for exactly this kind of water emergency, and getting them moving toward the scene as early as possible closes that dangerous timing gap mentioned earlier. The second is to look for anything nearby that floats and can be thrown or extended toward the animal without requiring anyone to enter the water themselves: a life ring if one's mounted nearby, a long branch, a rope, even a jacket tied to something sturdy. Reach-don't-enter is the guiding principle rescue trainers repeat for a reason; it's boring advice compared to a dramatic human chain down a spillway, but it's boring because it's designed to prevent exactly the kind of catastrophic chain-reaction failure that turns one victim into several.

If entering the water or a dangerous slope does happen — and, as this story demonstrates, sometimes it does, plan or no plan — doing it with support rather than alone matters enormously. A single person on wet concrete has nothing to arrest a fall. A chain of people, each anchored by the next, at least has a chance of holding if one link's footing slips. It's not a substitute for proper safety equipment, but it's a meaningfully less reckless version of the same instinct.

None of this is meant to lecture the people in this video, who did something brave and effective under real pressure with no equipment and no plan. It's offered instead for the next person who watches this footage and quietly wonders what they would do if they were the one standing at that railing when the dog went in.

A Small Postscript on Bystanders and Bravery

It's tempting, watching footage like this, to sort the people in it into "heroes" and "everyone else" — the men who climbed over the railing versus the crowd that stood and filmed. That framing misses something important, though. Every person in that crowd who pulled out a phone wasn't necessarily choosing spectacle over action; in the chaos of an unfolding emergency, documenting what's happening, calling for help, or simply staying put so as not to add another body to an already precarious human chain are all legitimate, useful roles. Not everyone needs to be the hand that grabs the dog for the rescue to succeed. Sometimes the most helpful thing a bystander can do is exactly what most of that crowd did: stay out of the way, keep watching, and be ready to help pull once the chain reaches the top.

Heroism, in stories like this one, rarely looks like a single person doing something extraordinary alone. It looks like a dozen ordinary decisions, made in the space of half a minute, that happen to add up to a life saved. A man who goes over a railing without a plan. A second man who follows him because the first one clearly can't do it alone. A crowd that doesn't scatter, doesn't just watch, but leans in at exactly the right moment with exactly the right number of extra hands.

None of them will likely think of themselves as remarkable. Ask any one of them afterward, and the answer is almost always some version of the same shrug: anyone would have done it. Anyone didn't, though. They did. And because they did, a small black dog that had every reason to disappear into a flooded canal that evening instead got to shake the water off its coat on solid ground, surrounded by strangers who, for about twenty seconds, had made its survival their only priority.

That's the story the video tells, frame by shaky frame. It doesn't need embellishment. It barely needs narration. It just needs to be watched — and maybe, afterward, remembered the next time it looks like nobody's going to do anything.

#STLCards - The Cardinal Chronicle: Completing the Comeback Season

When I launched the Cardinal Chronicle this spring, the purpose was to cover the 2026 St. Louis Cardinals season in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the 2006 World Series championship and the opening of Busch Stadium. This was always intended to be a one-season comeback, not the beginning of another long-term daily operation.

As the season draws to a close, it is time to honor that original purpose and bring this chapter to an end.

The Cardinal Chronicle will discontinue daily coverage. The website and Facebook page will be shut down by September 30.

My X account will remain active, but it will no longer provide daily Cardinals coverage. I may occasionally share thoughts about the Cardinals, respond to questions, or join a baseball conversation from time to time—but without the demands of operating a full-time publication.

This was not an easy decision. Baseball writing has been part of my life for nearly three decades, from The Birdhouse and the opportunities that followed to covering the Houston Astros and returning once more to cover the Cardinals in 2026.

I am grateful to everyone who read an article, shared a post, offered encouragement, or joined the conversation this season. Whether you were with me years ago or discovered the Cardinal Chronicle during this comeback, thank you for allowing me to share the game with you.

We came back to celebrate the past, cover one more season, and honor a special chapter in Cardinals history. We did that—and now it is time to step away from daily coverage.

Thank you for being part of the journey.

Kindest regards

Ray Mileur
