Appendix A — What Does It Actually Take to Build and Deploy Advanced AI?

Compute, Cost, Accessibility, and the Unknown ASI Threshold

This appendix is intended to provide policymakers with practical scale.

Artificial intelligence is often discussed as though a consumer workstation, an autonomous AI application, a datacenter GPU cluster, a frontier-model training run, and hypothetical artificial superintelligence represent different sizes of the same activity.

They do not.

The computational, financial, infrastructure, and operational requirements can differ by many orders of magnitude.

Most importantly:

There is currently no scientifically established hardware configuration, GPU count, training-compute threshold, parameter count, electrical requirement, or dollar amount that constitutes AGI or ASI.

The following estimates describe existing AI development and deployment scales.

They are not AGI or ASI thresholds.

Level 1 — Individual AI Development

Typical user: Independent developer, student, researcher, hobbyist, small business.

Typical hardware:

Consumer or professional workstation.

One capable GPU, sometimes several.

32–128+ GB system memory.

Fast SSD storage.

Consumer or workstation-class CPU.

Approximate cost:

Roughly $2,000–$10,000+, depending upon GPU, memory, storage, and configuration.

Cloud resources can reduce the upfront cost further.

What can be done:

Run open-weight models.

Build RAG systems.

Develop AI applications.

Perform smaller fine-tuning workloads.

Build coding agents.

Use persistent memory.

Connect AI to tools and APIs.

Create browser-using agents.

Execute code.

Experiment with robotics and computer vision.

Develop autonomous workflows.

This level can produce useful and increasingly sophisticated autonomous systems.

It is not equivalent to independently training a modern frontier foundation model from scratch.

Suggested policy posture:

Freedom to build.

Existing law applies to harmful conduct.

Voluntary S³P Layer 1 practices encouraged.

No general compute registration.

Level 2 — Advanced Individual / Small-Team Compute

Typical user: AI startup, research team, well-funded independent laboratory, advanced developer.

Typical resources:

Multiple GPUs locally or rented cloud accelerators.

Large system memory.

High-speed local storage.

Potential access to H100-, H200-, B200-class datacenter accelerators through cloud providers.

Approximate cost:

A sophisticated locally owned system may reach tens of thousands of dollars or more.

Cloud access changes the economics dramatically because the hardware does not have to be purchased.

As of 2026, commercial providers offer individual high-end datacenter GPUs by the hour.

This means significant AI compute can be temporarily accessed for hundreds or thousands of dollars rather than requiring ownership of a datacenter.

What can be done:

Larger-model inference.

Model fine-tuning.

High-throughput experimentation.

Multi-agent systems.

Persistent autonomous operation.

Tool orchestration.

Code execution.

Large retrieval systems.

Synthetic-data generation.

AI research and evaluation.

Again, significant autonomy does not necessarily require frontier-scale compute.

A system may use an existing model and gain considerable operational capability by connecting that model to software, credentials, APIs, browsers, memory, infrastructure, or other tools.

Suggested policy posture:

Freedom to develop.

Voluntary operational logging.

Permission boundaries.

Human review for consequential actions.

S³P Layer 1 and, where meaningful autonomous operation exists, Layer 2 practices.

Level 3 — Dedicated Multi-GPU AI Infrastructure

At this level the economics begin changing substantially.

Commercial providers already rent interconnected high-end GPU systems.

For illustration, current commercial rates place individual H100-class GPUs at approximately several dollars per GPU-hour, with newer B200-class accelerators costing more.

Consider a simplified example using eight high-end GPUs continuously.

At approximately $4 per GPU-hour:

8 GPUs × $4 × 24 hours = approximately $768 per day.

Thirty days of continuous operation would approach:

$23,000 in GPU rental alone.

A full year at that utilization would approach:

$280,000.

At approximately $7 per GPU-hour for newer hardware:

8 GPUs × $7 × 24 hours = approximately $1,344 per day.

Thirty days approaches:

$40,000.

A year approaches:

$490,000.

These figures are illustrations rather than fixed market prices and exclude some associated engineering, storage, networking, staffing, data, and operational expenses.

What can be done:

Serious model training and fine-tuning.

Large-scale inference.

Extensive evaluation.

Large autonomous workloads.

High-throughput agent operations.

Research requiring substantial accelerator memory and compute.

But even this remains dramatically smaller than the infrastructure used to train some frontier foundation models.

Suggested policy posture:

Still not automatically a national-security issue.

Risk assessment should examine what is being deployed, what authority the system possesses, and what consequences it can produce.

Strong S³P Layer 2 controls may be appropriate for consequential autonomous deployments.

Level 4 — Large AI Cluster

Typical resources:

Tens to hundreds of interconnected datacenter GPUs.

High-speed GPU interconnects.

Dedicated storage infrastructure.

Large datasets.

Specialized networking.

Substantial electrical and cooling requirements.

Dedicated ML and infrastructure engineering.

Illustrative cloud economics:

At 64 GPUs costing roughly $6 per GPU-hour:

64 × $6 × 24 = approximately $9,200 per day.

Approximately $276,000 for 30 days.

At 256 GPUs costing roughly $5.50 per GPU-hour:

256 × $5.50 × 24 = approximately $33,800 per day.

Approximately $1 million for 30 days.

A six-month sustained workload at that scale could therefore move into several million dollars of GPU rental before considering many additional development expenses.

At this level, compute is no longer simply a workstation expense.

It is substantial organizational infrastructure.

Suggested policy posture:

Still evaluate capability and deployment rather than assuming dangerous intent.

However, voluntary security, observability, incident response, containment, and independent evaluation become increasingly reasonable expectations.

Level 5 — Frontier Model Development

This is where comparisons with ordinary AI development become misleading.

Meta disclosed that training Llama 3.1 405B involved more than 16,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs and more than 15 trillion training tokens.

Independent estimates compiled by the Stanford AI Index place training costs for several major models approximately at:

GPT-4 — $79 million

Grok-2 — $107 million

Llama 3.1 405B — $170 million

Gemini 1.0 Ultra — $192 million

These are estimated training costs, not the total lifetime cost of the companies, datacenters, researchers, failed experiments, data acquisition, inference infrastructure, product development, or ongoing operation surrounding the models.

Frontier development therefore involves more than purchasing GPUs.

It requires large accelerator fleets, networking, electrical infrastructure, cooling, storage, enormous datasets, distributed-training software, specialized engineering, research personnel, experimentation, evaluation, and significant capital.

Research into frontier-model economics has estimated that hardware represents approximately half or more of total development cost for major frontier systems, while research personnel represent another substantial portion.

The largest future training runs have been projected to potentially exceed $1 billion if historical scaling trends continue.

That puts contemporary frontier-model development beyond the realistic financial reach of the overwhelming majority of individuals and small businesses.

Training Is Not Deployment

This distinction is essential.

An independent developer does not need to train a $100 million foundation model to build a capable autonomous AI system.

Existing models can be downloaded, rented, accessed through APIs, fine-tuned, quantized, connected to retrieval systems, and integrated with tools.

Therefore:

Frontier training may be extremely expensive while meaningful autonomous deployment can be relatively inexpensive.

Congress should not confuse the two.

A $5,000 workstation could potentially operate software with substantial autonomous functionality by using existing models and external tools.

Conversely, an organization could spend millions on compute while performing benign scientific research.

Compute expenditure alone does not determine risk.

The Scale Distinction

The economics of artificial intelligence create an important distinction for policymakers:

Most Americans can increasingly afford to build with powerful AI. Almost none can afford to independently reproduce today's frontier-scale training infrastructure. And no one has established what compute would be required to create ASI.

All three statements matter.

The first means independent developers, researchers, students, startups, and small businesses increasingly have access to meaningful AI capability.

The second means this accessibility should not be confused with the enormous infrastructure required to reproduce today's largest frontier-model training programs.

The third means policymakers should not treat today's frontier-compute requirements as though they represent a scientifically established threshold for artificial superintelligence.

These are three separate categories:

Accessible AI development is already here.

Frontier-scale model training requires extraordinary capital and infrastructure today.

The compute required for ASI is unknown.

That distinction should remain explicit in any policy discussion involving compute restrictions, hardware controls, open-source development, or hypothetical future superintelligence.

The ASI Question

Artificial superintelligence presents an even more fundamental problem for compute-based regulation.

We do not currently know what would be required to create it.

It may require vastly more computation than today's frontier models.

It may require architectural advances.

It may require scientific discoveries that have not occurred.

Algorithmic efficiency could reduce compute requirements.

It is also possible that the concept will not correspond to a single meaningful hardware threshold at all.

Therefore statements such as:

"10,000 GPUs can create ASI"

or

"$100 million of compute creates superintelligence"

would not presently be scientifically justified.

That uncertainty should be acknowledged rather than hidden.

The Question Congress Should Ask

If hypothetical future superintelligence is used as justification for regulating present-day artificial intelligence, policymakers should ask:

What measurable capability are we regulating?

What evidence demonstrates the danger?

What computational resources are actually necessary?

Can the capability be reproduced independently?

Does owning the compute create the risk, or does deploying a system with particular autonomy and authority create the risk?

Would the proposed restriction meaningfully prevent the identified harm?

What legitimate development would the restriction prevent?

How will the threshold change as hardware and algorithms improve?

These questions should be answered before extraordinary restrictions are imposed.

A Better Risk Equation

AI risk should not be reduced to:

More GPUs = More Danger

A more useful conceptual model is:

Risk = Capability × Autonomy × Access × Authority × Scale × Consequence

Compute contributes to capability.

It is not the entire equation.

A system capable of acting independently with production credentials, financial authority, sensitive information, infrastructure access, and minimal human supervision may deserve substantially stronger safeguards than a much larger model operating inside an isolated research environment.

That is why S³P focuses on operational integrity and increasingly strong safeguards as autonomy and risk increase.

Policy Principle

The United States should preserve the ability of individuals, researchers, startups, universities, and businesses to own computing hardware and develop artificial intelligence.

At the same time, organizations deploying consequential autonomous systems should be encouraged to demonstrate:

Observability.

Auditability.

Permission boundaries.

Human review.

Rollback.

Containment.

Incident response.

Accountability.

And long-horizon stability monitoring.

If future evidence demonstrates that an extraordinary level of aggregate compute creates a specific national-security threat, Congress may then evaluate narrowly tailored safeguards directed toward that demonstrated threshold.

But extraordinary restrictions should follow extraordinary evidence.

They should not precede it.

Freedom to build should remain the default.

Responsibility should increase with capability and deployment risk.

Governance through accountability, not control.

text:
Shares of Oracle fell 5.3% to $144.20 Monday after a weekend of whiplash: 
co-founder Larry Ellison canceled his plan to sell as many as 50 million shares — a holding worth $7.5 billion
 — 
just a day after a regulatory filing disclosed the trading plan, which had been adopted on June 22 and was set to end Oct. 24.
 
The company did not offer a reason for the change in plans.
 The reversal lands at a fraught moment: Oracle is burning cash to fund an AI infrastructure buildout while broader tech stocks slide on interest-rate anxiety.

The Abrupt Reversal Spooked the Market Instead of Reassuring It. 
"No Oracle stock was sold under that plan, and he has no other plans to sell any of his Oracle stock," Oracle said.
 Bulls frame the cancellation as a founder betting on his own company after a 22% year-to-date decline. But the sequence — file, disclose, cancel within 24 hours — raises governance questions and injected volatility at the worst time. 
Oracle shares are down over 50% from their peak of $304.38 a year ago.

Oracle's AI Boom Is Real but Costs Are Staggering. 
Q1 revenue hit a record $19.3 billion, up 30% year-over-year, as cloud infrastructure revenue jumped 121%.
 
Contracted future revenue not yet recognized reached a record $664 billion.
 Yet 
capital expenditures for the quarter were $28 billion, leading to negative free cash flow of $5 billion, and full-year spending is projected at $90–$95 billion.
 Unlike competitors such as Meta or Alphabet, which self-fund data center expansions from enormous cash flows, 
Oracle is funding a hyperscaler-scale expansion from a BBB-rated balance sheet already generating negative free cash flow.

Ellison's Personal Stake Mirrors the Company's Dilemma. 
Ellison controls more than 40% of Oracle
, so any sale would weigh heavily on the stock. 
Oracle stock had fallen roughly 16% to 18% since the plan was adopted in late June, and a person close to Ellison said he views the shares as undervalued.
 Selling into that decline would have locked in steep losses. Keeping shares also keeps his paper wealth tied to an outcome that hinges on converting a $664 billion backlog into real revenue — while Oracle 
raised $43 billion in debt financing last fiscal year and expects to raise approximately $40 billion more through a mix of debt and equity in fiscal 2027.

Bottom line: Ellison's hold signals conviction, but conviction alone won't close the gap between Oracle's massive AI orders and the cash needed to fulfill them. Until free cash flow turns positive, every insider move will be read through that lens.

PAPE: IRAN JUST GRABBED THE OIL ARTERY — NEXT STOP: THE GULF BANKS AND IRAN BECOMES A WORLD POWER.

University of Chicago professor Robert Pape sat down on "At the Waters Edge" on September 13 and said the last three days were not noise. In his read, Iran just tightened a grip on the oil routes that feed the world — and the next move is not more missiles. It is politics over the governments that sit on hundreds of billions in U.S. Treasuries.

THE WEEKEND SHIFT
➡️ Pape says the Houthis now appear to control the Red Sea, and those three days are “shaking the world.”
He calls it pretty bad, and getting worse before it gets better.
➡️ The East-West pipeline that was supposed to bypass Hormuz has been hit and shut, he says, so there are no loadings at Yanbu.
That is not a side show. The host put it near 4% of global oil. Pape did not blink.

THE PLAN HE SAYS WAS ALREADY ON THE CALENDAR
➡️ On June 15 he mapped Iran’s “period of maximum leverage” as three buffers running down: the U.S. SPR, China’s extra buying, and the Houthis.
➡️ Starting July 20, after IRGC advisers landed in Sanaa, the Houthis began hitting Saudi tankers — not random ships.
➡️ Hormuz shipping was already being squeezed again. Then Iran-backed militias in Iraq hit the land pipe.
Pape’s line is blunt: this is a coherent, multi-prong offensive, not a weekend accident. 

THE BYPASS THAT ARRIVED TOO LATE
Scott Bessent’s idea that Hormuz becomes “irrelevant in two years” because of new bypasses is, in Pape’s words, three months late and about $300 billion short.
➡️ “Right in front of our eyes they’re becoming a world power.”
He does not mean Turkey and Pakistan. He means a Persian Gulf core, then a “security resistance belt” from the Mediterranean to the Red Sea to the Gulf.

NO FLEET IS STEAMING IN
Europe, he says after Brussels, is not mustering for the Red Sea. It is staring at Ukraine, Russia, and a dark winter at home.
➡️ The U.S. Navy is tapped out in Hormuz. Japan, Britain, and France cannot magically reopen Bab el-Mandeb.
Flag officers talking B-2 carpet bombing miss the point he has taught for 30 years: air power without a ground or surface “anvil” just scatters the enemy. The Houthis will not sit in a kill box and wait.

THE PRICE PATH HE IS WATCHING
➡️ Oil has gone “straight up” since mid-July. Trump can talk. The tape is not listening.
➡️Diesel, Pape says, is already at a historic U.S. high. Pump prices around $4.30–$4.45 a gallon jumped almost 20 cents in a week. He sees a path over $5, maybe $5.50 — with food riding diesel, not gasoline.
➡️If SPR draws keep the current pace, his sketch has the reserve effectively gone by early April. That is his scenario, not a printed date.

WHAT HE SAYS COMES NEXT
The last three days, in his framing, already put a tight grip on “our artery of oil.”
➡️ The next six months are political: more influence over frontline Gulf capitals — because those central banks hold the Treasuries.
Regime-change logic, he says, is realism 101. If Washington treated it as fair game against Tehran, do not be shocked when Tehran treats Gulf governments the same way. He is describing a trajectory, not announcing a coup.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Pape’s warning is simple. The off-ramps are gone, the buffers are thinning, and the fight has moved from tankers to the map itself. First the oil artery. Then the governments that sit on the money.
Iran is not waiting for a better offer. It is building the leverage while the West argues about who should sail first.

text:
🚨 The active compound in 'magic mushrooms' can prevent debilitating chemotherapy-induced nerve damage.

Chemotherapy is a cornerstone of cancer treatment, yet it often inflicts a grueling toll on patients in the form of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). This condition — characterized by persistent pain, numbness, and extreme sensitivity to cold — frequently forces physicians to prematurely halt or reduce life-saving treatments. 

However, a landmark study published in Science offers a glimmer of hope. Researchers from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center discovered that administering just two doses of psilocybin before chemotherapy cycles protected sensory nerves from damage. Strikingly, this neuroprotective benefit was achieved without compromising the chemotherapy's ability to destroy cancer cells.

The key to this protective effect lies in preserving mitochondrial function. Chemotherapy typically halts the transport of mitochondria, the cellular energy powerhouses, leaving long nerve fibers starved of fuel. 

The researchers demonstrated that psilocybin keeps these energy factories moving, shielding axons in both mouse models and human tissue samples. Impressively, the nerve protection persisted through multiple chemotherapy cycles, marking a monumental shift from traditional palliative care to proactive prevention. Because psilocybin's safety profile is already well-documented, the research team is initiating human clinical trials to fast-track this potential game-changer for cancer survivors worldwide.

source: Heles, M., Pasvolsky, L., Sathishkumar, H., Naara, S., Vu, Y., Stewart, C. L., & Amit, M. (2026). Psilocybin prevents chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy through mitochondrial trafficking preservation. Science, 393(6815).

text:
Senate Republicans dropped their "last, best and final" CLARITY Act text Sunday night ahead of Tuesday's cloture vote. 

The headlines are about Trump agreeing to ethics restrictions. The real story is what got traded away.

The Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act took a serious hit.

The BRCA was the industry's red line. The provision that would settle once and for all that writing non-custodial software, mining blocks, or validating transactions doesn't make you a money transmitter. 

Previous drafts cited 18 U.S.C. Section 1960 twice, explicitly shielding developers and miners from criminal prosecution under the statute DOJ used against Tornado Cash.

The new text cites Section 1960 zero times.

What remains is a civil safe harbor. Developers avoid registration requirements and BSA financial institution treatment. But the explicit criminal shield that would have stopped prosecutors from wielding 1960 against people who write code or run nodes was removed. 

The civil protections are real, and earlier versions already preserved liability for knowingly moving criminal proceeds. But stripping the criminal-code language leaves developers with meaningfully less certainty than previous drafts offered.

Galaxy Digital's Alex Thorn flagged it immediately. "All refs to 18 USC 1960 are GONE."

In exchange? Permanent ethics bans on officials holding crypto, state AG enforcement, a stablecoin "circuit breaker," and tighter exchange conflict-of-interest rules. These are real, documented concessions. But it's hard to ignore that politicians spent a year negotiating who can hold bags while the provision protecting the people actually building got quietly narrowed.

The BRCA was supposed to fix developer ambiguity. This version leaves the question half-answered.

IMHO, the value of commissaries go beyond groceries, they offer a piece of America to the troops, especially those stationed overseas. It's a bit of the familiar, and I fully support that and the discounts that put more money back into the pockets of those in service to this country. I'm glad some of my tax dollars go toward this effort.

Mamdani stores are a gimmick. No reasonable person will agree 1 store, or even 5 stores, can adequately serve a city of 8 million. They will be heavily subsidized and even won't pay taxes; all so they can aim to break-even. There are also numerous existing businesses in the immediate areas, so is it even needed?

Sun Fresh in Kansas City was getting $18M in subsidies, and still closed. In Baldwin FL, the city took over the store, put its staff on municipal payroll, and floated operation costs and expenses, and the store still was forced to close.

This is an exercise in futility, proven in many previous attempts. The money for this performative political stunt can be better used to provide actual goods and services to those in need, i.e. Costco/Sam's Club/BJ memberships. Instead, it will be a yearly guessing game as to how much the subsidies will increase for each store based on its operations and performance.

These stores will become a continuous drain on the tax base and may force the administration to increase the tax burden of residents and/or rob from Peter to pay Paul by shifting budget priorities; all for soundbites, stump speeches, and fleeting self-congratulatory parades on social media.

text:
Kansas taxpayers deserve a government whose authority is measured by faithful performance. BlueprintLiberty’s proposed safeguards begin with a direct principle: tax on authorized events, never existence. Buying a taxable new product or consumer service may trigger a defined tax. Continuing to own a home, farm, or piece of equipment should not. Ownership should provide security, with families able to remain on their property without a recurring tax claim arising simply because another year has passed.

The next principle follows naturally: property rights must be established before government pools resources. Under this proposal, government administers tax dollars as a steward. Taxpayer ownership continues until the corresponding constitutional covenant obligation has been faithfully fulfilled and that fulfillment verified. Collection does not prove fulfillment. Appropriation does not prove fulfillment. Even payment does not prove fulfillment. If Kansas taxpayers finance a road project, the relevant question is whether the authorized work meets its established requirements.

That obligation receives one authorized work cycle, with its boundaries and acceptance standards defined beforehand. Established failure requires immediate correction. It creates no automatic extension, second cycle, or entitlement to additional money. Failure is not an enumerated power. Recoverable amounts go to the taxpayer sinking fund, preserving ownership and attribution rather than becoming an unrestricted balance officials can spend elsewhere.

These protections require clear and fast signals. Taxpayers must be able to distinguish money collected, money committed, money spent, work delivered, and obligations still unmet. Information must arrive while corrective action and meaningful choices remain possible. A report issued after renewal cannot adequately inform the renewal decision.

Liberty also requires built-in exit points. A declining tax provides partial release from government’s claim; terminating that tax completes the exit from that particular obligation. Exempt alternatives and permitted withdrawal offer other pathways. As proposed, NBBF’s four-month decision event can trigger an exit under its governing rules, creating a recurring opportunity to reduce or end a claim. The review itself is not the exit; the enforceable outcome is.

Together, these safeguards establish a practical covenant between taxpayers and government: define ownership, authorize the event, limit the appropriation, verify the result, expose deficiencies, and recover resources when required. Enforcement must use clear evidence, defined responsibility, and due process. Kansas can pursue these changes peacefully through constitutional and legislative reform. The goal is a government that earns continued authority through faithful stewardship, with taxpayers retaining enforceable rights throughout the process and meaningful protection when public obligations go unfulfilled.

text:
It's worth stating the cost differences too. The need for green energy is more likely a desire to keep prices lower for these large corporations so they maximise profits. Green is then subsidised by the general consumer under the guise of net-zero requirements to save the planet.  So as large industrial and hyperscale buyers typically pay far less per kilowatt-hour than households because they take power at high voltage, use it almost continuously, and negotiate special tariffs or long-term contracts. 
https://t.co/0W2C7pgr6h

In the United States the latest EIA figures show residential customers paying about 17–18 ¢/kWh on average, commercial users around 13–14 ¢/kWh and industrial users 8–9 ¢/kWh. That puts typical industrial rates at roughly half the household price. 
https://t.co/eCoYv3BqNS

The very largest data-centre operators go further still. Many lock in power-purchase agreements (PPAs) for new solar, wind or gas generation at 2–6 ¢/kWh, and some reports put Virginia data-centre rates near 5.5 ¢/kWh versus 9–14 ¢/kWh for other local customers. These deals also include demand charges and minimum-load commitments that smaller users never see. 
https://t.co/CxwAyvFo2V

The gap exists because serving a few giant, high-voltage loads is cheaper per unit than serving millions of small homes, and because utilities and generators compete hard for the predictable, creditworthy demand that hyperscalers offer.

text:
Iran War Day 199 SITREP WATCH — WEEKEND READER INSIGHTS

THE DOUBLE WHAMMY: MASS MANPOWER + COMMERCIAL TECHNOLOGY

QUANTITY HAS A QUALITY ALL ITS OWN

14 September 2026 UTC

WARNINGS

Watch developments in the Strait of Bab al-Mandab (BaM). Per prior reporting the pincer movement has been closed and key locations in strait taken to control it.

Upcoming Jewish holidays are not the time for IDF leave (+ have reserve forces ready for deployment) or Israel to let its guard down - just look at history.  

ANALYSIS

The commercial-technology revolution has a second half that may be even more important than AI, drones or satellite imagery themselves:

technology does not replace manpower.

It amplifies manpower.

Iran’s distributive war network is increasingly combining two things that Western military thinking too often considers separately:

large pools of locally available manpower

and

increasingly capable commercial technology available at a fraction of traditional state cost.

That combination is changing the economics of asymmetric warfare.

Weekend Reader — the deeper analysis of Iran’s distributive network, commercial technology and global economic war:

https://t.co/pyzZcpCnQX

YOU CANNOT IRON DOME 10,000 MEN

Northern Israel provides the simplest example.

Israel developed one of the most sophisticated missile- and air-defense architectures in the world.

It can intercept rockets.

It can intercept missiles.

It can intercept drones.

But Hezbollah spent years preparing more than 9,000 Radwan fighters — roughly a 10,000-man assault force — to cross into northern Israel, seize territory and take hostages.

That creates a completely different military problem.

You cannot Iron Dome 10,000 men.

Stopping them requires other men.

Infantry.

Ready reserves.

Local defense.

Persistent surveillance.

Fortifications.

Commanders.

And enough manpower physically present to deny terrain.

A missile interceptor can destroy a missile.

It cannot hold a border.

A fighter aircraft can destroy a target.

It cannot permanently occupy a village.

A drone can observe terrain.

It cannot control that terrain by itself.

Mass still matters.

Now add the commercial-technology revolution to that mass.

Those 10,000 fighters no longer have to operate like the comparatively unsophisticated irregular forces of previous generations.

Increasingly, even a non-state force can gain access to:

commercial satellite imagery;

cheap reconnaissance and attack drones;

AI-assisted analysis;

commercial communications;

smartphones;

digital mapping;

commodity navigation;

computer vision;

open-source software;

and increasingly capable inexpensive precision weapons.

The sophisticated portion of the system does not have to reside inside every fighter.

The technology can reside in the network around him.

That allows relatively ordinary fighters to benefit from reconnaissance, communications, navigation and precision capabilities that once required the infrastructure of a state military.

That is the double whammy:

MASS × COMMERCIAL TECHNOLOGY

The technology raises the capability of the manpower.

The manpower gives the technology dispersion, persistence and the ability to control geography.

Each compensates for the limitations of the other.

Missiles can attack territory but cannot occupy it.

Infantry can occupy territory but historically lacked the surveillance, communications and precision available to advanced states.

Commercial technology is beginning to close part of that gap.

THE HOUTHI AI CELL IS THE MICRO OF THE MACRO

This is why the Houthi AI weapons-development cell revealed by Anthropic matters far beyond one program.

Anthropic identified actors in northern Yemen using Claude to develop guidance, navigation and control software for guided weapons.

They used AI for coding, simulation, guidance development and post-test analysis.

They conducted an actual guided-rocket test and returned to the AI system after it failed.

Anthropic describes the actors as using Claude Code in place of human software engineers for portions of the program. (Anthropic)

That is one detected cell.

One AI company.

One window into the battlefield.

There are other commercial models.

Open-weight models.

Locally hosted systems.

Commercial imagery providers.

Cheap electronics.

Open-source flight-control software.

Millions of commercially available drones.

The identified cell should therefore be viewed as a micro example of the macro transformation.

Commercial technology is lowering the amount of traditional state infrastructure required to generate useful military capability.

The asymmetric actor does not need to reproduce the entire American reconnaissance-strike complex.

It needs enough of its functions to become dangerous.

Good enough to see.

Good enough to communicate.

Good enough to navigate.

Good enough to guide.

Good enough to hit.

That is sufficient lethality.

And sufficient lethality can be obtained at a small fraction of the historical state cost.

NOW ADD THE MANPOWER RESERVOIR

Where does the mass come from?

There is no single cause.

It is the interaction of several conditions.

High fertility and demographic momentum.

Large birth cohorts become large military-age cohorts years later.

Yemen illustrates the scale.

Its population increased from approximately 13.9 million in 1990 to 41.8 million in 2025. (DataBank)

Its fertility rate was approximately 8.6 children per woman in 1990 and remained about 4.5 in 2024. (DataBank)

At the same time, infant mortality fell from approximately 97 deaths per 1,000 live births in 1990 to about 34 in 2024. (DataBank)

That combination matters:

high fertility + improved survival = very large future cohorts.

Then add economics.

Yemen entered the current era with severe unemployment and a labor market incapable of absorbing its rapidly growing youth population.

UNDP was warning before the present war that demographic pressure and youth unemployment were major threats to stability. In 2014 almost half of Yemeni youth were neither in school, training nor employment. (UNDP)

War made the economic alternatives worse.

Then add the social structure.

Tribal and communal networks remain important parts of local organization in Yemen.

Those networks can provide identity, protection, leadership and ready-made structures through which people mobilize.

Then add years of war.

A generation grows up with weapons, checkpoints, militias, political violence and armed organizations as ordinary features of daily life.

Armed groups offer something dysfunctional civilian economies frequently cannot:

money;

food;

status;

belonging;

protection;

purpose;

and a social role.

The United Nations has specifically documented poverty, unemployment, lack of education, ideological indoctrination and the need to support families as drivers of recruitment into Yemen’s armed organizations. (Children and Armed Conflict)

And the scale changes everything.

An armed organization does not need to recruit every young man.

It does not need half of them.

It does not need ten percent.

If the underlying population contains millions of military-age men, recruiting even a small percentage produces an enormous military manpower pool.

Iran’s distributive model is particularly powerful because Iran does not have to supply those people itself.

The nodes supply much of their own manpower.

Yemen supplies Yemenis.

Lebanon supplies Lebanese fighters.

Iraq supplies Iraqi formations.

Iran supplies technology, weapons expertise, components, training, operational knowledge and the network connecting them.

Commercial technology then raises the military value of that locally generated manpower.

THAT IS THE NEW ASYMMETRIC EQUATION

The asymmetric opponent does not need an American-quality force.

It needs enough people.

Enough technology.

Enough weapons.

And enough geography to impose problems upon a much more expensive military.

The defender then faces both dimensions simultaneously:

LOOK UP: drones, missiles and inexpensive precision weapons.

LOOK OUT: thousands of fighters capable of exploiting and controlling the terrain underneath them.

Those threats consume different defensive resources.

That is why manpower remains indispensable.

And it is why commercial technology is potentially revolutionary.

It allows an adversary to keep mass while making the mass substantially more capable.

The West has increasingly pursued another model:

fewer people;

more expensive people;

fewer platforms;

more exquisite platforms;

and technology intended to compensate for shrinking mass.

Iran’s distributive network is moving in the opposite direction:

retain the manpower and add increasingly sophisticated technology to it.

That produces the equation:

COMMERCIAL TECHNOLOGY × ABUNDANT MANPOWER = LOW-COST MASS WITH INCREASINGLY HIGH-END EFFECTS

And because Iran distributes that combination through Yemen, Iraq, Lebanon and other regional nodes, the result is not merely greater tactical lethality.

It produces geographic power.

Relatively inexpensive forces can threaten maritime chokepoints, energy infrastructure, borders, pipelines, cities and military bases across an enormous oil-rich region.

That is how manpower and inexpensive technology become strategic.

AND THERE IS AN UNCOMFORTABLE FINAL PIECE

We did not create Yemen’s high fertility.

We did not create its tribal system.

We did not create its wars, ideology, poverty or political culture.

But the United States and the wider international community have spent billions of dollars sustaining the population through war, famine risk and state collapse.

By February 2023, the United States alone reported more than $5.4 billion in humanitarian assistance to Yemen since the conflict began, explicitly describing that assistance as keeping millions from acute food insecurity and tens of thousands from famine-level conditions. (U.S. Department of State)

That aid saved lives.

It also means something strategically unavoidable:

by helping sustain the population, we also helped sustain the demographic reservoir from which the armed organizations recruit.

The manpower pool did not appear from nowhere.

It was produced by demographics, survival, economics, social structure, ideology and decades of conflict.

And outside aid helped preserve much of that population through the period in which the pool expanded.

That deserves its own analysis.

The next boost will examine U.S. and international aid, Yemen’s population growth from 1990 to today, declining mortality, high fertility and the unintended strategic consequence of helping sustain the manpower base from which an enemy recruiting system draws.

The central point here is simpler:

Technology did not eliminate mass.

Commercial technology is making mass more dangerous.

And Iran’s distributive network possesses both.

If you value analysis that looks past individual attacks to the methods and means changing modern warfare, like and follow the account.

Analysis: my own.

SOURCES FOR ANALYSIS

Anthropic — Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI, September 2026. Primary reporting on the Yemen guided-weapons engineering cell and AI use in conventional-weapons development. (Anthropic)

Anthropic — Measuring Tactical Intelligence Targeting and Conventional Weapons Capabilities of AI Models, September 2026. Anthropic testing showing frontier models performing some military/intelligence tasks historically requiring scarce trained specialists. (Anthropic)

Israel Defense and Security Forum — Turning Point in the North / Israel Weekly War Summary. Source for Hezbollah’s preparation of more than 9,000 and up to approximately 10,000 Radwan fighters for an assault into northern Israel. (IDSF)

World Bank — World Development Indicators. Yemen population: approximately 13.9 million in 1990 to 41.8 million in 2025; fertility and mortality series. (DataBank)

UNDP — Yemen Youth Employment / Country Programme reporting. Youth unemployment, demographic pressure and lack of economic alternatives. (UNDP)

United Nations — Children and Armed Conflict, Yemen. Recruitment drivers including poverty, unemployment, limited educational opportunity, family economic pressure and ideological indoctrination. (Children and Armed Conflict)

U.S. Department of State — Humanitarian Assistance for Yemen. More than $5.4 billion in U.S. humanitarian assistance by February 2023 and documented effects on food security and famine prevention. (U.S. Department of State)

text:
Iran War Day 199 SITREP WATCH — WEEKEND READER

IRAN’S GLOBAL ECONOMIC WAR

14 September 2026 UTC

The five most important developments of the weekend are not five separate stories.

They are parts of one emerging system.

Iran is using geography, a distributive proxy network and rapidly improving commercial technology to turn a regional war into a global economic war.

The battlefield remains concentrated around Iran, the Arabian Peninsula and the two great maritime chokepoints.

The economic effects do not.

Iran does not have to defeat the United States conventionally.

It does not have to sink an American carrier.

It does not have to completely close Hormuz or Bab el-Mandeb.

It only has to make the arteries, bypasses and refining systems connecting Gulf energy to the world sufficiently dangerous, unreliable and expensive that the damage propagates outward through the global economy.

At the same time, commercial technology is lowering the cost of building the weapons, intelligence and targeting systems required to impose that damage.

That combination—geography + distributive warfare + commercial technology—is the larger story.

⸻

1. COMMERCIAL TECHNOLOGY AMPLIFICATION OF ASYMMETRIC WARFARE

The Houthi AI weapons cell is not the story.

It is a micro example of the macro transformation occurring across Iran’s distributive network and modern warfare generally.

Anthropic identified a northern Yemen cell using Claude as part of an actual guided-weapons engineering program.

The cell worked on three programs:

a guided rocket using a commodity phone-class flight computer and terminal guidance;

a multistage ballistic missile with a stated range goal above 2,000 kilometers;

and a missile family containing a hypersonic-glide variant.

The operators used Claude Code in place of human software engineers to develop guidance, navigation and control software.

They assigned different AI instances different engineering jobs, using one for coding, another for research and another to review the first model’s work.

They built flight-control software.

They integrated an open-source autopilot.

They performed simulations.

They optimized guidance algorithms.

They developed firmware.

Then they conducted an actual guided-rocket test.

When it failed, they returned to Claude to diagnose the failure.

Anthropic also found that the group had built an offline simulation environment that no longer depended upon Claude. (Anthropic)

But one detected cell should not be mistaken for the size of the phenomenon.

Anthropic caught activity visible to one AI company on accounts it identified.

There are other commercial AI systems.

There are open-weight models.

There are locally hosted models.

There are accounts that have not been detected.

There are actors operating entirely outside American commercial platforms.

And Anthropic found conventional-weapons development activity involving actors in China and Russia as well as Yemen. (Anthropic)

Inside the Iranian ecosystem, Anthropic separately uncovered an Iran-nexus actor using AI to generate targeting recommendations against U.S. naval forces.

That actor combined publicly accessible ship and aircraft transponder identifiers, military photographs, vulnerability research, public sources exposing naval movements and commercial satellite-imagery query scripts to help construct targeting handbooks. (Anthropic)

We are therefore already seeing AI operating on multiple parts of the kill chain:

AI helping build the weapon.

AI helping find the target.

AI helping analyze the target.

The identified Yemen cell is a visible sample of something much larger.

And the deeper change is economic.

For most of the precision-war era, sophisticated strike capability required enormous state infrastructure:

specialized engineers;

national intelligence organizations;

military satellites;

expensive simulation software;

large computing establishments;

specialized guidance expertise;

proprietary communications networks;

and major weapons-development laboratories.

That barrier is collapsing.

Commercial AI can perform portions of work once requiring scarce engineers and intelligence analysts.

Commercial satellite companies can provide militarily useful imagery.

Commodity processors can become flight computers.

Smartphones contain cameras, processors, inertial sensors, navigation capability and communications.

Open-source autopilots provide mature flight-control architecture.

Commercial communications move information globally.

Cheap drones provide expendable test platforms and weapons.

AI increasingly provides the integration layer connecting those systems.

The new standard is not technological equality with the United States.

The standard is good enough.

Good enough to locate the target.

Good enough to identify it.

Good enough to write the guidance software.

Good enough to navigate.

Good enough to fuse commercial data.

Good enough to strike a refinery, pipeline, radar, ship, airfield or command center.

That is a fundamentally different technological threshold.

The asymmetric actor does not have to reproduce America’s multibillion-dollar reconnaissance-strike architecture.

It needs only enough pieces of that architecture to achieve sufficient lethality.

Commercial AI + commercial ISR + commodity electronics + open-source software + inexpensive weapons can increasingly produce state-like effects without state-like infrastructure or state-like cost.

That creates an exchange-rate problem for the United States and its allies.

The attacker increasingly operates with commercial-priced technology.

The defender continues to rely on state-priced platforms, scarce trained manpower, exquisite sensors and expensive interceptors.

A cheap weapon does not have to equal the sophistication of the system defending against it.

It has to force the expensive system to respond.

And if inexpensive systems can repeatedly threaten high-value targets, the weaker actor can lose individual engagements while still impose the better economic exchange.

Iran’s distributive network is almost perfectly structured to exploit this.

Iran no longer has to provide every Houthi, militia or proxy node with every engineer, imagery analyst, programmer and specialist.

The commercial economy increasingly supplies part of the missing technical infrastructure.

Iran supplies the military layer:

weapons knowledge;

components;

training;

operational experience;

target priorities;

and the network connecting geographically separated actors.

Commercial technology therefore multiplies the effectiveness of distributive warfare.

It makes individual nodes more capable.

It reduces reliance on centralized Iranian expertise.

It lowers the cost of experimentation.

It accelerates regeneration.

It makes failed tests cheaper.

And knowledge developed by one node can increasingly move across the network at almost zero marginal cost.

There is a second-order consequence here that deserves its own analysis later:

commercial technology is beginning to take scarcity value away from portions of the traditional U.S. defense-industrial model.

Capabilities once available almost exclusively through governments and major defense contractors—computing, simulation, imagery exploitation, software engineering, data fusion and elements of targeting—are increasingly being commoditized by civilian technology companies.

The American defense primes still produce the exquisite aircraft, missiles, propulsion systems, radars and hardened military systems.

But they increasingly do not own the entire technological advantage surrounding those machines.

Some of the intelligence of the weapons system is migrating into the commercial marketplace.

That is a conversation for another day.

For this war, the conclusion is already visible:

The price of entry into precision warfare is collapsing.

And Iran’s distributive network is using the falling price.

⸻

2. IRAN IS USING GEOGRAPHY TO WAGE A GLOBAL ECONOMIC WAR

Now look at the theater as one map.

Iran sits over the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis now exert increasing military and geographic pressure around Bab el-Mandeb.

Between them sits Saudi Arabia—the historical shock absorber of the global petroleum system.

Saudi Arabia’s principal solution to an impaired Hormuz was the East–West Pipeline.

Move the crude across the Arabian Peninsula.

Load it at Yanbu.

Bypass Hormuz.

That relief valve has now been attacked and shut down.

Saudi Arabia says the drones that struck the pipeline originated in Iraq. (Saudi Press Agency)

The pipeline had become critical to moving roughly 4 million barrels per day toward the Red Sea while Hormuz remained impaired. An extended outage places as much as approximately 4% of global supply at risk, with available Yanbu stocks providing only a short bridge if flows are not restored. (Reuters)

Think about what that means strategically.

Hormuz is the artery.

The East–West Pipeline is the bypass around the artery.

Then move south.

The Houthis expanded their position around Yemen’s Red Sea coast and Perim Island at the entrance to Bab el-Mandeb, adding pressure on the western maritime exit. (Reuters)

Then look at Jazan.

The Houthis struck Saudi energy infrastructure there.

Jazan is not simply another oil facility.

It is a 400,000-barrel-per-day refinery on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea side.

At design capacity it produces approximately 250,000 barrels per day of ultra-low-sulfur diesel. (Aramco)

That changes the meaning of the strike.

It was part of the global economic war.

Attack Hormuz and you attack the primary export route.

Attack the East–West Pipeline and you attack the bypass around Hormuz.

Pressure Bab el-Mandeb and you attack the western maritime exit.

Strike Jazan and you attack the downstream refined-product system on that western side.

Iran’s distributive network is therefore not merely attacking oil.

It is attacking the system used to move around the attacks on oil.

That is the encirclement.

The network does not have to completely close every route simultaneously.

It has to make every alternative progressively worse.

⸻

3. THE WORLD’S OIL SHOCK ABSORBER IS ITSELF BEING SHOCKED

This is why the Saudi production number matters.

Saudi Arabia reported August crude production of approximately 6.238 million barrels per day—its lowest reported production level since 1990.

The IEA independently assessed Saudi August crude supply at approximately 5.97 million barrels per day, down from 8.24 million in July.

Those are different measurement universes—Saudi-reported production versus IEA market supply—but they tell the same strategic story: the kingdom’s ability to put oil into the global system has collapsed. (IEA)

That is not merely another OPEC statistic.

Saudi Arabia historically performs a unique function in the world economy.

When supply disappears elsewhere, Saudi capacity is supposed to compensate.

Saudi Arabia is the shock absorber.

Now the shock absorber is itself being hit.

Its eastern route is constrained.

Its western bypass has been attacked.

Its Red Sea infrastructure is being struck.

Bab el-Mandeb is under increasing pressure.

And Saudi production has fallen to a level not reported since the year Iraq invaded Kuwait.

Meanwhile, the IEA reports:

507 million barrels of observed global inventories drawn since February.

95 million barrels drawn in August alone.

Global supply projected to fall 5.7 million barrels per day in 2026.

Record Atlantic Basin refining margins driven by sharply higher diesel cracks.

Gulf diesel/gasoil exports down to roughly one-quarter of prewar levels. (IEA)

This is where Iran’s regional war becomes global.

The transmission chain is straightforward:

energy → diesel → freight → food → construction → manufacturing → inflation → interest rates → debt service → reduced economic slack.

Diesel is particularly important.

It moves trucks.

Farm machinery.

Construction equipment.

Ships.

Generators.

Mining equipment.

Industrial logistics.

That is why the Jazan refinery belongs in the same analytical frame as Hormuz.

The attack was not simply damage to Saudi Arabia.

It was pressure applied to a refined-product system already transmitting the war into the global economy.

Iran’s battlefield is regional.

Its economic battlespace is global.

⸻

4. THE FIRST TEST OF THE NEW SUNNI ALLIANCE FAILED

The Saudi military story also has to be read as a sequence.

In simplified operational terms, Saudi Arabia re-entered this round of the Houthi fight believing it could handle the problem.

Washington remained behind the curtain with intelligence and targeting support.

Then the Houthi offensive accelerated.

Saudi-backed forces lost strategically important territory.

Saudi cities and energy installations came under attack.

The Houthis expanded toward Bab el-Mandeb.

Saudi Arabia reached the clutch and needed additional kinetic power.

It turned to Pakistan.

Pakistan declined kinetic participation during an active Houthi offensive.

Pakistan’s own Foreign Ministry made clear on September 10 that Islamabad was pursuing diplomacy and was not operationalizing the Makkah agreement for military action against the Houthis. (Ministry of Foreign Affairs Pakistan)

The Houthi offensive succeeded.

That makes this the first meaningful test of the new Saudi–Pakistan–Türkiye Sunni collective-security architecture.

It failed.

Not because the alliance lacked enough committees.

Not because headquarters had not been constructed.

Not because Pakistan lacked aircraft.

The failure was political.

Pakistan would not kinetically strike the proxy army of neighboring Iran.

That exposed the first political ceiling on the alliance.

Iran’s distributive method therefore accomplished something bigger than another battlefield success.

It found the political seam inside the new Sunni alliance.

Tehran does not have to attack Pakistan.

It does not have to attack Türkiye.

It can apply pressure through the Houthis against Saudi Arabia while forcing Islamabad to choose between its Saudi defense commitment and direct kinetic confrontation with an Iranian proxy tied to its immediate neighbor.

On the first test, Pakistan chose not to cross that threshold.

Then Saudi Arabia turned to Washington.

MBS called President Trump twice asking for direct American strikes against the Houthis.

The United States declined kinetic intervention as well.

Washington continued intelligence and targeting support but declined to open another direct front in Yemen while American forces remained committed against Iran and around Hormuz. (Axios)

That produces the strategic sequence:

Saudi Arabia believed it could handle the Houthis.

It could not.

Pakistan declined kinetic help.

The United States declined kinetic help.

The Houthi offensive succeeded.

That is more than a Saudi embarrassment.

It is a force-structure and alliance disclosure.

The United States retains enormous destructive power.

But available combat power is not infinite.

Iran’s distributive strategy creates simultaneous geographically separated problems and forces the stronger power to decide which ones receive scarce high-end kinetic resources.

Saudi Arabia just discovered what happens when it is not the selected front.

⸻

5. SAUDI ARABIA NEEDS A WESTERN-PILOTED FOREIGN AIR LEGION — WHILE CHINESE COMMERCIAL ISR SHOWS WHERE WARFARE IS GOING

Saudi Arabia does not lack advanced aircraft.

It owns one of the world’s most expensive collections of Western combat aviation equipment.

What this war has exposed is the difference between owning advanced machines and possessing the human combat system capable of extracting their full value during a sustained adaptive fight.

The deficiency is not solved by buying another aircraft.

It is not solved by another security agreement.

And it cannot be solved by assuming Washington or Islamabad will provide the missing kinetic force when the decision becomes politically difficult.

Saudi Arabia needs a Western-piloted Foreign Air Legion.

Not simply hired pilots.

A standing Saudi-controlled combat aviation formation built around experienced Western combat aviators and the full ecosystem required to generate combat power:

pilots;

weapons officers;

mission planners;

maintainers;

EW specialists;

intelligence personnel;

battle managers;

tanker crews;

and experienced operational commanders.

The aircraft would be Saudi.

The command authority would be Saudi.

The decision to fight would be Saudi.

Foreign combat human capital would be imported into a sovereign Saudi military structure while Saudi personnel were developed alongside it.

The objective would be simple:

when Saudi Arabia decides it must fight, Riyadh should not have to telephone Washington or Islamabad to obtain the human kinetic capability required to use machines it already owns.

This war has reinforced the larger manpower thesis:

equipment overmatch is not enough.

Saudi Arabia possessed enormous equipment overmatch.

The Houthis repeatedly achieved human, adaptive and decision-cycle overmatch.

That is the weakness the Foreign Air Legion would address.

And another development this weekend shows why that problem is becoming more urgent.

U.S. officials have linked high-resolution satellite imagery supplied by Chinese entities to Iran’s July 17 missile attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan that killed three American soldiers.

Iran obtained imagery before and after the attack, placing Chinese commercial imagery inside the targeting and battle-damage-assessment portions of the Iranian strike cycle. (The Wall Street Journal)

This is the same technological revolution seen in the Houthi AI cell from another direction.

Chinese commercial ISR entered the Iranian kill chain.

Iran did not need to build its own American-scale military reconnaissance-satellite constellation.

Commercial imagery supplied part of the function.

And the commercial layer matters because it creates separation between military effect and formal state military involvement.

A PLA reconnaissance satellite does not have to be visibly tasked against an American base for Chinese-origin imagery to help an Iranian missile strike.

Commercial technology creates deniability while still producing military effect.

Combine that with the Anthropic discoveries and the pattern becomes clear.

Commercial AI lowers the engineering barrier.

Commercial satellites lower the reconnaissance barrier.

Commodity electronics lower the guidance barrier.

Open-source software lowers the integration barrier.

Iranian military technology supplies weapons expertise.

The distributive network supplies geography and manpower.

No individual component has to equal the American state system.

Together they only have to become sufficiently lethal.

⸻

THE WEEKEND VERDICT

The strategic picture coming out of this weekend is larger than Iran.

Larger than Yemen.

Larger than Saudi Arabia.

A new model of warfare is becoming visible.

Iran possesses uniquely powerful geography.

Its distributive network expands that geography outward.

Commercial technology increases the capability of each node in the network while lowering its cost.

Chinese commercial ISR demonstrates how capabilities once monopolized by major states can enter someone else’s kill chain without conventional military deployment.

AI increasingly supplies engineering and intelligence labor.

Cheap weapons create expensive defensive requirements.

And geography allows relatively inexpensive attacks to produce global economic effects.

This is why the refinery strike matters.

This is why the East–West Pipeline matters.

This is why Bab el-Mandeb matters.

This is why Hormuz matters.

They are not disconnected targets.

They are components of the same global economic system.

Iran does not have to physically occupy that system.

It has to disrupt the points where geography concentrates it.

The resulting strategy is increasingly clear:

Attack the artery.

Attack the bypass.

Attack the alternate exit.

Attack the refinery.

Use distributed forces so the enemy cannot concentrate everywhere.

Use commercial technology to make each distributed force increasingly capable at a fraction of traditional state cost.

That is the emerging architecture of the war.

Iran is waging a global economic war through regional geography.

And commercial technology is lowering the price at which its distributive network can participate.

The final strategic equation is therefore:

GEOGRAPHY × DISTRIBUTIVE WARFARE × COMMERCIAL TECHNOLOGY = GLOBAL ECONOMIC EFFECT AT ASYMMETRIC COST

That is the larger lesson of the weekend.

The blockade is the south.

The encirclement is the blockade plus the destruction, disruption or coercion of the relief valves.

And increasingly:

the technology required to enforce that pressure is no longer exclusively a state resource.

If you value analysis that looks beyond the daily headline to the underlying methods and means of the war, like and follow the account.

text:
It does seem like today's reaction to the AI slowdown statements by large AI companies is overdone. 

Everything has gapped down this morning at the open.

Although I just got the alert that $IWM closed the morning gap.

Small cap is worried more about what the Fed does this week and interestingly a rate hike may end up being bullish after all is said and done.

Coming back to the AI slowdown - looks like the semis $SMH are affected the most. That would make intuitive sense. If there is AI slowdown there shuld be less need for chips.

I do think the streets will settle back to the realization that AI slowdown as being discussed relates only to the slowdown in the future releases of "frontier" models. 

Not to inference. And the AI statements will end up increasing the volume of inference because there is far more risk for companies to not use AI. So AI use overall will increase even if there is slowdown in the pace of new frontier models being released.

It gives a chance to companies (enterprise users) to "catch up" to current levels of what the frontier models offer and worry a little less about what is being released tomorrow. 

Of course, all this is my personal optinion and I am a tech investor - so I am biased. 

The streets will do what the streets thinks is best and what it thinks is right to do.

And I will follow. 

I still think this reaction is way overboard.

‼️UK | BREAKING || 'WESTMINSTER'S TIME IS COMING TO AN END' -- WALES, SCOTLAND AND N. IRELAND  NATIONALIST LEADERS SIGN CARDIFF PACT 

Cardiff -- The nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have signed a joint declaration demanding Westminster prepare for constitutional change and recognise their nations' right to decide their own future.

Plaid Cymru's Rhun ap Iorwerth, the SNP's John Swinney and Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill signed the pact as party leaders, joined by Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald.

For the first time since devolution, all three First Minister posts are held by parties seeking independence or Irish reunification.

The pact declares that no Westminster government may block democratic change. Swinney went further, predicting Andy Burnham would be "the last prime minister of the United Kingdom."

Ap Iorwerth, however, offered no referendum timetable. Plaid has ruled out a Welsh vote before 2030, while Downing Street and unionist parties accused the nationalists of seeking to break up the country.

PIRA in 2002: “Sunday 21 July marks the 30th anniversary of an IRA operation in Belfast in 1972 which resulted in nine people being killed and many more injured.

While it was not our intention to injure or kill non-combatants, the reality is that on this and on a number of other occasions, that was the consequence of our actions.

It is therefore appropriate on the anniversary of this tragic event, that we address all of the deaths and injuries of non-combatants caused by us.

We offer our sincere apologies and condolences to their families.

There have been fatalities amongst combatants on all sides. We also acknowledge the grief and pain of their relatives.

The future will not be found in denying collective failures and mistakes or closing minds and hearts to the plight of those who have been hurt. That includes all of the victims of the conflict, combatants and non-combatants.

It will not be achieved by creating a hierarchy of victims in which some are deemed more or less worthy than others.

The process of conflict resolution requires the equal acknowledgement of the grief and loss of others. On this anniversary, we are endeavouring to fulfil this responsibility to those we have hurt.

The IRA is committed unequivocally to the search for freedom, justice and peace in Ireland.

We remain totally committed to the peace process and to dealing with the challenges and difficulties which this presents. This includes the acceptance of past mistakes and of the hurt and pain we have caused to others.”

P O'Neill, Irish Republican Publicity Bureau, Dublin.

text:
The reality is that Irish people’s online behaviour is notably highly aggressive, abusive, and mob-like towards those  with differing political opinion, particularly on the issue of Israel/Palestine and Irish antisemitism. 

Obviously, my own experience speaks to that. For calmly and rationally speaking openly about my sincerely held position that antisemitism is a serious problem in Ireland I have been relentlessly attacked and abused. I have been viciously and conspiratorially attacked as a ‘traitor’, ‘anti-Irish’, and ‘a paid agent of subversion’. I have had multiple people publicly say that I should be charged with treason.

I have been harassed and intimidated by powerful figures in Irish society, including a senior politician operating behind an anonymous account who posted about my family and I multiple times a day for weeks. A known hotelier created a parody account of me using photos I never shared on this platform, in addition to threatening to call up my dad’s business mere weeks before his retirement.

But it is not just me. At this point I have multiple British and American friends, and even two Palestinian friends, who have remarked to me the toxicity of Irish people online on this issue. Specifically the fact that every time the mere *suggestion* is made that Ireland may have an antisemitism problem, Irish people online will viciously intimidate that belief into silence. 

When @DrDominicGreen wrote for the WSJ about Ireland’s antisemitism, wherein he was most clear to say that he did not believe the average Irish person was antisemitic but rather that this was a phenomenon pushed by Official Ireland, he said he had never received such vicious backlash in anything he had ever written on a range of contentious geopolitical issues. So great was the outrage that a former ambassador was quick to write a rebuttal that contained minimising inaccuracies about the ongoing push to rename Herzog Park. I sincerely wish this outrage was felt for the experiences of antisemitism and intimidation the Irish Jewish community - who are just as Irish as anyone else - have felt in recent years. 

The extent of Ireland’s antisemitism problem is a matter of ongoing debate and, unfortunately, denial. But what there simply cannot be a denial of is that Irish society is highly intolerant of dissent, and intensely fragile to any criticism of our ‘Most Oppressed People Ever (MOPE) and therefore most moral’ self-styled image. It’s a profound hypocrisy because Irish pro-Palestine people often will highly praise Israelis with dissenting opinions, for example Gideon Levy who has been regularly platformed in Irish media. 

This intolerance and fragility results in intense intimidation against those of us who do not toe the line. Such that goes far beyond the bounds of what one would expect from a Western nation and liberal democracy. 

The greatest irony is that, through this behaviour, they have shot Ireland in the foot. Not only because their own abhorrent conduct speaks for itself, but also because it means that Irish people with nuanced opinions on the issue of antisemitism in Ireland and Israel/Palestine have been intimidated into silence. 

I was at a Rosh Hashanah dinner on Friday and was speaking with one Irish Jew about how Ireland’s reputation for antisemitism was solidified internationally and how much we had encountered it. Both of us *do not* believe that Ireland is the most antisemitic country in the world, or even in Europe on certain metrics. But because Irish people with opinions such as ours have been intimidated into silence, the platform is ceded to non-Irish sensationalists, such as Alan Dershowitz, who have no love for or knowledge of our country. 

And so an international perception of Ireland as being more antisemitic than it is has taken hold, all while, conversely, domestically there is a denial that this problem exists at all. It’s a massive and ever-widening gap, and one that I am losing hope of ever being filled.

🇾🇪|Yemeni missiles are turning the myth of Saudi air defense invincibility into an expensive fireworks display. As hangars at King Khalid Air Base burned under the impact of ballistic missiles, the Saudi Air Force’s most advanced F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets along with the "precision strike" tactics learned from U.S. and NATO pilots were being humiliated by Yemeni armed forces in the most primitive yet effective way: having their very nests wiped out by direct missile strikes.

💥 First: On September 14, Yemeni Armed Forces spokesman Yahya Saree announced that, in response to over 300 Saudi airstrikes, Yemeni missiles and drones had precisely struck fighter jet hangars, radar systems, runways, and ammunition depots at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait.

This base is no ordinary target; it is the central launch point for Saudi airstrikes against Yemen the very place where F-15 and Typhoon jets conducting bombing missions take off. The logic of the Yemeni armed forces is simple yet lethal: wherever you take off to bomb us, we will hurl missiles right back at your runway.

Following the attack, the Saudi General Directorate of Civil Defense issued safety alerts for several southwestern cities; residents of Khamis Mushait and Abha received mobile phone warnings late at night. This is not what a "successful interception" looks like. This is what it looks like when air defense systems are penetrated.

🎯 Second: The performance of the Saudi Air Force on the Bab al-Mandab Strait front has devolved into a slaughter of its own allies.

On September 13, officers from the "Southern Forces" (aligned with the Aden-based Yemeni government) reported that the Saudi Air Force had launched seven unprovoked airstrikes against Yemeni government positions on the Lahj–Bab al-Mandab front, resulting in numerous deaths and injuries among the troops. On this same front, Saudi warplanes also mistakenly bombed positions held by the "Giants Brigade."  Despite receiving systematic training from the US and NATO, Saudi pilots have been involved in "so many massive accidental bombing incidents." There is only one reason: the Saudi Air Force is acting as an "enforcement squad" bombing anyone who surrenders. Unable to tolerate another instance of "entire brigades defecting" from the Yemeni government forces, Saudi Arabia uses F-15 bombs to threaten its own proxies: if you lay down your arms against the Yemeni armed forces, we will blow you to kingdom come.

Saudi bombs are not meant to defeat Yemen; they are meant to stop their own proxies from fleeing.

🛢️ Third, Saudi Arabia has attempted to downplay the consequences of the attack on the East-West Pipeline. Satellite images, however, do not lie.

Satellite photos published by *The Guardian* reveal severe damage to a pipeline pumping station southeast of Medina, with extensive scorch marks visible on the ground. Following the attack, Saudi Arabia announced a "precautionary shutdown" of the pipeline but refused to disclose the actual extent of the damage or a timeline for restoration.

Sources cited by Reuters offered two assessments: one suggesting full repairs could take six weeks, and another predicting a faster turnaround though even during repairs, only partial pumping capacity could be restored initially.

The most critical figures come from inventory levels at the port of Yanbu. Three industry insiders familiar with Saudi export operations revealed that current stocks at Yanbu are sufficient to sustain exports for only five to seven days. If the pipeline is not restored in time, the reserves will be completely exhausted.

This pipeline transports approximately 4 million barrels of crude oil daily, accounting for about 4% of the global supply. With the Strait of Hormuz blocked by Iran and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait controlled by Yemeni armed forces, the East-West Pipeline represents Saudi Arabia's only overland export alternative. Now, that alternative is burning too.

🚀 Fourth, In the Raghwan district of Yemen's Marib province, locals recovered the booster wreckage of a Chinese-made DF-15A tactical ballistic missile.  Open-source intelligence analysts have confirmed that this marks the first time Saudi Arabia has used the DF-15A in actual combat.

With a range of approximately 600 to 900 kilometers, the DF-15A is capable of covering the entirety of Yemen. Saudi Arabia had previously purchased DF-3As (around 60 units in the late 1980s) and DF-21s (around 2007) from China, but there had never been confirmation of its possession or use of the DF-15 series.

Saudi Arabia deployed Chinese missiles weapons that had never before seen combat against targets in Yemen. This was not a "strategic choice"; it was a signal that their munitions stockpiles were running dry. When a nation resorts to pulling its reserve medium-range ballistic missiles out of storage to strike at guerrilla forces, it is no longer conducting "military operations," it is merely venting frustration.

Even more ironic is the fact that the booster stage of one of these DF-15As fell into an area controlled by Saudi-backed forces, causing civilian casualties. Saudi Arabia ended up bombing its own allies with its own missiles.

🏴‍☠️ Fifth, On September 14, the UAE Ministry of Defense officially acknowledged that two Emirati servicemen, Major Abdullah Shams Al-Manhali and Saeed Abdullah Al-Shamsi had "fallen while performing a training mission."

While official UAE statements described the deaths as occurring during a "training mission," training exercises do not take place on the front lines in Yemen. The UAE's military presence in Yemen has long been an open secret one that the country publicly denied. Now, with the return of two coffins, those official denials have come to an end.

The UAE has consistently sought to position itself as a "safe haven," a land of Dubai skyscrapers, Abu Dhabi financial centers, and a commercial paradise insulated from the flames of war. Yet, missiles and drones launched by Yemeni armed forces are erasing that boundary. When Emirati soldiers die on the front lines in Yemen, the notion of Dubai as a "safe haven" rings hollow. 

🏔️ Sixth, In the early hours of September 14, Yemeni armed forces captured four key high points in the Kahboub mountain range: San Sanfah, Sanfah, Al-Jaroubah, and Al-Hamra. This mountain range overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the entire western coast of Yemen.

The capture of Kahboub means that Yemeni armed forces control not only the waters of the strait but also the high ground used to monitor it. While the Saudi Air Force can continue its bombing campaigns, it cannot retake the mountain peaks. During the operation to capture Kahboub, Yemeni armed forces killed five commanders from Saudi-backed proxy forces including a battalion commander from the "4th Brigade" and wounded four officers of chief-of-staff rank.

The chain of command for Saudi proxies on the Bab al-Mandab front has been severed.

🇾🇪 Seventh, What is happening in Yemen cannot be reduced to a mere victory for "Iranian proxies."

This is an independent Islamic revolution one that has grown from Yemeni soil, aimed at resisting foreign aggression and internal puppets. While its ideological roots trace back to the 1979 Islamic Revolution in Iran, it is not a carbon copy. It represents a second phase living proof of the prophecy made by Imam Khomeini and Imam Khamenei that "this revolution will give birth to other revolutions."

The "reformists" within Iran those who argue that the revolution is over and that Iran should function like an ordinary republic are being proven wrong by the reality in Yemen. The revolution has not ended; it is continuing in Yemen. The Yemeni armed forces liberated the entire western coast in 18 hours, struck Saudi airbases with missiles, and secured naval control over the Bab al-Mandab Strait feats beyond the capability of mere "proxies." These are the capabilities of revolutionaries.

text:
The Atlantic has gone 103 days into the 2026 hurricane season without forming a single hurricane, the longest wait on record since satellites started reliably tracking storms in 1966. The previous latest starts were Gustav in 2002 and Humberto in 2013, both by September 11. According to Colorado State University hurricane expert Phil Klotzbach, this is now also the least active Atlantic season since 1950, with just five short-lived tropical storms so far. The only system that came close to hurricane strength was Tropical Storm Edouard, which made landfall near the Texas-Louisiana border on September 1 while still 14 mph shy of a hurricane. History offers a reminder not to relax: Category 5 Hurricane Andrew's catastrophic landfall in South Florida happened in 1992, a season with just seven storms total.
