text:
Why do Newars offer alcohol, eggs, meat and even animal sacrifice to Ganesha? 

If you know Ganesha mainly as the gentle god of Modak, you may find this surprising. 

But in traditional Newar Hinduism, Ganesha has a much wider ritual identity.

In the Kathmandu Valley, Ganesha is worshipped not only as Vighnaharta, the remover of obstacles, but also as a powerful Tantric and threshold deity. 

He can remove obstacles, but is also traditionally understood to have the power to place them. 

Therefore, different forms of worship developed around him.

This is why, in certain Newar traditions, offerings can include ayla (ritual alcohol), eggs, meat and animal sacrifice.

Alcohol is not simply offered because the deity "likes drinking." Within Tantric ritual, substances normally avoided in ordinary worship can become sacred offerings after ritual purification. 

They belong to a broader Tantric vocabulary in which ordinary distinctions between pure and impure are ritually transformed.

The egg also has a ritual significance. In Newar traditions such as sagan, it forms part of a set of ritual substances representing different elements and principles. 

Eggs, meat, fish and ayla can therefore appear together in sacred contexts.

Animal sacrifice has another dimension. It is connected with blood, life-force, power, protection and the ritual fulfillment of vows or wishes. 

In some Newar communities, Ganesha receives sacrificial offerings for success in important undertakings and the removal of obstacles.

But this does not mean every Newar worship of Ganesha involves sacrifice. 
Practices vary greatly according to the temple, locality, caste/community, guthi, family tradition and ritual occasion.

So, Newar Ganesha worship cannot always be understood through the familiar image of the vegetarian, modak-loving Ganesha alone.

He can be both the gentle remover of obstacles and the powerful Tantric guardian of the threshold.

And that diversity is one of the fascinating features of the living Hindu traditions of the Kathmandu Valley.

text:
The President held a working meeting with Novgorod Region Governor Aleksandr Dronov. The Governor briefed the President on the socioeconomic situation in the region. Specifically, the discussion focused on projects being implemented to support healthcare workers, improve the demographic situation, and develop the educational sector.

Here is what they discussed at the beginning of this meeting (with my translation):

Pres. Putin: Aleksandr Valentinovich, a special economic zone has been established in your region—let’s start with that. How is it operating?

Dronov: One of the critical issues for us is creating new engines of economic growth. Thanks to you, Vladimir Vladimirovich, a special economic zone was established here in 2021. It focuses on creating new high-tech manufacturing facilities. Investments totaling over nine billion rubles have been announced, involving 16 resident companies and the creation of approximately 2,600 new jobs. We can already report that eight resident companies have launched production, created 612 jobs, and invested 4.5 billion rubles.🚀🚀🚀

Pres. Putin: And what kind of production facilities are these?

Dronov: Specifically, this refers to a plant for the production of reinforced concrete slabs for the construction of the Moscow–St. Petersburg High-Speed Railway. 🚀🚀🚀Our project has officially become a resident. A year ago, in August 2025, together with the Minister of Transport, Andrey Sergeyevich Nikitin, we laid the foundation stone. Today, commissioning and testing have already begun, and starting this October, products will ship directly to the construction site.

And this involves the Sber Group and the 'GigaFactory' project. This allows us to revive the manufacturing and assembly of televisions right here in Veliky Novgorod.

And of course, it is crucial that alongside economic development, we are also training personnel tailored to the needs of the region. One of these key initiatives is the construction of a university campus with a capacity of 4000 in Veliky Novgorod. It is being built on your instructions—thank you very much—as part of the 'University City' project. The Novgorodskaya Special Economic Zone serves as our concessionaire. It will house students and young scientists, and it will feature new hubs for science and sports. In fact, this creates an integrated ecosystem: high-tech manufacturing, science, and workforce training specifically tailored to these needs. Commissioning is scheduled for 2027.  🚀🚀🚀🇷🇺

Vladimir Vladimirovich, you are well aware that, for historical reasons, the Novgorod Region lags behind other regions of our country across many indicators. We are below the national average on a number of socio-economic metrics. For me—both as governor and as the head of the region—it is critically important that we move forward at an accelerated pace to ensure the region’s development. There is plenty of room for growth.

The key indicators are presented on the slide here, and as we can see, they are above the Russian average. This allows us to work within the budget. We took sixth place and moved up three spots in a year in the regional investment attractiveness ranking conducted by the Agency for Strategic Initiatives. Many thanks to Svetlana Vitalyevna Chupsheva for our collaboration.

Demography. I am a father of many children myself, and I know what families have to face. The Novgorod Oblast is among the regions of the so-called demographic winter, which is why for us, support measures for families with children are among the priority ones in our work.

At the last meeting, I reported to you on those measures that will be implemented starting from 2026; they have all been launched. We have strengthened support for young families, student families, and families with many children, and this is already yielding the first result.

In the first half of this year, we saw an increase in the number of first-time babies compared to the same period last year. We rank third in the Northwestern Federal District in terms of the total fertility rate.🚀🚀🚀

We are not stopping there, Vladimir Vladimirovich; starting in 2027, we are launching our "Novgorod Family" project. What does it entail? Every family will receive one million rubles for their fourth child and each subsequent child, and these funds can be used for essential needs: improving housing conditions, paying for kindergarten, or purchasing a vehicle. Furthermore, for families with five or more children, we will fully cover the cost of housing and utility services. It is fundamentally important to us that a family’s decision to have a third or fourth child be a completely logical choice, backed by appropriate state support measures.

Healthcare is a critically important issue. It is essential that the quality and standard of healthcare be uniform across the entire region—not only in the regional center but also in all our municipalities. And here, of course, the key issue is personnel and their training.

We currently have nine support measures in place, which have been utilized by more than 280 medical professionals between 2025 and the first half of 2026 alone.

We launched a new project 'Novgorod Nurse (Novgorod Male Nurse). This also allows mid-level medical personnel, whether they have been working in the profession for a long time work or whether they have made their first steps, to receive measures of support.

Housing is a crucial support measure. We launched this initiative in 2019, acquiring 283 apartments for medical professionals, with another 36 added in 2025. The terms are as follows: a medical professional works at a healthcare facility for seven years, after which they gain the right to privatize the property and retain ownership of it. The results speak for themselves: 353 medical professionals have chosen the Novgorod Region as the place to live and work since the program began.🚀🚀🚀

Naturally, we are training our own medical personnel. About 2,300 students are currently studying at the medical institute, including 461 in residency programs.

We launched the "Healthy Family" gubernatorial project. It began in June of this year, and within just three months, around 12,000 residents have already undergone screening.

What does the project entail? A team of doctors—including various specialists—travels to a municipality and examines the entire family on-site in a single day. Both older adults and the youngest children can get screening. One thousand people were referred for further medical examination. 🚀🚀🚀

Naturally, this systematic and complex effort—involving both medical professionals and the healthcare system as a whole—is yielding results. Mortality rates for the first seven months of 2026 show a decline compared to the same period last year.🚀🚀🚀

I would like to extend special thanks to Evgeny Vladimirovich Shlyakhto, an Academician of the Russian Academy of Sciences; Dmitry Olegovich Ivanov, Director of the St. Petersburg Pediatric Institute; and all our colleagues from St. Petersburg for their support and cooperation under our existing agreements. Their assistance is invaluable, and we are continuing to work with them.

Vladimir Vladimirovich, it is crucial to develop our workforce potential and train personnel specifically to meet the needs of the region's economy. We rank second in the country for the employment of graduates from secondary vocational education institutions. We are among the top 25 regions in Russia in terms of education quality, holding the 23rd spot. Virtually 90 percent of ninth-grade graduates remain in the region, which is a very positive outcome for us.

As part of the federal "Professionalitet" project, we are establishing educational-industrial clusters in partnership with enterprises. We have already implemented this model in the chemical industry, radio-electronics, construction, agriculture, transport, and mechanical engineering. I would like to extend my sincere thanks to the Minister of Education, Sergey Sergeyevich Kravtsov, for his support of the region and for this work.

One of the tools is the High-Tech Championship. This year, we are hosting the finals for the fourth time. The entire championship is dedicated to the transport industry. For us, this involves 20 skill categories and the arrival of over 15,000 participants from across the country—offering a chance to see which professions will be in demand in the future.

Preserving our historical and cultural heritage is of great importance. Vladimir Vladimirovich, acting on your instructions, we identified 37 cultural heritage sites of federal significance and designated five of them as priorities. We are already seeing initial results.

Work has been completed on the Church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul on Sinichya Gora. The project was finished in June, and the Bishop conducted the first service there in July. The site now functions as both a place of worship and a museum.

Work has begun on the Church of the Intercession of the Theotokos and the Pokrovskaya Tower within the Kremlin—the site of the original citadel. I am personally overseeing this project, which was initiated under your directive, and we are on track to complete the work by 2029.

Last year, we opened the country’s first branch of the Polytechnic Museum 🚀🚀🚀under the patronage of Mikhail Valentinovich Kovalchuk 🤮🤮🤮 . We restored a designated regional cultural heritage site using regional budget funds and handed it over to the museum; a full schedule of events is already taking place there. Most importantly, however, we were the first in the country to do this.

And, Vladimir Vladimirovich, construction of the Academician Yanin National Center is proceeding as you directed. I would like to express my sincere gratitude to Mikhail Vladimirovich Mishustin; the construction is being carried out under his personal supervision. Everything is progressing according to plan, and the work will be completed in 2027.

Thank you for the decision to re-register GTLK [State Transport Leasing Company] within the Novgorod Region. This will enable us, over the next five years, to restore key landmarks: the "Millennium of Russia" monument—a symbol of our country—as well as the St. Sophia Cathedral belfry (bell tower) and two 14th-century churches: the Church of the Savior at Kovalev and the Church of the Assumption on Volotovo Field.

A vitally important program involves creating comfortable living conditions and fostering a comfortable urban environment—an initiative carried out under the auspices of the Ministry of Construction and Housing and Utilities. I would like to express my sincere gratitude to Minister Irek Envarovich Faizullin in this regard. The Novgorod Region ranks 21st in terms of quality of life, with 665 areas having undergone improvement; notably, 100 percent of the region's cities are officially recognized as having a favorable urban environment.

We actively participate in the All-Russian competition for urban development projects in small towns and historical settlements, having won 17 projects since 2019. This year, we secured four winning projects, which we will implement next year. As you can see, each project is carried out with due regard for the specific characteristics of the respective municipality.

Our duty is to support our service members participating in the special military operation and their families. We approach this work proactively and with great care. 🌹We collaborate actively with the "Defenders of the Fatherland" Foundation branch—and I would like to extend a huge thank you to Anna Yevgenyevna Tsivileva 🌹; you have visited our branch yourself. A social coordinator is assigned to each family. We have cut the number of documents required to access support measures by half. The average timeframe—from document review to the actual provision of support—has been reduced from thirty days to five working days. And this is yielding results.

First of all, the men underwent training through the "SVOi Heroi 53" program. Many of them have already found employment. For some, we have mapped out a career path to facilitate their professional growth.

On October 1 of last year, the "Help Is Nearby" project was launched in the Novgorod Region. This initiative involves a mobile multidisciplinary team that travels to municipalities to provide on-site assistance to the men. It also includes consultations with veterans of the special military operation, who offer support to those adjusting to civilian life.

Pres. Putin: I see. Good.  You haven’t mentioned anything about school facilities. Yet I know that over 50 percent of schools are in need of repair.

Dronov:    Vladimir Vladimirovich, that is indeed an issue we face. We carry out school repairs every year. We have also built a new school; a new facility with a capacity of 1,500 students opened its doors on September 1st last year. Since this single legal entity comprises two schools—one for 960 students and the other for 1,500—it is the largest educational institution in the region, offering a wide range of extracurricular activities where children can spend practically the entire day. We are undertaking major renovations and participating in all the relevant programs. Naturally, we will continue this work.

Pres. Putin: Make a note of this; we need to keep it under close supervision. Over 54 percent require major repairs. That is quite a challenge. 

Dronov:  We are addressing this issue systematically and comprehensively. After all, federal funds are allocated specifically for the major renovation of the buildings themselves. We coordinate with our municipalities: yes, we start by renovating the building and classrooms and equipping them with educational gear, but we simultaneously develop the surrounding school grounds—installing playgrounds, sports courts, and stadiums. We are working systematically and will continue to do so. I am personally overseeing this work.

Pres. Putin:  Good.

<…>

Sophia:  The rest of this meeting was not open to public.  If you wish to read the RUSSIAN transcript of what I translated above, please go to:  https://t.co/9OrQ9AOXxJ

text:
Warren Buffett stood at a white lectern at the University of Florida in October 1998 and walked a room of finance students through the exact math of the $25 million candy company deal that taught him everything he now knows about buying a business.

His name is Warren Buffett.

He is 95 today and worth roughly $150 billion.

He has been the CEO of Berkshire Hathaway since 1965.

He gives roughly one full university talk a year and has never raised his fee above zero.

The clip in this video is 84 minutes from the Graham-Buffett Teaching Endowment series, funded by fund manager Mason Hawkins.

His framework fits on a napkin.

Only invest inside your circle of competence.

Not the biggest circle. The one where you actually know what you do not know.

Buy pricing power, not cheap multiples.

See's Candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 in 1972. Thirty cents more per pound doubled the pretax profit overnight.

If the brand raises the price without losing the customer, the moat is real.

Ignore the macro forecast.

The 1973 recession was already loud when Berkshire signed the See's deal. Every macro reason to wait would have cost them ten billion dollars in compounded value.

Read annual reports for the rest of your life.

Buffett has read one every day since he was ten. His edge is not information. It is the database in his head.

Go to work for the person you want to become.

Take zero salary at the right desk before you take six figures at the wrong one. Ten years next to a great operator beats every MBA in the country combined.

Right price on a business you understand. That is the whole trade.

Every founder chasing revenue in a business he cannot explain to his mother is inside the same lecture.

Every investor buying a tech stock because the ticker is up forty percent this quarter is inside the same lecture.

Every graduate taking the higher offer at the worse boss is inside the same lecture.

"That's all we'll get paid for doing."

That is Warren Buffett describing sixty years of buying companies in one sentence.

The full lecture is free on YouTube. Every Berkshire shareholder letter since 1965 is on Berkshire's website.

Almost no student picking a first job next month has watched a minute.

text:
TAKE OWNERSHIP OF YOUR UROLOGIC HEALTH

Prostate cancer often causes no early symptoms. Know your risk and when to begin PSA screening.

During Prostate Cancer Awareness Month, urologist Sijo Parekattil, MD, FACS, encourages men in their 30s and 40s to prioritize urologic health, especially with a relevant family history, symptoms or a sense that something is not right.

His recommendation reflects his clinical experience. Current guidance from the American Urological Association and the Society of Urologic Oncology (AUA/SUO) takes a risk-based approach to routine prostate cancer screening.

CURRENT AUA/SUO GUIDANCE

The 2026 guideline says clinicians may offer a baseline PSA blood test between ages 45 and 50 for men at average risk. Screening should be offered between ages 40 and 45 for men at increased risk, including Black men, those with certain inherited gene mutations or a strong family history of prostate cancer.

Regular screening every two to four years is recommended between ages 50 and 69. Decisions should be individualized with a clinician.

PSA stands for prostate-specific antigen. It helps assess prostate cancer risk, but an elevated result does not by itself mean cancer.

Routine screening guidance is intended for men without symptoms. Symptoms or unusual changes should be medically evaluated regardless of age.

Dr. Parekattil directs Avant Concierge Urology and is Associate Professor of Urology at the University of Central Florida. Learn more at https://t.co/Da7rx97UTN.

Blue Cure encourages men to ask questions and take an active role in their healthcare. Do not wait for symptoms to start the conversation.

Learn your family history. Ask when you should begin PSA screening. Speak up when something does not feel right.

Download Blue Cure’s Know Your Numbers Men’s Health Checklist at https://t.co/oPzsULh8gl.

Ask more questions. Start the conversation.

This edited excerpt is from an interview recorded in September 2025.

For education only. This is not a substitute for professional medical advice.

text:
What “Grid First, School First” Actually Requires

The Memphis record points toward a different model for AI infrastructure.

1. Energy infrastructure before expansion

Permanent generation and grid interconnection should be established on a public timeline before additional computing capacity comes online.

Temporary or portable generation should not become a de facto permanent energy strategy.

2. Binding commitments with matching dollar figures

Community infrastructure commitments should be contractual.

Every major promise should identify:

• the project;
• the dollar value or maximum value;
• the responsible party;
• the completion date;
• the approval mechanism;
• and the enforcement mechanism.

If the commitment changes, the public should be able to see exactly what changed and why.

3. Environmental monitoring as a precondition

Air and water monitoring should begin before operations that can materially affect local conditions.

Monitoring should be independent, continuous and publicly accessible.

When there is a disagreement over environmental impact, the community should not have to build its own evidentiary infrastructure simply to determine what is happening in its neighborhood.

4. Notice before expansion

Communities should receive meaningful notice before a major expansion is announced or construction begins.

Notice is not the same thing as consultation.

A real process requires enough information, enough time and enough authority for residents to influence the outcome.

5. No poverty discount

A community-benefit package should not be calibrated to what a community with fewer resources can be persuaded to accept.

The test should be:

Would the same package be offered to a wealthier community with greater political and legal leverage?

If not, the difference deserves explanation.

6. Public accounting of benefits

The public should be able to see, in one place:

Promised → Contracted → Spent → Completed → Outstanding

That ledger should remain public throughout the life of the project.

A ribbon-cutting should never be allowed to close the ledger while commitments remain unfinished.

text:
Why This Is the Exhibit

Memphis demonstrates the pattern this project exists to name and correct:

A company makes a sweeping, specific public commitment.

A local institution with genuine unmet needs accepts the offer.

The community continues to bear environmental and infrastructure concerns associated with the underlying industrial project.

The implementation agreement narrows the original commitment through a cap and an expiration date.

Some benefits are delivered.

Other promised benefits remain outstanding.

Meanwhile, the industrial footprint continues to grow.

None of this requires assuming bad faith by every person involved.

The structural problem is enough.

One party has capital, lawyers, technical expertise, deadlines and the ability to move quickly.

The other has schools that need repairs now, neighborhoods that need investment now, and residents who may have far less institutional leverage.

That is precisely why community benefit cannot be allowed to become a substitute for community power.

text:
MEMPHIS IS THE EXHIBIT

A Case Study in What AI Infrastructure Owes the Communities Hosting It

The Promise

On July 15, 2025, xAI sent Memphis-Shelby County Schools (MSCS) a letter proposing in-kind improvements at four campuses near its Memphis data-center operations: John P. Freeman Optional, Fairley High, Mitchell High, and Westwood High.

The proposed work was extensive. It included plumbing, lighting and HVAC systems; windows; chemistry and technology labs; athletic facilities including an outdoor track and indoor basketball court; landscaping; and other building improvements. The letter stated that xAI would “assume all financial responsibility” for the additional repairs described in the proposal. (Tfp Dev)

Source: July 15, 2025 xAI letter to MSCS, as reproduced in reporting and the district’s board materials; see also MSCS-related reporting cited below.

On July 29, 2025, the MSCS board voted 7–2 to approve the arrangement. Board members Keith Williams and Stephanie Love voted against it. Williams raised concerns about the project’s impact on his Whitehaven constituents and questioned whether the school system should participate while residents were opposing the company’s data-center operations. (https://t.co/7gQ8l2EEFv)

The four schools were not chosen at random: they were among the district’s schools with significant building needs. Reporting at the time estimated the repair needs at the four campuses at approximately $61 million over the following decade, while MSCS’s district-wide maintenance needs exceeded $1 billion. (Chalkbeat)

Source: Chalkbeat, July 30, 2025; WMC/Action News 5, July 29–30, 2025. The $61 million figure reflects the scope cited for the four campuses; district-wide needs are reported separately and should not be conflated with that number.

The significance of the offer is therefore straightforward: xAI was offering improvements to schools with substantial existing infrastructure needs in communities immediately adjacent to a rapidly expanding industrial-scale computing operation.

text:
SCWA Announces 2026 Waterfowl Heritage Festival

📷

The South Carolina Waterfowl Association (SCWA) invites outdoor enthusiasts, families and waterfowlers from across the state to attend the 2026 Waterfowl Heritage Festival. The event will take place on Saturday, November 7 at the SCWA Wildlife Education Center in Pinewood, South Carolina.

The Waterfowl Heritage Festival celebrates the traditions, people, and outdoor experiences that have shaped South Carolina's rich waterfowl heritage. The family-friendly event will bring the waterfowl community together for a full day of competition, outdoor recreation, shopping, food, live entertainment, and activities for all ages.

Formerly known as Duckfest, the Waterfowl Heritage Festival begins a new chapter for the longstanding event while continuing its tradition of celebrating South Carolina's outdoor heritage.

Festival activities will include a Duck Call Competition, Sporting Clays Tournament, Waterfowl Gear Market, Kids Zone, live music, vendors, food trucks and more. Whether attendees are experienced waterfowlers, newcomers to the outdoors, or families looking for a fun fall event, the festival will offer opportunities to experience and celebrate the traditions that make South Carolina's outdoor heritage unique.

The festival will also provide an opportunity for attendees to learn more about SCWA and its mission to enhance and perpetuate South Carolina's wildlife heritage through education and habitat conservation.

Admission to the Waterfowl Heritage Festival is free, with parking available for $10.

Additional information about festival activities, competitions, vendors and entertainment will be announced as the event approaches.

Waterfowl Heritage Festival
Date: Saturday, November 7, 2026
Location: SCWA Wildlife Education Center, Pinewood, South Carolina
Admission: Free
Parking: $10
For additional information and updates about the 2026 Waterfowl Heritage Festival, follow the South Carolina Waterfowl Association and Waterfowl Heritage Festival on social media.

text:
Fathom and its 400k MAUs are getting acquired by Superhuman.

The move follows Notion, which acquired Embra - the tech that powers the hugely popular Notion AI Meeting Notes.

Why?

Transcripts are a dead end. I know (but can't prove) that a decent majority of users, never really did anything with these notes. Nobody reads meeting recaps.

A recorded call only has value if the context immediately triggers work where people actually work (email, docs, CRM).

Superhuman is buying a great platform and a bunch of users who can now pipe that meeting context straight into their email, calendar or document/storage products.

For example, once a Fathom-recorded sales meeting ends,
1. An offer recap email is drafted in Superhuman.
2. A discovery analysis doc is written in Coda (Superhuman Docs).
3. A sales agent in Go is triggered to read both and advise on how to close the deal.

And all of it is tonally consistent thanks to what Grammarly knows about the company's language - smart!

P.S. I guess it's either Bending Spoons or the Coda/Grammarly/Superhuman rollup 🤣

text:
Aha!! It's the bubble. Always follow the money. 

"A central worry is recursive self-improvement: the prospect that tomorrow’s AI models might start designing and training their own successors, racing ahead before we have the right safety guardrails in place.

Another driving force is the need for breathing room—time for independent experts, scientists, and regulators to thoroughly test and audit AI systems before unleashing them into the world.

There is also a powerful incentive to avoid a race to the bottom, where fierce commercial or geopolitical rivalry might tempt companies to cut corners on safety just to stay ahead of the pack.

Unspoken but significant, economic realities and technical limits are quietly shaping the growing consensus for an AI slowdown.

While headlines spotlight existential safety and alignment, a parallel critique simmers among economists and tech insiders. They suggest that calls for a regulatory or industry-wide pause also offer strategic cover for companies grappling with technical and financial headwinds.

While researchers like Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton warn about genuine safety risks based on alignment theory, the business world is primarily driven by financial realities. 

For many companies, calls to slow down AI development also serve their own interests: they help justify rising hardware budgets, lower the hype and expectations around large language models (LLMs), and protect market share from fast-moving, open-source competitors.

If an AI bubble bursts and triggers a broader market slowdown, it’s not just Wall Street traders or tech investors who suffer the consequences. 

For millions of ordinary people—those who don’t own stocks, work in tech, or follow the markets—the impact can be deeply personal: layoffs, shrinking job opportunities, and tighter household budgets. 

When the wealthy gamble and lose, it’s everyday families, small businesses, and entire neighborhoods that often pay the real price."

Crypto, but on chain especially, is often fuelled by new dynamics that enable speculation and new buyers/flows to push valuations up

In essence you need people to be able to believe for a minute rather than destroying each other on what are largely solved for games. When we've played the game before, the participants know the outcome, the targets are known and rushes for the exit brings valuations/tops down - the euthanasia coaster essentially

Most chains/ecos in crypto suffer from this - you've got highly efficient tooling to smooth out inefficiencies, repeated ideas and a history of the userbase being fucked

RH will have many of the same things, no doubt, but so far it also has new dynamics other chains do not - a global leader in retail trading that can directly onboard users, a large amount of political and social capital that exists outside of crypto, coming to market in conjunction with other onboarding tools like FOMO, access to tech/legal abilities to introduce a new, larger asset class in RWA/stocks on chain in new innovative ways, and what appears to be a good, core group of builders on the chain

I don't think this gets rid of the same issues other chains have had, or makes it immune to them, but the dynamic of what it could be and the market it is open to means imo it offers a lot better opportunity to dream a little bigger than repeating the same games from previous cycles on previous chains

text:
A lot of you ask how I gained over 10,000 followers in under three months. It isn't easy, but it isn't complicated either. 

It comes down to combining skill with decisive action. Skill without decision is slow. Decision without skill gets you nowhere.

Here is what you might not know: I have been on X since 2011. I built audiences and left a footprint across multiple personal accounts in completely different fields, hitting numbers far bigger than what I am doing on Da7em. This isn't new to me.

First, identify your edge. For me, it's critique, evaluation, and breakdown. Once you find your skill, you face a choice: blend in and play it safe, or carve out a distinct identity and make an actual impact. The safe route is easy. The distinct route takes guts. I took the second path without hesitating.

That choice brings loyal followers, but it also brings hate. People will resent you because you are honest, because you are sharp, and because you say what they are terrified to voice. If everyone attacks you, you messed up. But if it is only a vocal few while you keep winning, you are on the right track.

Take labels like "ragebait" or "AI slop." They come from two camps: people with one working brain cell, or cowards who envy your craft.

If you write engaging, magnetic prose they could never pull off, they cope by claiming AI wrote it. They leave hate comments within two minutes on a post that takes fifteen minutes to read. 
That is pure jealousy.

Others are so desperate to please brands and appease their audience that any bold opinion looks like ragebait to them.
Don't let them derail you.

Find what you enjoy, hone your skill, and commit. Don't drown yourself in rigid schedules or overthinking. Accept the bad days with the good, just like hitting the gym or picking up a new craft. You put in the time, stay patient, and eventually hit an inflection point.

Building a community is non-negotiable. You can't take without giving. Give people your time, answer questions, listen, stay humble, and develop your skills. You start with three or four people, then ten, then twenty. The people who support you early will push you to the top. Never turn your back on them when new attention rolls in.

For writing, start walking. Ancient philosophers walked for a reason. My best, most viral posts were written on walks. That is when ideas flow.

Think of your mind as a vessel. If you fill it with trash and scrolling, you get shallow output. Fill it with literature, history, art, and philosophy instead.

You might ask what that has to do with AI or tech. Everything. Deep inputs build the substance you need to captivate people and offer something fresh.

Everyone uses AI now. Most creators look like carbon copies of each other, completely hollow and interchangeable.

Be the rare signal in all that noise.

Protect your health, guard your mind, walk, read, and write. That's the whole playbook.

I have plenty more to share, but I'll save it for next time. If you have questions, reach out.

Hope this gives you some clarity.

What is being described as the first combat encounter between two uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) has been reported in the Black Sea, marking a new stage in the naval drone warfare that has defined much of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

According to open-source naval analyst H.I. Sutton, writing for Naval News, the encounter involved a Ukrainian Sargan-3000 USV equipped with a remotely operated 12.7mm machine gun, reportedly mounted on a Norwegian-made remote weapon station and a Russian "Orcan" one-way attack craft, which appeared to carry no defensive armament.

Footage released by the Ukrainian Navy shows a short-range exchange in calm seas, with the armed drone firing short bursts into the opposing vessel's hull, mast and antennas until it sank stern-first. Russian officials have not publicly commented on the incident, and the footage has not been independently verified.

The episode points to a possible shift in how both sides approach drone warfare at sea. Russia and Ukraine have each used explosive-laden USVs against ports and ships, and both have struggled to intercept incoming craft. Gun-armed drone boats, deployed in numbers, could offer a counter, a scaled-down echo of 20th-century gunboat actions, adapted to conditions in the Black Sea.

The Ohio River is one of North America's most historically important waterways.

Critical route for agricultural exports

text:
A forgotten $75 fee ended with a family losing nearly everything.

In rural Tennessee, Gene Cranick had missed South Fulton’s annual fire-protection subscription for residents outside city limits.

When an emergency reached his home, crews responded—but because the property wasn’t enrolled for that year, they did not extinguish the house.

Gene reportedly offered to pay whatever it cost.

The policy still stood.

Then the situation threatened a neighboring property.

That homeowner had paid the $75 subscription, so crews stepped in to protect it.

The Cranick family lost their home, belongings and four beloved pets.

The aftermath became even more complicated. Gene’s son, Timothy Cranick, later confronted the fire chief and was arrested. He was charged at the time with felony aggravated assault.

All of this came from one forgotten $75 payment.

The policy was clear. The outcome was devastating.

More than a decade later, it remains one of those stories that makes people think hard about where policy ends and compassion begins.

text:
📷Calling Bullshit on James Talarico

Jesus Is Not Your Campaign Surrogate

abstractruth

Sep 14📷 📷📷📷📷

I don’t normally comment on political races, but when I see someone who is as fundamentally full of shit as James Talarico, I believe it is my duty to say something about it. James Talarico is now the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate from Texas, having defeated Jasmine Crockett in the 2026 primary. He has discovered a political instrument more powerful than a Super PAC, more versatile than a focus group, and considerably harder to interview: Jesus Christ. After generations of right-wing Protestant pastors hijacking the message of Jesus and turning him into some kind of political football, you have to hand it to James. After all, he is shameless enough to say, why not me?
📷
Down in the backwater leftist stronghold of Austin, Texas, Talarico is selling progressive politics with a halo. He has shamelessly transformed Jesus into a mouthpiece for leftist progressivism. But that same feeling that we used to get when we watched the PTL Club pervades his aura. I have to hand it to American Protestantism, despite its amazing versatility, it can still make you feel dirty, cheap and used.
Talarico’s maneuver is a simple one for the simple-minded. He selects biblical passages that he can bastardize and put into the service of leftist progressivism, as if it were a direct command from the Lord Jesus Christ to the White House and the U.S. Senate. Jesus becomes a mouthpiece for the massive expansion of government, open borders and illegal immigration, and NGOs. However, the clarity of his stance  rolls into the fog the moment that the fate of an unborn child enters the discussion.
It would be too simple to call him a political whore. But I have to say that hearing him speak makes me nostalgic for Jasmine Crockett. Talarico has shamelessly peddled the God-loves-abortion argument that was vomited out by his professors at the far-left seminary he attended in Austin. Just a quick review of the course catalogue puts the “seminary” in the same political hotbox as any American progressive propaganda center these days. As a survivor of Harvard Divinity School, I can recognize all the usual fluff: Activism and the Old Testament Scriptures, Womanist and Feminist readings of the New Testament, Immigration and the Old Testament, Communication for Ministries of Social Justice. At Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary, there is not even a pretense to read the Bible through anything other than a Marxist, feminist lens. The historical texts never stood a chance.
📷
The faculty includes Cynthia Rigby, who is a constructive theologian, as in “makes shit up.” I studied under a “constructive theologian” named Gordon Kaufman all the way back in 1980, back when “constructing the concept of God” was an off-the-wall idea posited by professors desperately trying to be provocative to obtain tenure. Now it’s mainstream. It’s the same old eggheads treating the Christian tradition as oppressive and patriarchal and all the usual crap, using a version of analysis that posits that everything they believe now is wonderful, and everyone else in the entirety of human history is simply not as smart or as evolved as they are.  It’s aggressively stupid.
One of the other professors over there is a guy named Gregory Cuéllar whose books include Resacralizing the Other at the U.S.–Mexico Border and Empire. His research concerns Global Justice within the framework of border enforcement. What the hell any of this has to do with the actual proclamation of Christ, who was decidedly apolitical and steadfastly refused to get into politics, we’ll never know. But Cuéllar, like his colleague Rigby, seems to like to make stuff up.
📷
What is especially loathsome about these seminaries is that they seem to barely read the printed word and have no real interest in what the gospels actually say. Their efforts have been directed toward “demythologizing” the gospel (Rudolf Bultmann), finding the secular meaning (Paul van Buren), secularizing the message (Harvey Cox, The Secular City), or drawing a picture of God to their liking literally conjured up from thin air (God the Problem, Gordon Kaufman). Then there are the feminist wackos like Mary Daly, the “theologian” who despised all men, would not accept men into her classroom, and would only refer to God as “Goddess.” For any serious scholar that actually wants to study Augustine, Aquinas, Athanasius, Luther or the actual Bible, stay the hell away from a mainstream Protestant seminary. They wouldn’t know a Bible if it fell off the shelf and hit them over the head. They haven’t even lifted their heads out of Das Kapital for the last seventy-five years.
So this helps explain Talarico, who wandered out of this environment into progressive politics which is tame by comparison. Talarico is what we would call a “liberation” theologian, which means that he accepts as true all the presuppositions of Karl Marx and Lenin, and then mixes in a few Bible passages as necessary. We are all supposed to be one big global community with no borders, with a bunch of bureaucrats running everything, splitting everyone’s candy bars into perfectly equal geometric squares so no one person gets more than another, before they are sent back to live in their climate-controlled cube.

📷
The point they miss is that giving to the poor, loving your neighbor and loving your enemy does not mean that a nation cannot police its borders from drug cartels and rapists who traffic children. I might even agree, as I have written before, that we should find a way to welcome law-abiding, hard-working families into the country in a way that does not penalize those who played by the rules.
But, there is nothing in the Bible that exhorts us to ensure that federal agencies lose contact with hundreds of thousands of unaccompanied minors at the border, some of whom end up involved in sex trafficking or worse. Moreover, I must have missed the part about the Bible prohibiting showing a government ID when voting.

All of this would be enough to call Talarico a fraud and a demagogue, but his argument on abortion is even more astounding for its duplicity and lack of shame. Talarico has now engaged in an acrobatic sleight of hand that advocates a “double-consent” on the part of the woman before giving birth. For Talarico, the original sex act is not consent to give birth. How he arrives at this, fuck if anyone knows. Perhaps in Austin they are still figuring out whether the act of coitus has anything to do with conceiving a child. I suppose that’s entirely possible. No, even after having sex, now the woman has to consent to have the child. The only one in the whole deal who never has a choice is the kid whose life is up in the air while his mother is determining whether to conceive the child, or kill him so she won’t have to miss a month or two of yoga.

📷

How does Talarico come to the conclusion that this is “Biblical”? Well, in one of the biggest asshole moves of all time, he decides to pollute the story of the Annunciation of the Virgin—one of Christianity’s most sacred narratives—and turn it into a decision point as to whether or not to have an abortion. Because Mary is informed and delighted that she will bear God’s son, Talarico makes the leap to argue that this reaction demonstrates that she “consented” to have God’s son. Luke 1 does contain Mary’s response—“Let it be with me according to your word”—which Christian traditions frequently understand as assent to a divine blessing.  The narrative does not say Mary was choosing between continuing or terminating an existing pregnancy, and such a reading is ridiculous.  A “divine right to abortion” isn’t even remotely what is offered in the Gospel of Luke. And this interpretation is so extraordinarily half-cocked that I would bet anyone a Starbucks Venti Latte that he heard this kind of idiotic argument from one of his professors over at the seminary.
We could be cruel and say that Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary likely contains no learning, no faith, and no serious Christians. But let’s be charitable and say that it has a roving theological imagination that appears to be uniformly one-directional. Finding a conservative in the place is probably even more difficult than finding a conservative in Austin. Or better yet, they are in the business of trying desperately to translate leftist progressive Marxist politics into the Christian vocabulary. Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary is about as far away from teaching the Christian proclamation of love, life and sacrifice as the white-shoed preachers who proclaim that the promises of God will make you rich. It is a factory that produces Biblically illiterate, historically illiterate arch-leftists who preach a message as alien to Christianity as Mao’s Little Red Book.
📷

I would be remiss if I did not also call out Talarico’s fraudulent claim that he is a champion against billionaire mega-donors and puppet politicians. Despite his claim that it has all been done with $100 donations, there is the little matter of the widely reported $6.2 million his Senate campaign raised in its first twenty days, along with significant outside spending by super PACs supported by wealthy donors. Talarico has accepted donations from the Texas Sands PAC, linked to who else, billionaire arch-abortion advocate and casino owner Miriam Adelson. The Texas Tribune reports that Texas Sands PAC was funded by Adelson; the verified figure is $59,000 from that PAC during Talarico’s 2024 Texas House campaign.

📷
Talarico wants voters to believe that he has rescued Jesus from the Republican Party, but what he really did was recruit Jesus for the Progressive Leftist Democrats, assign him a communications director and limit his personal appearances to approved campaign stops. Talarico directs Jesus to what desks he wants him to overturn in the Senate, and you can bet it won’t be Chuck Schumer’s. He may be the first candidate in history to turn the Annunciation into an abortion brief, but he won’t be the first candidate who has turned the Gospel into campaign literature. That’s been done before.
This guy is nothing new. He’s just a little sneakier than some of the others.

text:
In December 2019, Toney Maguire played a private heads-up match in Dallas against Andy Beal, the Texas banker and longtime ultra-high-stakes player (the subject of Michael Craig’s book The Professor, the Banker, and the Suicide King). Beal lost about $15.6 million in that session. Maguire’s personal share was $7.8 million, the rest involved side bets / other participants. Court documents treat the $7.8 million figure as Maguire’s cut of a staked or syndicated action, which is common at that level.

   Neither man was a casual. Maguire has been a serious private-game player since the early 2000s Hollywood boom and was a fixture in the circle later depicted in Molly’s Game. Beal has spent two decades playing heads-up for huge sums against pros. Beal did not settle promptly. Filings say he also owed side bettors hundreds of thousands and “failed to timely pay.” 

      Into 2021 he offered a settlement for significantly less than the full amount. Maguire refused. Maguire already knew Goldstein from poker circles and hired him in 2020. Goldstein raised the prospect of a lawsuit. Beal then paid the $7.8 million in June 2021. Maguire paid Goldstein a $500,000 fee.

   Goldstein told Maguire to wire the $500,000 not to him or his firm, but to real-estate investor Bob Safai, another poker player to whom Goldstein owed a large gambling debt (reported around $14 million). Maguire testified that three-way, lightly documented transfers are normal in that world. Prosecutors used the payment as part of their picture of Goldstein moving money outside ordinary books. Goldstein was later convicted on most counts and sentenced in July 2026 to six years in prison plus restitution. Maguire was not accused of any crime.

text:
Nobody was laid off when we handed marketing and leasing to AI at our Texas communities. The on-site roles got lighter, not smaller.

At each community the property manager and the leasing assistant did both jobs themselves — listings and ads on one side, Facebook, the phone and the inbox on the other. Neither is what they were hired to do, and more than half the leads were lost.

Now the thinking happens for them. A board stays open on their screens all day: which guests are coming in, who to call next, what to say when the call connects. What used to take their judgment is now an instruction they carry out.

Across 14 communities and 4,000+ units, leads and signed leases are up 40-70% on average versus before launch. At our best community, tours in the first two months rose 186%, and that lift took the property from 86% to 95% occupancy in those same two months. The tours are the cause; the occupancy move is what followed.

The line I hold is: AI thinks, people act. It recalls and tracks more than any of us can. It can't offer warmth. So judging, sorting and scripting go to the AI; meeting the guest, answering the phone, hosting the visit stay with a person.

Neither role was removed. Nobody was cut, no retraining, and hiring is easier now that the job doesn't ask for ad buying or copywriting. Managers are back with residents and on the property itself.

I would like to hear how other operators split this — what do you insist stays with a person?

text:
In many ways, Illinois is a tale of two states: Chicago, and everyone else.

At least, that’s what many people in Southern Illinois -- a region commonly known as “Little Egypt” -- told us.

As an aside, exactly how Southern Illinois got its Egyptian nickname is a matter of debate, and over the years, locals have offered plenty of explanations.

One man we met told us that Chicago mobsters came south, opened casinos, and wanted an exotic-sounding name for the area.

The popular online explanation is that during and after the brutal winter of 1830–31, also known as the “Winter of the Deep Snow,” poor harvests left parts of central and northern Illinois short on grain. Farmers traveled south, where crops had fared better, to buy corn and other supplies. According to the story, some farmers compared the journey to Jacob’s sons traveling to Egypt for grain during a famine in Genesis 42.

Southern Illinois became “Egypt,” and eventually, “Little Egypt.”

🏥 One patient made a hospital emergency department into one of the greatest mysteries in medicine.

In February 1994, Gloria Ramirez was brought to a California hospital for her late-stage cervical cancer. While in the hospital, doctors mentioned an unusual ammonia smell and odd symptoms, and not long afterward, 20 or more staff members showed symptoms like difficulty breathing and dizziness.

The case came to be known as "The Toxic Lady."

Various theories have been offered, such as the occurrence of a rare chemical process in relation to a painkiller and the possibility that at least some of the symptoms may have had a mass psychogenic component. Her family disagreed with those findings, and no theory has emerged as conclusive.

The case remains unsolved more than three decades later, as one of the greatest mysteries of modern medicine.

The Attic, Leeds

Maria Taylor is a singer-songwriter celebrated for her hushed vocals, cinematic atmospheres, and emotionally resonant storytelling — both as a solo artist and as a founding member of Azure Ray. Her forthcoming album, Story’s End, unfolds like a hazy, widescreen narrative, with each song acting as a chapter tracing love, loss, fracture, and the quiet search for solace in the aftermath. Written over several years and shaped by profound personal upheaval, the record finds Taylor expanding the signature elements of her work — bell-like piano, sweeping strings, and intimate lyricism — into something more nuanced, expansive, and ultimately life-affirming. Recorded between her California home studio and ARC Studios in Omaha, Story’s End features collaborations with Mike Mogis, Ben Brodin, Brad Armstrong, Conor Oberst, Nate Walcott, and others. The album gradually arrives at a fragile but powerful sense of transformation and hope. At once journal-like and cinematic, Story’s End offers listeners a space for reflection and consolation, paying close attention to the fleeting moments that quietly give life its meaning.

"The English Set The Scottish and Irish Free"

The Scottish and Irish were suppressed. They went to America because America had something Ireland and Scotland, under British rule, did not: a legal and political tradition that treated liberty as a birthright, not a gift from the state.

That tradition did not arrive from nowhere. English settlers carried it across the Atlantic: common law, trial by jury, habeas corpus, property rights, limits on the Crown, and the idea that government exists to secure rights rather than invent them. 

Those ideas were the product of centuries of English resistance to arbitrary power, kings who overreached, parliaments that claimed too much, courts that were bent, taxes imposed without consent, and liberties slowly worn down by central authority.

America was not founded by people who hated England. It was founded by people who believed they were being denied the rights of Englishmen and offered those rights to all.

Speaking to reporters in Ireland alongside Taoiseach Micheál Martin, U.S. President Donald Trump predicted that his administration could reach a trade deal with Canada "fairly soon"—even while doubling down on claims that the U.S. has been "ripped off for 50 years" and jarringly grouping Canada in the same breath as Iran as reported by CTV News. The remarks—made after Trump was asked whether he plans to formally withdraw from the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA)—swing between classic dealmaker optimism and aggressive grievance, targeting Canadian dairy tariffs of "400 per cent" while Canadian trade strategists and political veterans warn that Ottawa cannot return to the table on Washington's one-sided terms. It’s "The 'Fairly Soon' Negotiation Tease & Dominance Framing" vs. "The Sovereignty Defense & Anti-Capitulation Resolve Matrix"!

THE SYSTEMATIC BREAKDOWN
THE "FAIRLY SOON" PREDICTION & 50-YEAR GRIEVANCE:
Taking questions alongside Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, Trump was asked directly whether he is considering withdrawing from CUSMA:
"We're going to have a great relationship with Mexico. We actually have a good one with Canada, but the United States has been ripped off for 50 years by Canada... We don't need their product, and they need our product. They do all of their business almost with us and we do very little with them."
Despite the rhetoric, he predicted an agreement could materialize "fairly soon".

THE JARRING "CANADA AND IRAN" COMPARISON:
In a comparison that ignited immediate political blowback across Canada, Trump linked prospective negotiations with Ottawa to the monthslong military standoff in the Middle East:
"Canada wants to make a deal very badly... Canada wants to make a deal, and Iran wants to make a deal. And at the right time both of those things could happen. I hope Canada appreciates being in the same sentence with Iran."
Canadian Reaction: Scott Reid, former communications director to Liberal Prime Minister Paul Martin, noted on CTV News that placing Canada alongside a wartime adversary "really speaks to the destructive nature of Donald Trump's foreign policy... We are now treated expressly as an enemy"—adding that the rhetoric will only "stiffen the spine" of Canadians resisting U.S. pressure.

TARGETING "400 PER CENT" DAIRY TARIFFS:
Trump took aim once again at Canada's agricultural supply management system:
"They were charging our farmers 400 per cent tariffs."
Former Canadian cabinet minister Ralph Goodale, an adviser on Prime Minister Mark Carney's Canada-U.S. advisory council, called Trump's characterization "factually wrong" and "part of the PR game," while reiterating that the previous U.S. proposal walked away from in August was "one-sided" and "fundamentally uneconomic".

CANADIAN NEGOTIATORS' REALISTIC THRESHOLD:
Policy and trade strategist Diamond Isinger (former adviser during NAFTA/CUSMA renegotiations) cautioned that resuming talks cannot mean capitulation:
"If they (the U.S.) simply would like to resume talks at the same starting point things were severed, those were not realistic expectations for Canada to agree to... Canadians wouldn't accept the status quo of what was on the table weeks ago."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford strongly backed Carney's initial walkaway, declaring that the U.S. offer would have "destroyed our economy from top to bottom".

THE CLASH OF TIMELINES:
While Trump dangles a deal "fairly soon," the economic reality on the ground continues to harden:
Canada's ~$28 billion in reciprocal counter-tariffs on 700+ U.S. items remain fully active.
U.S. executive import bans on Canadian beer, wine, liquor, dairy whey, and motorcycles take effect September 29.
New 50% tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, and furniture roll out September 15.

THE DIPLOMATIC STRATEGY & TRADE JURISPRUDENCE VERDICT
"Donald Trump’s prediction of an imminent deal with Canada represents the classic 'maximum pressure followed by sudden optimism' negotiation cycle. However, by publicly pairing Ottawa with Tehran and reiterating asymmetric grievances over trade deficits and dairy tariffs, the White House is maintaining rhetorical dominance while testing whether Ottawa's united front will splinter. Given Canadian domestic political unity and the activation of multi-billion-dollar counter-tariffs, any genuine off-ramp will require substantive American concessions rather than a mere return to the rejected August terms."— International Trade Negotiations, Bilateral Diplomacy & CUSMA Jurisprudence Assessment.

text:
Look At Rosengård. Then Look At Us: Forty-Two Per Cent Of The Dublin List Is Not Irish

Is This Where We Are Heading?

A clip from Malmö has been doing the rounds. Rosengård Centrum voted 54 per cent Social Democrat and 41 per cent Left Party in Sweden’s 2026 election ,  95 per cent together, Herrgården the same. Commentary said 98 per cent and that no Swede can set foot there. The first figure is a stretch; the second is a slogan.

Police call it a particularly vulnerable area. What is not a slogan is the demography: eight or nine in ten with a foreign background in parts of the estate, native Swedes a remnant, the old Swedish left hoovering the vote. Sweden was the sermon of kindness. Rosengård is compound interest.Put the Swedish tape beside last Saturday’s Dublin tape and the rhyme is not subtle. 

In Malmö: Palestinian flags, flares, “Malmö till Palestina” in a district that barely votes Swedish. In Dublin, during the Trump visit: Palestinian flags down O’Connell Street, then a masked breakaway burning the American flag outside the Dáil, a spectacle unknown on the streets of Ireland, now performed as if it were as Irish as the Angelus. Compare the two videos and the destination is the same. We are heading that way.

That is the future this country’s political class has been walking us toward. Government and opposition alike treated immigration as a moral accessory and a labour-market convenience. Identify the trend and you were tarnished a far-right racist. 

International protection applications peaked at 18,553 in 2024 and were still 13,146 in 2025. Net migration to April 2025 was almost 60,000. Hotel bills ran toward a billion while the housing list lengthened. The parties of the left called restriction racism. The parties in office discovered “capacity” about five years after the capacity was gone. The public was ahead of both.

Then there is the list. Gavin Pepper, independent for Ballymun-Finglas, has published figures from the Dublin housing authority. Of 15,005 households waiting: 8,706 Irish (58 per cent) and 6,299 non-Irish (42 per cent). Somali households alone: 1,320 — 8.8 per cent of the entire list. The non-Irish share of accepted housing offers rose from 21.8 per cent in 2023 to 32.9 per cent in 2025. Approved Housing Bodies now provide almost 63 per cent of those accepted offers. 

Dublin City Council admits it does not monitor allocation outcomes or waiting times by nationality. It cannot say who waits longest, who refuses offers, why AHB nominations fail, or explain the shift. A system handing out thousands of homes is running without the data that would settle the argument.

They will call that noticing “disinformation.” The file says otherwise. Forty-two per cent of the Dublin wait is non-Irish. Nearly a third of the accepted offers in 2025 went the same way. Somali households alone are approaching one in eleven on the list. Homeless priority does the rest: people still in the asylum process are not eligible; people granted status and then assessed as homeless are. That is the scheme.

That is why a family ten years on the ordinary list watches a house go next door and is told the problem is their tone. Ireland has no Rosengård. Not yet. It has Pepper’s Dublin numbers, a flag in flames on Molesworth Street, a council that will not track the outcomes of its own allocations, and a political settlement that treated numbers as unmentionable until the list changed colour.

Demography is not a tap. Once a waiting list, a school and a ballot box change, they do not change back because a minister said cohesion. Someone saw it coming. They were told to shut up. That is how the irreversible usually begins.

The “COVID 2.0 / coordinated op to run out the clock” part is an inference, not something the public record can prove. What can be checked is whether his three predictions are showing up this week.

The predictions that match current events

House Democrats have asked Speaker Mike Johnson to cancel or delay the recess and stay in session until Congress advances AI safeguards, citing “catastrophic risk.” Signers and amplifiers include Reps. Ted Lieu, Lori Trahan, Sam Liccardo, George Whitesides, and Greg Stanton; Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has also said the House should “act urgently.” That is close to Ceren’s third test: treat AI as the reason Congress should not go home.

The pause language is also real. Sen. Bernie Sanders has introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, called for an immediate pause on advanced AI, a permanent ban on superintelligence, and a Trump–Xi treaty to freeze development. Other Democrats have backed data-center moratoriums or “pause until rules exist” language. That matches the first two predictions on safety rhetoric and an opening “pause.”

The media–expert–politician loop is visible too. Warnings from former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon and related incident reporting were quickly cited by Democrats and covered as an emergency. Industry figures (Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, Elon Musk) separately argued for slowing or “pacing the frontier,” which then became source material for the congressional pause push.

What does not cleanly fit the “op” claim

The coalition is not only Democratic, and the demand is not only “shut it down.” There are bipartisan bills (FRONTIER Act, kill-switch proposals) and some Republicans who also want action. Trump and Johnson are resisting an emergency pause, arguing a rushed U.S. slowdown would help China. That is the opposite of a unified elite consensus.

A pause that gets “extended as long as it is politically useful” cannot be confirmed yet. Ceren said to check at week’s end; as of today the spike is days old. Also, “same small donor ecosystem flipped a switch” is not established by these stories. A party letter plus TV hits is ordinary midterm politics. June reporting that some Democrats were reluctant to cut a deal before November is consistent with electoral timing, not unique proof of a manufactured panic.

Bottom line

The observable pattern supports Ceren on tactics and timing: safety language, pause proposals, and an attempt to keep Congress in session on AI grounds are happening now. It does not by itself prove the stronger claim that the campaign is a fabricated operation whose real purpose is to paralyze Republican governance. Genuine risk concern, industry self-interest, China-race politics, and midterm positioning can produce the same surface pattern. The useful test is the one he offered: whether the pause demand hardens and crowds out other business after this week, or whether it stays one faction’s position in a split Congress.

text:
The U.S. bond market is approaching a level that investors can no longer ignore.

The 10-year Treasury yield has climbed to around 5%, recently touching 4.99%, its highest level in nearly three years. The yield briefly crossed 5% during the 2023 bond selloff, but a sustained move above that level would push markets into territory rarely seen since before the Global Financial Crisis.

On the surface, the difference between 4.9% and 5% looks small. In practice, however, 5% matters because Treasury yields sit at the foundation of the global financial system. They influence mortgage rates, corporate borrowing costs, private credit, commercial real estate financing and, perhaps most importantly for equity investors, the discount rate used to value future corporate earnings.

There is nothing magical about exactly 5%. But the closer yields move toward that level — and the longer they remain there — the harder it becomes for investors to justify paying very high prices for risky assets.

The bigger concern is that this rise in yields is not being driven by one temporary factor. Several forces are pushing in the same direction at the same time.

The first is fiscal pressure. The U.S. federal budget deficit reached roughly $2 trillion during the first 11 months of fiscal 2026. That means the Treasury must continue issuing enormous amounts of debt into a market that is already being asked to absorb historically heavy supply.

Large deficits do not automatically mean bond yields must rise. But when government borrowing remains elevated while inflation is still uncomfortable and investors demand greater compensation for holding long-duration debt, the clearing price of that debt can become increasingly expensive.

In simple terms, Washington needs buyers.

And those buyers are asking for higher yields.

The second pressure comes from inflation. Oil has surged back above $100 a barrel as geopolitical tensions and disruptions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies. Brent crude recently traded above $107, while WTI moved above $100. Energy prices can feed directly into transportation, manufacturing and consumer costs, making the Fed's job considerably more difficult.

This is particularly uncomfortable because inflation was already proving sticky before the latest energy shock. Markets had spent much of the previous period assuming that inflation would continue moving gradually toward the Federal Reserve's 2% target. That assumption is now being questioned.

A renewed energy shock changes the equation.

If companies face higher fuel, electricity, transport and input costs, some of those costs eventually reach consumers. Workers may then demand higher wages to compensate for lost purchasing power, while businesses raise prices to protect margins. If that process continues for long enough, what initially looks like an isolated oil shock can begin feeding into broader inflation expectations.

That is the scenario bond investors are increasingly worried about.

And there is now another major borrower competing for global capital: the AI boom.

Artificial intelligence is often discussed as a technology story, but it is increasingly becoming a financing story as well. Building the infrastructure required for AI means spending enormous amounts of money on data centers, semiconductors, networking equipment, electricity generation, cooling systems and transmission infrastructure.

That capital has to come from somewhere.

Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle issued roughly $194 billion of bonds in 2026 through early July, already far above their combined issuance for all of 2025. Goldman Sachs has estimated that issuance from the major hyperscalers could reach around $250 billion this year and $400 billion in 2027.

Morgan Stanley has separately estimated that global AI-related debt issuance could approach $570 billion in 2026, while the largest hyperscalers are expected to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on AI infrastructure.

This does not mean AI borrowing directly causes Treasury yields to rise one-for-one. But it does mean governments and corporations are increasingly competing for the same pool of global savings.

The U.S. government needs capital.

Technology companies need capital.

Data-center developers need capital.

Energy infrastructure needs capital.

And investors are no longer willing to provide that capital at near-zero interest rates.

This may be one of the most important structural changes happening in financial markets.

For much of the period after the Global Financial Crisis, the defining problem was too much money chasing too few attractive bonds. Central banks were buying government debt, interest rates were extremely low, and investors were pushed further out on the risk curve in search of returns.

Today, the situation increasingly looks reversed.

There is an enormous amount of debt and an enormous demand for capital, while central banks are much less willing to suppress yields because inflation has returned as a genuine constraint.

That changes the price of money.

And when the price of money changes, almost every asset has to be repriced eventually.

This is where the 5% Treasury threshold becomes particularly important for stocks.

Imagine an investor deciding between a Treasury bond yielding around 5% and an equity market trading at historically elevated valuation multiples. The Treasury offers a contractual return with minimal credit risk. Stocks offer potentially higher returns, but investors must accept earnings uncertainty, economic risk and much greater volatility.

When Treasury yields were 1% or 2%, investors had little choice. They were effectively pushed into equities.

At 5%, they have an alternative.

That does not mean investors suddenly sell every stock and buy bonds. But the hurdle rate becomes much higher. A company trading at 30 or 40 times earnings has to offer sufficiently strong future growth to justify taking equity risk when a government bond already provides a meaningful return.

The higher yields go, the more difficult that calculation becomes.

This helps explain why equity investors are watching the bond market so closely. In Bloomberg's latest Markets Pulse survey of 122 market participants, roughly 30% said a 10-year Treasury yield between 5% and 5.25% could be enough to trigger a 10% stock-market correction. Another 22% placed the danger zone between 5.25% and 5.5%.

Again, 5% is not a magic number that automatically causes stocks to fall.

What matters is what pushes yields there — and whether they stay there.

If yields rise because economic growth and corporate earnings are extraordinarily strong, equities may be able to absorb some of the pressure.

But if yields rise because inflation is accelerating, oil prices are surging, Treasury supply is overwhelming demand and the Federal Reserve is forced to tighten monetary policy again, the outcome becomes much more dangerous.

That is because both sides of the equity valuation equation begin working against investors.

The discount rate rises while the economic outlook deteriorates.

That combination is far more damaging than higher yields alone.

There is also a historical warning investors should not ignore: the experience of the 1970s and early 1980s.

One of the biggest mistakes policymakers made during the Great Inflation was believing inflation had been defeated too early.

The Federal Reserve tightened policy in the early 1970s, but later eased as unemployment increased before inflation had been fully contained. Inflation subsequently fell, with the year-over-year rate reaching around 5% by the end of 1976.

It looked like progress.

But inflation came back.

By the end of the decade, another energy shock, persistent price pressures and increasingly entrenched inflation expectations pushed inflation sharply higher again. When Paul Volcker became Fed chairman in 1979, inflation was running at extremely elevated levels, eventually forcing the Fed into one of the most aggressive tightening campaigns in modern history. The federal funds rate ultimately approached 19%, and the U.S. economy went through two recessions before inflation was finally brought under control.

Today's economy is obviously not identical to 1980.

Inflation is far below the double-digit levels seen during that period. The structure of the economy is different, central-bank credibility is stronger, and inflation expectations have so far remained much better anchored.

But history does not need to repeat exactly for the lesson to matter.

The important lesson from the 1970s and early 1980s is that inflation can come in waves.

The first decline can create confidence that the problem has been solved. Financial conditions loosen. Asset prices recover. Consumers and businesses become more comfortable again.

Then another supply shock arrives.

Oil rises.

Demand remains strong.

Wages remain firm.

Inflation stops falling — and begins climbing again.

Suddenly the central bank that markets expected to cut rates has to start raising them instead.

That is why today's combination of strong economic activity, sticky inflation, rising oil prices and Treasury yields approaching 5% deserves attention.

The risk is not necessarily that the United States is about to repeat the 1980s.

The risk is that investors have underestimated the possibility of a **second inflation wave**.

If inflation genuinely continues falling, the current rise in yields may eventually reverse and markets could stabilize.

But if energy prices remain high, fiscal borrowing stays enormous, AI investment continues absorbing huge amounts of capital and inflation begins accelerating again, then 5% may not represent the ceiling for Treasury yields.

It could represent the beginning of another repricing.

And that is where the danger for equities becomes much greater.

For years, investors became accustomed to the idea that every major market disruption would eventually bring lower interest rates, easier monetary policy and central-bank support.

The next cycle may work differently.

If inflation is the problem, the Fed cannot simply rescue asset prices every time financial conditions tighten. In fact, weaker asset prices may become part of the mechanism required to slow demand and bring inflation back under control.

That is why the bond market may now matter more than the stock market itself.

The key number to watch is no longer simply the S&P 500.

It is the 10-year Treasury yield.

At 4%, equities can still argue with bonds.

Around 5%, the competition becomes serious.

And if yields move decisively above 5% because inflation is returning rather than because growth is booming, investors may discover that the biggest market risk is not recession.

It is the return of inflation after everyone thought the battle had already been won.

That was one of the defining lessons of the early 1980s.

And it is a lesson markets should be very careful about forgetting.

text:
Concord’s Christ the King pantry rebuilt last year and stopped handing people a box. Now they walk in and pick their own food.

571 people a month in 2023. 1,371 last month. Almost a quarter of which are children.

A volunteer who’s been there 38 years called it a dignity outfit, not a charity outfit. They built a porch so nobody has to wait outside. Hood sends milk. Knights and Lions fill a truck. The food bank keeps up. Other groups hold clinics in the extra space.

Nobody passed a bill. Rent and heat went up, so people cut groceries, and a church and a pile of volunteers just… handled more of it.

That’s the part the state never quite figures out. Unlike a state program, they also offer solutions on how to budget, and fix your situation. If less people need help, the resources immediately get reallocated to another arm of needed charity, with no red tape.
