September 14, 1913: Ben Hill Will Go On Fulton Bench As Fourth Judge 

Reading Time: 24 minutes, [4111 words]

The Atlanta Constitution, Sunday, 14th September 1913.

PAGE 1, COLUMN 1

Roan Takes the Court of Appeals Vacancy; Reid, Stone

Mountain; George Napier, Solicitorship.

FOUR CHANGES MADE TO FILL ONE OFFICE

Appointments Effective October 6 Judge Roan Will Probably Hear Motion in Frank Case.

The fourth judge of the Fulton county superior court is Benjamin H. Hill, chief judge of the court of appeals.

L. S. Roan, judge of the Stone Mountain circuit, will take Judge Hill's place as a member of the court of appeals.

Charles S. Reid, solicitor general of the Stone Mountain circuit, has been elevated to the bench to succeed Judge Roan.

George M. Napier, of the firm of Napier, Wright & Cox, succeeds Mr. Reid as solicitor general of the Stone Mountain circuit.

All these appointments announced by Governor Slaton Saturday are to go into effect on Monday, October 6, the day of the opening of the October term of the court of appeals, or as soon thereafter as is predictable, in order to allow Judge Hill to wind up his business as a member of that court.

Four Appointments Instead of One.

It will be seen that the governor in filling the new judgeship in Fulton county created by the last legislature has made four appointments instead of one. The acceptance by Judge Hill of a position on the superior court bench and the elevation of Judge Roan to the court of appeals made it necessary to find a new man to fill the judgeship of the Stone Mountain circuit. This Governor Slaton' did by elevating to the bench Solicitor General Reid.

It was then necessary to fill Mr. Reid's place, and when this was done by the appointment of Mr. Napier, a lawyer to private life, with offices in Atlanta, the round of appointments ceased.

The public will, of course, be interested in knowing whether or not Judge Roan or another judge is to hear the motion for a new trial in the Frank case, which is set for October 4. In all probability he will. While October 6 has been fixed by the governor as the earliest date when the new appointments are to become effective. It is not unlikely that it will be several days later before they take effect, owing to the business of Judge Hill in the court of appeals. It is the intention of the governor to give him time to wind up that business and to write his opinions on the cases assigned to him.

Ross to Hear Frank Motion.

So that, ever if there should be a continuance of the motion for a new trial in the Frank case, it will in all probability be up to Judge Roan to hear it. Besides, it is understood that if Judge Roan desires time to wind up his motion docket before going on the higher court, the governor will grant him a reasonable length of time in which to do so.

All of the men named are well known to the people of Georgia, and particularly so to the people of Atlanta. Judge L. S. Roan, the new judge of the court of appeals, was born in Henry County in 1849. He was given a common school education and received his legal training in the firm of Peeples & Griffith at Griffin, Ga. He was admitted to the bar in 1871.

Ten Years on Bench.

He located in Fairburn, where he soon built up an active practice. Before his elevation to the bench to succeed Judge John S. Candler as judge of the Stone Mountain circuit, which was on October 29, 1902, he had never held other public office than that of county solicitor and mayor of the town of Fairburn. He has been on the bench nearly eleven years.

Judge Roan's services on the bench since 1902 are too well known to need recalling here. His presiding in noted murder cases in Atlanta, such as the Grace case, the Appelbaum case, and then the Frank case has given him a reputation throughout the south.

New Fulton Judge.

Judge B. H. Hill has been presiding judge of the court of appeals ever since that court was organized, January 1, 1906. He is a son of the famous statesman and United States senator, Benjamin H. Hill, and was born in LaGrange, the home of his distinguished father. At the time of his elevation to the court of appeals, he was a practicing lawyer in Atlanta, being in partnership with his brother, the late Solicitor-General Charles Hill.

That he should consent to take a place on the superior court bench, a lower court than that in which he has presided for more than seven years, is probably to be found in the fact that, while the Fulton County judgeship is really a lower office in rank than the one he now holds, it pays a higher salary. The salary of the Fulton County judgeship is $5,000 per year, while that of the court of appeals is only $4,000. This anomaly of having inferior judges paid higher salaries than the judges of the courts of review has often been called attention to by members of the bar, but the legislature has never seen fit to change it.

Who Charles S. Reid Is.

Charles S. Reid, who becomes judge of the Stone Mountain circuit as successor to Judge Roan, is also well known to the people of the state. He is about 50 years old and has practiced law in Fairburn, Ga., ever since he was admitted to the bar. He repre-

Continued on Page Seven

PAGE 37, COLUMN 2

BEN HILL WILL GO

ON FULTON BENCH

Continued from Page One.

APPOINTED TO NEW PLACES

BY GOVERNOR JOHN SLATON

JUDGE L. S. ROAN,

Appointed on court of appeals.

GEORGE M. NAPIER,

Solicitor Stone Mountain circuit.

sented Campbell County in the legislature for a number of terms, though all of them were not consecutive. In the general assembly of 1909-10 he was chosen chairman of the important committee of ways and means of the house. It was during his chairmanship that the general tax act was made a permanent statue instead of being enacted every two years as it had been up to that time.

C. S. REID,

Judge Stone Mountain circuit.

New Fulton County Judge

JUDGE BENJAMIN H. HILL.

Shortly after the expiration of his last term in the legislature, he was appointed by Governor Brown as solicitor general of the Stone Mountain circuit, to succeed William Schley Howard, who had been elected to represent the fifth district in congress. Subsequently, he was elected solicitor by the people and has remained in that office ever since.

Napier an Eminent Mason.

As grand master of the Masonic fraternity of Georgia for several terms. Georgia M. Napier, the new solicitor general of the Stone Mountain circuit, is probably as well known to the people of the state as any of the others. He was born in Walker County and began the practice of law at Monroe, Ga., where he practiced for a number of years. Later he moved to Decatur and opened a law office in Atlanta, becoming head of the firm of Napier, Wright & Cox. He also served for a time as judge advocate of the military forces of the state.

It is not unlikely that Judge R. B. Russell, who will now be senior member of the court of appeals, will be elected presiding judge by the court to succeed Judge Hill.

PAGE 19, COLUMN 3

Plennie Minor Entertains Friends at Barbecue

Photo by Francis E. Price, Staff Photographer.

Front row, reading left to right: Jurors in Frank case: O. L. Wisby, M. Johenning, M. S. Woodward, W. M. Jeffries and F. V. L. Smith. Back row: Deputy Plennie Minor, and Jurors T. B. Higdon, Fred E. Winburn, C. J. Bosshardt and J. T. Osborn.

Dignity and decorum of the courtroom relaxed and scattered on the wind Saturday when Deputy Sheriff, Plennie Miner, entertained scores of his friends among the courthouse office, lawyers and newspapers men at a barbecue and fish fry and, lest it be forgotten, "And So Forth," at Germania pars.

Judge L. S. Roan was there, but he was not the man with the austere countenance, relieved only by the kindly eye, whom court spectators see. He was not the man on the bench, but the man among his friends, and in his quiet way he was as congenial as the most effusive and hearty as any who attended.

The occasion proved a love-feast which will not soon be forgotten by some sixty or one hundred who were fortunate enough to attend, and good-fellowship abounded. All else was left behind.

Roan Praises Host.

To tell of the barbecue and fried fish and drinkables that Plennie (for his other name has long ceased to be used) provided would be cruelty to those who did not attend. Judge Roan, in a brief speech, said that Plennie was the best deputy sheriff he had ever seen in his years of experience, and the same might be said of the barbecue Plennie provided for his friends. Of the fried fish, well there's hardly use to waste words in telling about the detectable eating they furnished. Anyone who has not tasted a fresh-caught fish, friend by Deputy Lon Burdette over an open fire, has missed something that not even the classiest restaurant in Atlanta could provide.

Eating was not the entire order of the day, and neither was speaking, for the occasion was, to use a slang expression, "long on eats and short on talk." When a crowd of men who know and like each other get together there is much talking, but all of it is not done from the stump, and that was the condition of Plennie's barbecue.

Congenial groups, ever changing, gathered here and there, and jokes and stories passed round while the crowd was waiting for the feast to be spread.

After the crowd had been thoroughly satisfied and begun to return to good

Photo by Francis E. Price, Staff Photographer.

Judge L. S. Roan, seated. Left to right, standing: Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey, E. A. Stephens, his assistant, and Deputy Sheriff Plennie Minor, host at the barbecue, serving them.

cigars and quiet reflections, someone called on Judge Roan for a speech. Standing on a little bridge in the edge of the wood and with a small creek rippling beneath his feet, the judge told of his pleasure in being there and also expressed his own personal opinion of Plennie as deputy sheriff, as host and as friend. Somebody shouted for three cheers for Plennie as he finished, and they came with a roar.

Not Opposing Mangum.

After the first speech, Plennie responded to the calls for him, and jumping to a rock in the middle of the creek, spoke his appreciation of his friend's many kind words.

"Gentlemen, I want to set one thing straight," he said before he closed, "and that is the report that I'm going to run for sheriff against Dad' Mangum. My friends haven't believed that, for they know I wouldn't try to defeat the man who placed me in my position and the man whom we all love. I am not going to run against Dad.'"

Solicitor Hugh Dorsey followed with appropriate words, and then the crowd called for Deputy J. W. Poindexter, the preacher-member of the sheriff's office.

In truly characteristic style he told things on Plennie that kept the merrymakers laughing from start to finish. He ended by saying that as it was against the law to sell beer to a minor, that Plennie had given the barbecue, so he could get a glass for himself.

PAGE 28, COUMN 1

JUST UNDERTAKERS:

The why and the wherefore of them

How a man becomes one---Some

Grewsome experiences of beginners

BY NED McINTOSH.

"I wonder why he went into the undertaking business?"

Of course, you have asked yourself that questions time and time again. To be sure, somebody has got to be an undertaker, but just why would any man pick out that particular vocation as a life's work?"

There is not an undertaker in the city of Atlanta but will tell you that he likes his work. Whether in his boyhood dreams his fondest ambition was to sit up with corpses and drive a hearse is another question. That, at least, is the case of one.

Let us consider for a moment the jolly undertaker as he goes merrily about his business, and see just what lured him into the funeral directing game.

LET'S FIND OUT

THE REASON WHY.

There are six establishments in Atlanta, and surely from some of these we should find somewhere a reason.

Incidentally, all of them report that business is very dull just now.

I was down playing checkers with Pat Bloomfield, at his place on South Pryor street, the other day while he was waiting on somebody to die, and I asked him:

"How did you happen to go into the undertaking business?"

He jumped two men and went into kingdom before he answered.

"Well," he said, "that was a good while ago. "I just sort of loafed into the job, I guess."

"You see, I had a government job, and naturally had plenty of loafing time. I did most of my loafing around at Hilburn & Bowden's undertaking place, down there in the same building where Harry Poole used to be before he moved down here next to me.

WHEN HE

ENTERED BUSINESS.

"Sometimes, when I had nothing else in particular to do, I would answer calls with them, so I got pretty used to handling dead people before I ever really went into the business."

"I think the time I really got broken in was one night they had a call out to Fort McPherson. That was during the Spanish-American war, when the fort was used as a general hospital, and a good many of the wounded died there. The call came about midnight, and I was already undressed, so I wasn't much stuck on going along. But I agreed to go. I don't think I was waked good when we got out to the fort. Soon after our arrival, though, I woke fast enough."

"There was a little house out there based as a morgue. Bowden was busy about something, and I stepped in the morgue to see what sort of a job we had to do. I couldn't find a light switch, so I struck a match. I saw the body lying in front of me, and was about to leave, when I glanced around and saw another, and another and another. Well, sir, when I had looked around a minute I found I was standing in the midst of an assemblage of seven corpses. I tried to

"I HAD JUST STARTED TO MOVE HIM WHEN HE LOOKED AT ME!"

tough it out, but my feet got the best of me and I came out of there good and quick. I met Mr. Bowden at the door, and he laughed at me."

"That's about the last time I ever felt anything out of the ordinary about a dead person, though."

"Soon after that I got to thinking that I might stick around at my government job the rest of my life without getting along any better, and besides a political job is a little uncertain, so I made up my mind to go into business for myself. Well, the undertaking business was about all I knew anything about."

MOST PEOPLE NOT

AFRAID OF CORPSES.

"I want to tell you, though, that this talk about most people being afraid of a corpse is all tommyrot. I never realized that so much as I did while the body of Mary Phagan was e. I believe that fully 8,000 people walked through the building and looked at that body!"

W. A. Gheesling, who is connected with Mr. Bloomfield, chimed in:

"Well, it's different here. I simply never had a chance. I was raised up in the business and became an undertaker almost before I knew it. I started out as an office boy for Mr. Barcley when I was 9 years old, and I have never been out of the undertaking business since."

Incidentally, Mr. Gheesling has handled many of the most famous cases in Georgia, and was for three years of his career the youngest embalmer in the United States.

"As long as I have been in the business, though, I don't believe that I was ever good scared but one time. That was a number of years ago."

"I got a call to a little street out in the edge of town about midnight on a suicide case. There were no lights on the street and I had considerable difficulty in locating the house."

"I finally found it, though. A poor devil had fought booze about as long as he could and had ended the fight with a bullet in his head."

"He was in a stuffy little room upstairs over a small grocery store. The only light in the room was a candle stuck in a beer bottle."

"The body was lying on an old bed, and was doubled up until the knees almost touched the chin. It was impossible for me to move it in that shape, so I undertook to straighten it out. It had already grown stiff."

THOUGHT MAN

WAS ALIVE.

"With the assistance of an officer who was there, I turned it over on its back and bore down on the knees. I found that the knees straightened out quite readily, but something happened that I had not figured on. The hip joints remained stiff and my pressure on the knees made the body rise up in a sitting posture, so that when I turned around that dead man with his eyes bulging out was sitting up staring me in the face. Believe me, I wanted to run that time!"

In the case of Mr. Brandon, of the Barclay & Brandon company, the veteran undertakers of Atlanta, we find a man who gave up the business of decorating live people for that of decorating dead ones.

"The primary reason, though," says Mr. Brandon, "why I went into the undertaking business was for my health. I was out of bread and meat, which, I am told on good authority, is an extremely unhealthful condition."

"I was working in a jewelry store in Dalton for half the profits. At the end of the year the man for whom I was working owed me some $600 or so and was unable to make a settlement. I saw that wouldn't do and I'd have to get another job."

"It so happened that the jewelry establishment was in part of a furniture store, so I went to the proprietor of the furniture store and asked him for work, which he gave me."

ONLY THREE UNDERTAKERS

IN ATLANTA THEN.

"And again it so happened that the stock and trade of the furniture store was in part coffins and the undertaking business. It sort of fell to me to look out for the undertaking end, and in that way I learned the business."

"In 1893, I believe it was, I came to Atlanta and bought out Captain Dave Wiley, of the firm of Wiley & Brandon. There weren't but three undertakers in the town then."

"I remember when I went into business here I bought the finest hearse in town, a black concern it was, with five turns on top of it. The memory of it seems rather quaint now, when I look at that new automobile hearse I bought the other day!"

"Exciting?"

"Oh, yes, at times. I had the experience once of being called upon to embalm a live man. Of course, it would not do to mention names, but one day I had a call to take charge of a body that wasn't as dead as it looked."

"When I arrived at the house I was shown into the room where the body lay. To all appearances the man was dead, and I did not pay any particular attention to him. I had just started to move him when he opened his eyes. It was rather weird and funny, too, of course, but his relatives were so overjoyed to find him still alive that no one thought of that side of it at the time."

"They have told the tale on me that he laughed at me when he come to, but he didn't."

FROM CURING SICK

TO BURYING DEAD.

S. R. Greenberg, of Greenberg & Bond, went form the business of curing the sick to burying the dead. That

"MY FEET GOT THE BEST OF ME AND I CAME OUT OF THERE GOOD AND QUICK!"

is not to say, however, that his observation in the former vocation offered him "a word to the wise" so to speak.

Mr. Greenberg, reclining at Oriental ease among coffins and fixtures, spoke thusly:

"I was in the drug business in my younger days, but had very good friends connected with C. H. Swift in the undertaking business. Often they had tried to prevail upon me to become associated with them, but I was more or less shy upon the subject. In 1908, though, I finally agreed to go."

"After becoming accustomed to it, I find that I like the work. It does not keep a man tied down to his office and gives him plenty of resting time."

BUSINESS

"LOOKS PRETTY SOFT."

Harry G. Poole, who has just moved into his new building on South Pryor, makes no bones about the fact that he went into the undertaking business, because it "looked pretty soft." Neither does Mr. Poole hesitate to say that it "was not so soft as it looked."

"It was this way," says he. "I was raised out here in the woods about six miles from Atlanta and used to come to town every once and awhile with a load of cotton and wood, and nearly every time I came, I would see a funeral procession going along. I was an unsophisticated country boy and it looked to me like the undertaker didn't have a thing in the world to do but ride to the cemetery and back on top a fine-looking hearse."

"I used to picture myself riding on top that hearse and figure what a fine time an undertaker must have."

"About the next thing I did was to pack up my duds and come to Atlanta to get a job as an undertaker."

"Needless to say, I had my eyes opened considerably. But at that, I have learned to like the work. I have made hundreds of friends in Atlanta and good friends, too, and it is a source of considerable gratification to me to know that I have been able to be of service to them."

ROY DONEHOO

OFFERS SOLUTION.

A solution to the question of the unanimous love of undertakers for their apparently grewsome work may be found in the following from Roy Donehoo:

"The horror with which the public at large usually looks upon the business of undertaking and funeral directing was never a part of my makeup on the contrary, the work always possessed a kind of fascination for me; not that I was morbidly fond of standing in the presence of death, but because I was able to see those phases of the work which relieved it of its grewsome elements, and then rendered it a work of service and mercy to those who were bereaved and sorrowing."

"Just how I happened to go into the business is difficult to say; but I recall that when a mere child, possibly not more than 7 years old, occasion required the presence of an undertaker in my own home. The whole atmosphere around the place before his coming was that of awe and expectancy. When he came, he was ushered immediately into the death

"HE WAS SITTING UP STARING ME IN THE FACE!"

chamber, and the room was cleared of all except one or two, who were invited to assist in the preparation of the remains. I was one of those who were excluded, and the air of mystery about the whole situation the awe which seemed to envelope the undertaker attracted and fascinated me.

"Then, too, when a mere child, the beauty of a hearse, which I still consider one of the masterpieces of art, appealed to me; and I used to gaze upon the man who sat beside the driver with admiration and longing and wonder if I could ever occupy so enviable a position."

"Later, when I grew into maturity, one of the most fascinating tasks of which I could conceive was that of beautifying a corpse, and putting into condition so that those who had loved the person in life might think of him, not as one cold and deathlike, but as one who, though dead, still retained a beloved, life-like appearance."

"And the possibility, too, of handling a situation in such a manner as to less the grief of those who were left, made the work appeal to me as very beautiful."

"For these reasons, when only 18 years old, I left a position which was paying me a much better salary, to become an apprentice in an undertaking office; and since that time my choice has been fixed."

text:
My son told me he's moving across the country, and I said, "That's great," even though I wanted to ask him not to.

He got a job offer. Good one. Better pay, better title, better everything.

He called to tell me, excited.

I said, "That's great, buddy. I'm proud of you."

And I meant it.

But after I hung up, I just sat there.

My wife asked what was wrong.

"He's moving to Oregon."

She nodded. "I know."

"That's really far."

"I know."

We didn't talk about it much after that.

A few weeks later, he came over to tell us the details. When he's leaving, where he'll live, all of it.

I smiled. Asked questions. Acted supportive.

Because that's what you do.

You don't tell your kid not to take the better job because you'll miss them.

You don't make it about you.

But when he left, my wife and I sat on the couch, and she said, "This is hard."

I nodded.

He moved last month. Calls every week. Sends pictures.

It's fine. It's good, even.

But the house feels a little quieter.

And I'm still getting used to that.

text:
And another.

NOMOTO MEDIA

How does the battle of AI dominance end? And will it?
Originally published 2025-02-12

ARTICLE ARCHIVE ← PREVIOUS NEXT →DOWNLOAD THIS TEXT ↓
Some see a stable equilibrium, where multiple powers each have strong AI capabilities but keep them in check through treaties or mutual deterrence, a lot like nuclear-era standoffs. Others foresee a lopsided world, where a single giant AI system sets the rules and leaves everyone else scrambling to adapt. Of course there’s also the chance that AI itself evolves in ways that outpace any control or oversight.
How we get there depends on choices made now. Government leaders can push for AI arms control agreements such as formal pacts or at least shared norms to prevent runaway weaponization. Tech companies could set up self-governance structures, pledging not to deploy certain systems without safety checks. Citizens might demand transparency, ensuring AI usage respects human rights. Or we might see a more chaotic scenario, with each player racing to deploy AI faster than the other, ignoring caution until something breaks. Maybe an unforeseen meltdown, a rogue deployment, or a massive social backlash when an AI-powered policy goes awry?

The major powers knows that unchecked AI rivalry risks mutual harm leading to a future when they are restricting or limiting certain categories of AI weapons or establishing oversight bodies. These bodies might look like early arms-control treaties of the Cold War, not perfect ,but better than total free-for-all. At the same time big tech will likely work under tighter government scrutiny. The West invests in robust public-private collaborations, reining in corporate secrecy while funneling money into fundamental AI research. China might do the same, though behind more opaque walls. The rest of the world aligns with whichever side offers reliable partnerships or invests in local data infrastructure.

Over time, we may find balance. AI becomes woven into daily life, factories, transport, communication, but the largest leaps will be more controlled. Some minimum standards of privacy or accountability might take root, especially in places where the public can pressure leaders. Its just the world we live in, espionage never stops, and smaller nations sometimes become pawns but at least the major players avoid total meltdown, and AI’s benefits, faster medical breakthroughs, improved logistics, advanced climate modeling promise to improve our lives.

Another scenario is no meaningful cooperation and repeated crises. One state fields advanced AI drones that strike with minimal human input, prompting others to follow suit. A glitch or misread data triggers conflict. Meanwhile, governments push AI-driven domestic surveillance to clamp down on dissent possibly fueling unrest. Entire industries change from automation, with no safety net to help displaced workers. Misinformation flourishes as generative models flood every channel. Trust in shared facts collapses completely, fracturing societies. Eventually, as by necessity a major incident will occur, a near-war triggered by AI miscalculations shocks us into last-minute treaties. But by then, public faith in institutions has eroded, and large areas of the global economy revolve around AI systems beyond easy governance. That future is bleak, a world of patchwork controls, skyrocketing inequalities, and fearful populations. Some pockets might thrive, but widespread anxiety festers.

Is there a middle way? Perhaps. We might see a push for “AI alignment” research not just in labs but as part of global policy. Nations could invest in ways to ensure advanced systems remain responsive to human intent and ethical constraints. They could also structure alliances that share certain breakthroughs, reducing the panic that leads to arms races. Such alliances would still compete, no illusions there, but they’d treat AI’s potential for catastrophe as a common threat, much like climate change. The biggest hurdle is political will. Trust is low, and each power suspects the other of covert infiltration and surveillance. Yet if leaders grasp that an uncontrolled AI race threatens everyone, they may accept uncomfortable compromises. We might see a new era of combined oversight, a council that audits advanced AI labs worldwide, staffed by rotating experts. Whether that’s realistic or naive is anyone’s guess. But the alternative may be waiting for disaster to force cooperation and that seems far riskier. So does it end in balanced progress, or fractious strife, or something in between? Much hinges on how fast AI matures and how far states push it before forging guardrails. In that sense, the conclusion isn’t set in stone. It unfolds through daily decisions, big or small, shaping which path becomes reality.

S0 how do we steer towards the less destructive outcomes? Some argue for immediate regulation, a framework that forces companies and governments to abide by shared standards. As in how nuclear technology was, in principle, open for any nation that could enrich uranium or design a reactor. Over time the global community devised treaties, monitoring agencies, and stiff penalties for violations. AI might need something like that to ensure advanced models aren’t misused. Mandatory fail-safes in critical systems, and open registers that track large-scale AI deployments will become reality

But AI isn’t like uranium, algorithms are intangible, easily duplicated, and modified. Even if a leading country imposes tough rules, others might not follow. That sparks a “why should we handicap ourselves?” debate. Second, regulation can chill innovation. Startups can’t bear the costs of compliance if the rules are too strict. The best minds might move to jurisdictions with fewer constraints, draining talent from the places that attempt to do AI “right.”

Another path to stability might come from a fundamental shift in public attitudes. If societies become more aware of how AI can manipulate or surveil them, they might demand transparency at every level. If knowledge is widespread that advanced AI propaganda can affect public opinion, entire populations could become more skeptical of content that seems too tailored or divisive, blunting the effect of automated propaganda. This occurred in Social Media.

That cultural shift might reduce the risk of AI-fueled chaos, but it won’t solve the arms race problem by itself. Governments could still chase advanced AI for strategic advantage. The best outcome might be a world where most citizens understand AI’s power and pitfalls, pressuring leaders to handle it responsibly. This moral check could keep ambition in line, somewhat.

AI development may also finally hit a plateau. In that scenario, the rapid leaps slow down, and progress becomes more incremental. If so, we’d see near-equal capabilities among major nations. Each can do advanced data analysis or field capable drones, but no one drastically outstrips the rest. That staves off one-sided dominance. The arms race evolves into a stalemate, with each side responding to the others’ breakthroughs in a tit-for-tat. It’s not exactly peaceful, but less prone to total upheaval than a single runaway lead.

Many doubt a true plateau is close though, especially with the influx of computing power and ongoing algorithmic innovations. They warn that progress might accelerate unpredictably, especially if a single breakthrough multiplies learning speed. That’s the nightmare scenario: one lab or one nation cracks an approach that unleashes a sudden AI dominance, overshadowing all competition.

In terms of public debate, we face a communication gap. AI experts talk about alignment challenges, existential risks, or moral hazards. Policymakers talk about job losses, trade advantages, or national security. The average citizen has almost no idea of what is happening. Bridging that gap is crucial. If the public sees AI as mere gadgetry, they won’t push for meaningful policy. If they see it as having capacity for unstoppable doom, they might slow down progress. We need a nuanced conversation, acknowledging all of AI’s benefits, medical diagnostics, climate science, improved education, aging, robotics and its threats.

Some nonprofits already monitor AI usage, releasing reports on potential abuses or biases. Others gather academic research to present in plain language for lawmakers. An engaged public that demands accountability can force even large tech companies or powerful governments to consider the social cost of reckless AI deployment. This doesn’t guarantee a peaceful path, but it can slow the race for a moment of reflection.

Ultimately, “the end of AI progress” might not be a single event. It could be an extended era of partial agreements, partial conflicts, and partial solutions. We might see bursts of AI-driven prosperity and waves of AI-driven disruption. Over decades, new norms could settle in, just as the world adjusted to space travel, and the internet. Each of those technologies brought its own set of hopes and terrors. AI, being more intangible and adaptable, will somehow weave itself into every life, from personal relationships to global finance.

AI has the power to transform the human plight and make life better for all us. The question is will we let it?

text:
Fathom and its 400k MAUs are getting acquired by Superhuman.

The move follows Notion, which acquired Embra - the tech that powers the hugely popular Notion AI Meeting Notes.

Why?

Transcripts are a dead end. I know (but can't prove) that a decent majority of users, never really did anything with these notes. Nobody reads meeting recaps.

A recorded call only has value if the context immediately triggers work where people actually work (email, docs, CRM).

So Superhuman is buying a great platform and a bunch of users who can now pipe that meeting context straight into their email, calendar or document/storage products.

For example, once a Fathom-recorded sales meeting ends,
1. An offer recap email is drafted in Superhuman.
2. A discovery analysis doc is written in Coda (Superhuman Docs).
3. A sales agent in Go is triggered to read both and advise on how to close the deal.

And all of it is tonally consistent thanks to what Grammarly knows about the company's language - smart!

P.S. I guess it's either Bending Spoons or the Coda/Grammarly/Superhuman rollup 🤣

text:
The first message is where 95% of people quit.

Not the build. The build is fifteen minutes and a free trial.

The message. The one you have to send to a stranger who owns a business.

So here's every version of it I'd actually send, and the one thing that makes all of them work.

FIRST — THE MESSAGE EVERYBODY SENDS

"Hi! I help local businesses use AI to automate their customer service and never miss a lead again. Would you be open to a quick 15-minute call this week?"

That gets ignored 100 times out of 100, and it deserves to.

Read it again and count what it asks for versus what it gives.

It asks for 15 minutes of a working man's day and gives him nothing but a sentence he's read forty times this year.

→ No proof you've done anything

→ No evidence you know his business exists

→ No reason today is different from yesterday

→ And "AI" in the first line, which to him reads as "expensive, complicated, probably a scam"

THE ONE THING THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING

You build the thing first. Before you talk to him. For free. Without asking.

Fifteen minutes, his real website, his real prices, his real service area. It answers the phone in his business's name.

Now you're not a stranger with an offer.

You're a stranger holding something that already has his name on it.

That's the whole trick. There isn't a second one.

THE MESSAGE, FOUR WAYS

The DM / text:

"Hi [name] — I rang you Tuesday around 7pm about a [job type] and nobody picked up, so I assume you were out on a job. I build phone systems for [trade] companies and I've already set one up using your website — it answers in your business's name, knows your prices and books straight into a calendar. Not selling you anything today. Can I show you four minutes of it?"

The walk-in (yes, walk in — nobody does this any more, which is exactly why it works):

"Is [owner] around? I'm not selling anything, I just built something using your business's info and I'd rather show him four minutes of it than email him about it."

Then show it on your phone. In the shop. Standing up.

The email:

Subject: your phone, Tuesday 7pm

"I called Tuesday evening about a [job]. No answer — no criticism, you were obviously working. I've built a system that would have answered that call, in your business's name, using your own pricing and hours. It took me fifteen minutes and I've already done it. Four minutes of your time to hear it. Reply 'ok' and I'll call you."

The phone call, if you're brave:

"Hi, this isn't a sales call and I'll be 30 seconds. I called you Tuesday at 7 and nobody answered. I've set up a system that would have taken that call and booked the job. It already exists, it already has your business in it. Can I show it to you Thursday?"

WHAT THEY ALL HAVE IN COMMON

→ A specific, dated, verifiable fact about his business (you called, he missed it)

→ Zero AI vocabulary — "phone system," "answers calls," never "agent," never "automation"

→ The work is already done, so there's nothing for him to commit to

→ The ask is four minutes, not a call, not a meeting, not a demo, not a discovery session

→ You explicitly take selling off the table in the first three lines, and you mean it

WHEN HE SAYS NO

Most will. Say this, exactly:

"No problem at all. I'll leave it running for a couple of weeks in case you change your mind — if you want to hear it, just text me."

Then actually leave it running. Then actually text him in two weeks: "still running if you want to hear it."

A quarter of everything I'd expect to close, closes on that second message, from people who ignored the first one entirely.

Nobody follows up. It is the cheapest advantage available to you and it costs one text message.

THE PART THAT'S HARD, HONESTLY

Not the tech. Not the script. You now have the script.

It's sending number twelve after eleven people either ignored you or were short with you.

That's the whole job. Everything else is fifteen minutes and $0 for the first month.

If that part is a dealbreaker, this business isn't for you, and I'd rather say that than sell you a dream.

THE MATH, BRIEFLY

One client at $1,500/month is roughly $18,000 a year.

The platform it all runs on is $97/month, flat, however many clients you have. Free for the first 30 days.

Realistic ranges, not guarantees — it depends entirely on who you approach and how long you keep going.

And it doesn't matter if you're 16 or 70. Nobody doing this was born knowing it — I spent years on dropshipping, print on demand, affiliate marketing and trading before any of it worked. ☀️

The full playbook — the build, the prompts, the seven questions, the pricing, the objections — is free in my bio. No email, no form.

text:
GRAND MARSHAL FRIJOLERO

Ifebi brings the flag.
Mamdani wears the sash.
Trump promises the $5,000.
Vance gets the Greyhound.

In Dallas, JD Vance thought mocking the Mexican flag might win him a few more supporters. But that calculation could backfire.

Anthony Nwanneka Ifebi, a Black man from Grand Prairie, Texas, waved a Mexican flag during the Republican convention. Vance saw him and fired back: “If you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.”

Ifebi, brother: you’re Mexican now.

Three days later, Brooklyn.

Zohran Mamdani, the son of immigrants, an admirer of Claudia Sheinbaum and mayor of a city of 8.5 million people, walked through Sunset Park during the 32nd Mexican Independence Day Parade, Mexican flag in hand and a tricolor sash across his chest:

GRAND MARSHAL.

The first New York City mayor to participate in the parade.

Someone in the crowd shouted:

“Zohran, brother, you’re Mexican now!”

Dallas offered the exit ticket. Brooklyn handed over the sash.

Mamdani recently told El País that democracy doesn’t work if people cannot afford their basic needs.

Childcare. Housing. Transportation. Food.

“Extreme left!” some shout.

Tell someone to leave the country for waving a Mexican flag.

What extreme is that?

Molotov turned the border insult into a classic more than two decades ago.

So here we are, heading into September 16.

Ifebi brings the flag.
Mamdani wears the sash.
Trump promises the $5,000.
Vance gets the Greyhound.

We’ll bring the cake.

Bean cake, naturally.

VIVA MÉXICO, CABRONES!

DON’T CALL ME GRINGO, YOU FUCKIN’ FRIJOLERO.

Inspired by Molotov — Frijolero (2003).

Not Left. Neither Right. Just Rights.

GACETA MIGRANTE
PERIODISMO 3.0™
The editorial decision remains human.

by: Ann Lipsett

SHAREBOSTON (WJW) — A new report is shedding light on the history of the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial.

Clancy has confessed to fatally strangling her three children in 2023. Prosecutors argued that during the murders, she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was overmedicated. The trial ended in a hung jury on Sept. 4.

Holdout in Lindsay Clancy trial said he had reasonable doubt but still wouldn’t acquit, juror saysAccording to NBC10 in Boston, the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder case had a history of domestic violence allegations against him.

That same news outlet in Boston also found that the juror had a pending eviction case against him, stemming from months of not paying rent. 

They also found that the juror had an active restraining order against him when he was serving on the jury.

The juror has not identified himself at this time, as he has not spoken publicly. Right now, the jury list is impounded.

An NBC10 investigative report dug into the juror’s domestic violence history.

In September of 2021, the juror faced a criminal charge for allegedly assaulting his wife.

The police report out of Massachusetts alleges that the juror’s 13-year-old nephew called 911 after claiming he saw his uncle grab his wife by the throat and throw her into a dresser.

Court records report that the couple divorced after the alleged incident. The criminal charge was later dismissed. The wife reportedly didn’t testify in court out of fear she would lose custody of her child.

Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer asks the judge to spare her a second trial for killing her childrenIn 2024, that same teenage nephew, regarding the 2021 incident, obtained a restraining order. 

The order came after the nephew said the juror allegedly pushed him to the ground and kept punching him in the face.

According to NBC 10, that restraining order was still active when the juror was selected to serve on the Clancy trial. 

He listened to evidence from both sides for weeks in the controversial case.  

According to People, Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida has offered the holdout juror asylum in the Sunshine State, although the juror has not been publicly identified.

A follow-up date in the Clancy case is scheduled for Sept. 29.
